sources.title: Amsterdam Wisselbank, 1609
sources.historical_claim: The Amsterdam Wisselbank institutionalized reliable payment settlement and monetary exchange in a multi-currency commercial environment before modern central banking.
sources.verification_status: Primary-source ordinance text located in W. C. Mees’s 1838 documentary reproduction; founding ordinance independently identified by Hans Bontemantel with reference to Noordkerk’s Handvesten; institutional context corroborated by Stadsarchief Amsterdam
sources.bn_title: আমস্টারডাম উইসেলব্যাংক, ১৬০৯

sources.notes: Hans Bontemantel's historical record explicitly identifies the Wisselbank's founding willekeur dated 31 January 1609 and cites its location in Noordkerk's Handvesten, p. 673. Amsterdam City Archives independently confirms the bank was established in 1609. This supports the founding claim; the database should distinguish the cited ordinance from the later descriptive account.

sources.publisher: City of Amsterdam; Amsterdam municipal records

sources.title: Stockholms Banco, 1656

Sveriges Riksbank independently reproduces wording from the oktroj and identifies it as the king's 1656 charter. The original 1656 manuscript/charter scan itself was not located, but the legal text is preserved in a dedicated royal-act compilation rather than only a later narrative history.

sources.title: Rothschild Portuguese Government Loan, 1823

sources.bn_title: রথসচাইল্ডের পর্তুগিজ সরকারি ঋণ, ১৮২৩
sources.bn_historical_claim: নাথান মেয়ার রথসচাইল্ডের লন্ডন ব্যাংক ১৮২৩ সালের £১৫ লক্ষের পর্তুগিজ ৫% সরকারি ঋণ গ্রহণের জন্য আলোচনা করেছিল; ঋণটি ব্রাজিলীয় রাজস্বের ওপর সুরক্ষিত ছিল।
sources.notes: The Rothschild Archive states that Nathan Mayer Rothschild contracted to undertake the Portuguese Government five per cent loan in 1823 and that a letter copybook records his approaches to Baron de Teixeira, Portuguese Minister of Finance, in July 1823. The archive's published transcription is used as the primary passage; the underlying loan contract is identified in the literature as Rothschild Archive RAL 000/401 A and dated Lisbon, 8 September 1823.
sources.primary_passage: The permanent interest of the Portuguese Governments will be best consulted by concluding the loan with ourselves, inasmuch as from the resources & credit we possess it would be more effectually in our power to advance and maintain the price of your securities than any other parties.
sources.passage_locator: Nathan Mayer Rothschild letter copybook, approaches to Baron de Teixeira, Portuguese Minister of Finance, July 1823; published by The Rothschild Archive in its Portugal collection. Related underlying loan contract: Rothschild Archive RAL 000/401 A, dated Lisbon, 8 September 1823.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — exact wording reproduced by The Rothschild Archive; underlying contract reference independently corroborated as RAL 000/401 A.
sources.source_identity: Nathan Mayer Rothschild correspondence concerning the Portuguese Government loan of 1823; The Rothschild Archive; underlying contract RAL 000/401 A.
sources.edition: The Rothschild Archive, Archivist's Choice: 200 years of Rothschild business with Portugal; underlying contract RAL 000/401 A.
sources.what_passage_establishes: The passage establishes Rothschild's contemporary proposal that his house undertake the Portuguese loan and his stated claim that its resources and credit would support the securities.
sources.evidence_limits: The passage does not establish that Rothschild ultimately won the Portuguese issue; contemporary contract evidence shows the loan was ultimately issued by B. A. Goldschmidt. It also does not establish broader Rothschild control of Portuguese finance.
scholarly_references: Marc Flandreau and Juan H. Flores, “Bonds and Brands: Foundations of Sovereign Debt Markets, 1820–1830,” *The Journal of Economic History* 69, no. 3 (2009), discussion and note identifying Rothschild Archive 000/401 A.

sources.title: Greek Loan Guarantee Convention, 1832
sources.historical_claim: The 1832 Convention among Great Britain, France, Russia and Bavaria provided for a Greek Government loan of up to 60,000,000 francs, guaranteed by Great Britain, France and Russia, with the interest and sinking fund secured on the first revenues of the Greek State and the loan to be raised in three 20,000,000-franc instalments.
sources.verification_status: Verified against the contemporary House of Commons record reproducing the Convention's financial provisions.
sources.primary_passage: The loan proposed was 60,000,000 of livres to be equally divided between the Three Powers, each of which was to be liable only for its own quota. This sum was to be advanced by instalments, with securities upon the revenues of the country for the payment of the interest, and for the accumulation of a sinking fund to discharge the principal itself.
sources.passage_locator: House of Lords, 13 August 1832, Greek Loan Convention, Hansard; Earl Grey's second-reading explanation of the Convention.
sources.passage_status: Exact contemporary parliamentary wording locked; the debate records the Convention's guarantee structure and revenue security. The original treaty scan remains a supplementary archival target.
sources.edition: Hansard, House of Lords, 13 August 1832.
sources.publication_status: A-grade — contemporary parliamentary evidence for the guarantee and security framework.
sources.evidence_limits: The passage establishes the governmental guarantee and security structure, not the later 1833 Rothschild contracting/issue terms, which are separately recorded in the 1833 Greek loan record.

sources.title: Rothschild Contract for the Greek Government Loan, 1833

sources.primary_passage: the two Commissioners, one a Greek, the other a Bavarian, met at Paris, and contracted with Messrs. Rothschild and Co. in January, 1833, for the whole 60,000,000f. at one and the same time, and at one and the same price—namely, 94 for a 5 per cent bond.
sources.passage_locator: House of Commons, 27 July 1855, debate on the Turkish loan; retrospective parliamentary account of the Greek loan of 1832/1833, Hansard.
sources.passage_status: Exact contemporary parliamentary wording locked as a retrospective record of the January 1833 contract; direct scan of the original Greek loan contract remains a desirable supplementary archival target.
sources.edition: Hansard, House of Commons, 27 July 1855.
sources.publication_status: A-grade — direct parliamentary evidence for the contract and terms, with original contract scan still a supplementary target.
sources.evidence_limits: The source is a parliamentary retrospective from 1855 rather than the original 1833 contract; it establishes the reported contract, amount and price but not every contractual security or distribution detail.

sources.title: Ottoman Turkish Loan, 1854
sources.historical_claim: The Ottoman Government's 1854 loan was raised in the English and French markets with the knowledge and stated satisfaction of the British Government, secured in part by an assignment of Egyptian tribute; contemporary parliamentary evidence also records that Rothschild had initially been entrusted with a proposed £6,000,000 Turkish loan before withdrawing that proposal.

sources.bn_title: অটোমান তুর্কি ঋণ, ১৮৫৪
sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৮৫৪ সালের অটোমান ঋণ ইংরেজ ও ফরাসি বাজারে তোলা হয়; ব্রিটিশ সরকারের জ্ঞান ও সন্তুষ্টির কথা সমসাময়িক ঋণ-প্রসপেক্টাসে উল্লেখ ছিল এবং ঋণের একটি নিরাপত্তা ছিল মিশরীয় খাজনার নির্দিষ্ট অংশ। একই সংসদীয় নথিতে প্রাথমিকভাবে রথসচাইল্ডদের হাতে £৬,০০,০০০ প্রস্তাবিত ঋণের দায়িত্ব দেওয়ার কথাও উল্লেখ আছে।
sources.primary_passage: The undersigned have the satisfaction to acquaint the public that they are authorized by the Earl of Clarendon, Her Majesty's Principal Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs, to state that this Loan is negotiated with the knowledge of the English Government; that Her Majesty's Government is satisfied that the Loan and the appropriation of the above-mentioned 30,000,000 piastres (£282,000 sterling) per annum of the Egyptian Tribute are duly authorized by His Majesty the Sultan.
sources.passage_locator: House of Commons, 21 July 1876, The Turkish Debt—The Loan of 1854—Resolution, Hansard; the debate reproduces the 1854 loan prospectus and general bond, including the 16 August prospectus statement and 24 August 1854 general bond.
sources.passage_status: Qualified contemporary-document reproduction locked — the parliamentary debate reproduces the 1854 prospectus/bond wording; direct scan of the original 1854 prospectus or bond remains a desirable supplementary target.
sources.source_identity: House of Commons, 21 July 1876, The Turkish Debt—The Loan of 1854—Resolution; reproduces portions of the 1854 prospectus and 24 August 1854 general bond.
sources.edition: Hansard, House of Commons, 21 July 1876, Turkish Debt—The Loan of 1854—Resolution.
sources.what_passage_establishes: The reproduced prospectus establishes that the 1854 Ottoman loan was negotiated with the knowledge of the English Government, that the Government was satisfied with the authorization of the loan and the allocation of 30,000,000 piastres of Egyptian tribute, and that the loan was secured by that tribute assignment.
sources.evidence_limits: This record does not establish that Rothschild ultimately issued the 1854 loan; the parliamentary account states that Rothschild withdrew their proposed £6,000,000 loan and that the subsequent issue was placed under Anglo-French auspices. The direct 1854 prospectus/bond scan remains a supplementary archival target.
scholarly_references: House of Commons, Hansard, 21 July 1876, The Turkish Debt—The Loan of 1854—Resolution.
sources.publication_status: A-grade for the reproduced contemporary prospectus/bond wording and government-knowledge claim; original 1854 document scan remains a supplementary archival target.

sources.title: East India Company £8 Million Home Loan Authority, 1858
sources.historical_claim: In 1858 Parliament authorized the East India Company to raise up to £8,000,000 by loan in the United Kingdom for the service of the Government of India during the financial emergency following the Indian revolt, while the contemporary debate addressed the relationship between Indian borrowing, the Bank of England, and possible British fiscal responsibility.
sources.verification_status: Verified against the contemporary House of Commons East India Loan Bill debate.
sources.primary_passage: Clause 1, empowering the Company to raise (£) by way of loan. THE CHANCELLOR OF THE EXCHEQUER proposed to fill up the blank with £8,000,000.
sources.passage_locator: House of Commons, 22 February 1858, East India Loan Bill, Committee, Hansard.
sources.passage_status: Contemporary parliamentary wording locked; the debate establishes the statutory borrowing authority and its purpose in meeting the Indian Government's financial emergency.
sources.edition: Hansard, House of Commons, 22 February 1858.
sources.publication_status: A-grade — contemporary parliamentary evidence for the £8,000,000 borrowing authority.
sources.evidence_limits: This record establishes parliamentary borrowing authority, not the precise amount ultimately drawn, final lenders, or complete contractual terms. The debate separately records an existing £1,000,000 Bank of England loan and earlier East India loans.

book_1_integration.part_label: Book 1 — Part II: National banking and nineteenth-century state finance

sources.title: East India £7 Million Loan on Indian Security, 1859
sources.historical_claim: In March 1859 the British Government sought parliamentary authority for a £7,000,000 loan on Indian security to meet the financial requirements arising from the Indian mutiny and its aftermath; the Government subsequently recognized that additional borrowing in England would be necessary.
sources.verification_status: Verified against the contemporary House of Lords Indian Finance debate.
sources.primary_passage: the reasons which induced the Government to believe at the time they made a proposition to raise a loan of £7,000,000 on Indian security, that that amount would be sufficient, and the circumstances which have induced them within the last few days to entertain a different opinion.
sources.passage_locator: House of Lords, 25 March 1859, Indian Finance, Hansard; statement concerning the £7,000,000 loan on Indian security.
sources.passage_status: Exact contemporary parliamentary wording locked; establishes the £7,000,000 loan proposal on Indian security and the Government's subsequent recognition of additional requirements.
sources.edition: Hansard, House of Lords, 25 March 1859.
sources.publication_status: A-grade — contemporary parliamentary evidence for the £7,000,000 Indian-security loan proposal.
sources.evidence_limits: This passage establishes the Government's loan proposal and financial context, but not the final lender, issue price, subscription result, or full statutory terms.

book_1_integration.part_label: Book 1 — Part II: National banking and nineteenth-century state finance

sources.title: East India £3 Million Home Loan Authority, 1860
sources.historical_claim: In August 1860 Parliament moved to authorize the Secretary of State for India to raise £3,000,000 in the United Kingdom by loan for the service of the Government of India, against a background of a projected Indian revenue deficiency of £7,472,000 for the year.
sources.verification_status: Verified against the contemporary House of Lords East India Loan Bill debate.
sources.primary_passage: its object to enable the Secretary of State for India to raise in this country by loan a sum of £3,000,000.
sources.passage_locator: House of Lords, 21 August 1860, East India Loan Bill, First Reading, Hansard.
sources.passage_status: Exact contemporary parliamentary wording locked; establishes the proposed £3,000,000 home borrowing authority and its Indian Government purpose.
sources.edition: Hansard, House of Lords, 21 August 1860.
sources.publication_status: A-grade — contemporary parliamentary evidence for the £3,000,000 borrowing authority.
sources.evidence_limits: This passage does not establish the eventual lender, issue terms, subscription result, or amount actually drawn. It is distinct from the earlier 1859 £7,000,000 Indian-security loan proposal.

book_1_integration.part_label: Book 1 — Part II: National banking and nineteenth-century state finance

sources.title: East India £4 Million Loan, 1861
sources.historical_claim: In June 1861 Parliament was asked to sanction a £4,000,000 loan for the service of India; the Secretary of State for India explained that the borrowing was required because railway receipts and expenditure had produced a shortfall, rather than because ordinary Indian government revenue was insufficient.
sources.verification_status: Verified against the contemporary House of Commons East India Loan Bill debate.
sources.primary_passage: the House was now asked to sanction a loan on account of India to the amount of £4,000,000.
sources.passage_locator: House of Commons, 13 June 1861, East India Loan Bill, Committee, Hansard.
sources.passage_status: Exact contemporary parliamentary wording locked; the debate establishes the £4,000,000 loan request and the associated increase in Indian debt.
sources.edition: Hansard, House of Commons, 13 June 1861.
sources.publication_status: A-grade — contemporary parliamentary evidence for the £4,000,000 Indian loan.
sources.evidence_limits: This record does not establish the final lender, issue price, subscription result, or complete contractual terms. It also does not imply that the borrowing was for ordinary Indian revenue needs; the debate specifically linked the loan to railway-related requirements.

book_1_integration.part_label: Book 1 — Part II: National banking and nineteenth-century state finance

sources.title: East India Railway Contingent Borrowing Authority, 1861
sources.historical_claim: In July 1861 the Secretary of State for India sought discretionary authority to raise additional money if Indian railway companies failed to furnish the funds required for railway construction; the proposed borrowing was to be used only if the companies did not raise the necessary sums themselves.
sources.verification_status: Verified against the contemporary House of Commons East India Loan debate.
sources.primary_passage: I now rise to ask for such powers to raise money to be used only in the event of the railway companies not furnishing the sum required.
sources.passage_locator: House of Commons, 25 July 1861, East India Loan, Hansard; Sir Charles Wood's explanation of proposed discretionary borrowing for Indian railway expenditure.
sources.passage_status: Exact contemporary parliamentary wording locked; establishes contingent borrowing authority tied to railway companies' failure to raise required funds.
sources.edition: Hansard, House of Commons, 25 July 1861.
sources.publication_status: A-grade — contemporary parliamentary evidence for the contingent railway borrowing authority.
sources.evidence_limits: This is distinct from the £4,000,000 loan already recorded for 1861. It establishes a contingent power, not proof that the additional power was exercised or that the Government ultimately borrowed under it.

sources.title: East India Railway Finance: Home Treasury Dependence on Company Payments
sources.historical_claim: In June 1861 the Secretary of State explained that Indian railway expenditure was paid through advances from the India Treasury while Home Government expenses were met from sums paid by railway companies into the Treasury in England; the shortfall in company payments created pressure for borrowing.
sources.verification_status: Verified against the contemporary House of Commons East India Loan debate.
sources.primary_passage: the expenditure for railways in India is paid by advances from the India Treasury, while the expenses of the Home Government are defrayed from the sums paid by the railway companies into the Treasury in England.
sources.passage_locator: House of Commons, 3 June 1861, East India Loan—Committee, Hansard.
sources.passage_status: Exact contemporary parliamentary wording locked.
sources.edition: Hansard, House of Commons, 3 June 1861.
sources.publication_status: A-grade — contemporary parliamentary evidence.
sources.evidence_limits: This establishes the financing mechanism and liquidity pressure; it does not identify a particular lender or prove that all railway expenditure was financed by borrowing.

sources.title: East India Railway Finance: Government Borrowing and Railway Company Payments
sources.historical_claim: In 1862 the Indian Government explained that railway expenditure was substantially financed through Government borrowing, while the railway companies were responsible for payments into the Home Treasury; contemporary debate recorded the resulting shortfall between railway expenditure and company payments.
sources.verification_status: Verified against contemporary House of Commons evidence.
sources.primary_passage: the money spent on railways is substantially borrowed by the Government.

sources.passage_status: Exact contemporary parliamentary wording locked.
sources.edition: Hansard, House of Commons, 19 June 1862.
sources.publication_status: A-grade — contemporary parliamentary evidence.
sources.evidence_limits: The passage establishes the financing structure at a high level; it does not by itself identify a particular lender, issue, interest rate, or loan contract.

sources.historical_claim: Contemporary parliamentary evidence reported that the £4,000,000 East India loan raised in London during the railway-finance pressure was subsequently repaid at 5 per cent after railway associations raised substantial funds as market conditions improved.
sources.verification_status: Verified against contemporary parliamentary evidence.
sources.primary_passage: they repaid the loan at 5 per cent

sources.evidence_limits: The passage establishes repayment at 5 per cent but does not by itself provide the original loan contract, exact repayment date, lender identity, or complete transaction terms.

sources.title: East India Loan: Railway Companies Ultimately Supplied the Required Funds
sources.historical_claim: The 1861 East India borrowing was ultimately not needed: Sir Charles Wood reported in 1864 that railway companies paid in the full estimated amount before the end of the year, leaving the £4,000,000 borrowed unnecessary.

sources.publication_status: A-grade — contemporary parliamentary retrospective evidence.
sources.evidence_limits: This establishes the reported outcome of the borrowing episode, not the original loan contract, issue price, lender, or a separate 1862 repayment instrument.

sources.title: Overend Gurney crisis, 1866
sources.historical_claim: The failure of Overend Gurney in 1866 produced a major financial panic and contributed to policy debate that shaped the Bank of England's lender-of-last-resort role.
sources.verification_status: Primary-source / contemporary official record verified
sources.bn_title: ওভারেন্ড গার্নি সংকট, ১৮৬৬
sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৮৬৬ সালে ওভারেন্ড গার্নির পতন একটি বড় আর্থিক আতঙ্ক সৃষ্টি করে এবং ব্যাংক অব ইংল্যান্ডের শেষ আশ্রয়ের ঋণদাতা হিসেবে ভূমিকা গঠনের নীতিগত বিতর্ককে প্রভাবিত করে।
sources.notes: The 11 May 1866 Hansard debate records the Government's contemporary response to the monetary panic, including the Bank of England's extraordinary expansion of loans and discounts, the sharp fall in its reserves, and the Government's decision to authorize action beyond the statutory Issue Department limits if necessary. The Bank of England archive separately preserves the Court of Directors minutes for 11 April 1866–4 April 1867, explicitly noting the Overend and Gurney collapse (G4/89). This provides direct contemporary parliamentary evidence plus a surviving institutional archival record. The broader later interpretation of the episode as shaping the lender-of-last-resort role should remain identified as historical interpretation rather than a direct 1866 statement.
sources.primary_passage: the Bank, moved by a just desire to sustain the commerce of the country, and to avert disaster, has extended its loans and discounts to-day to a sum of something more than £4,000,000.
sources.passage_locator: House of Commons, Hansard, 11 May 1866, vol. 183, cols. 840–842, “Suspension of the Bank Charter Act—Question”.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — contemporary parliamentary record
sources.source_identity: House of Commons Parliamentary Debates (Hansard), 11 May 1866, discussion of suspension of the Bank Charter Act and Bank of England advances during the crisis.; publisher/authority: Parliament of the United Kingdom; Hansard; year: 1866.
sources.edition: House of Commons Parliamentary Debates (Hansard), 11 May 1866, discussion of suspension of the Bank Charter Act and Bank of England advances during the crisis.
sources.publisher: Parliament of the United Kingdom; Hansard
sources.what_passage_establishes: The 11 May 1866 Hansard debate records the Government's contemporary response to the monetary panic, including the Bank of England's extraordinary expansion of loans and discounts, the sharp fall in its reserves, and the Government's decision to authorize action beyond the statutory Issue Department limits if necessary.
sources.evidence_limits: The passage establishes the cited institutional/legal/financial proposition; it does not by itself establish broader causal claims beyond the text and its documentary context.
scholarly_references: Sabine Schneider, “The politics of last resort lending and the Overend & Gurney crisis of 1866,” *The Economic History Review* 75 (2022), 579–600, DOI 10.1111/ehr.13113.
Marc Flandreau and Stefano Ugolini, “The Crisis of 1866,” in Nicholas Dimsdale and Anthony Hotson (eds.), *British Financial Crises since 1825* (Oxford University Press, 2014), pp. 76–93.

sources.title: Indian Railways Finance: No Additional Guaranteed Capital Announced, 1867
sources.historical_claim: In July 1867 the Secretary of State for India stated that no additional guaranteed capital was required for Indian railway works beyond amounts already announced, while the amount to be raised for 1867–68 to meet current expenditure, repay debt due to Government, and maintain a small balance was estimated at £8–9 million.
sources.verification_status: Contemporary parliamentary primary evidence verified from Hansard, House of Commons, 8 July 1867.
sources.bn_title: ভারতীয় রেলওয়ে অর্থায়ন: ১৮৬৭ সালে অতিরিক্ত গ্যারান্টিযুক্ত মূলধনের ঘোষণা নেই
sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৮৬৭ সালের জুলাইয়ে ভারতের সচিব জানান যে ইতিমধ্যে ঘোষিত অর্থের বাইরে ভারতীয় রেলওয়ে নির্মাণের জন্য অতিরিক্ত গ্যারান্টিযুক্ত মূলধনের প্রয়োজন নেই; একই সময়ে ১৮৬৭–৬৮ সালে চলতি ব্যয়, সরকারের কাছে বকেয়া ঋণ পরিশোধ এবং সামান্য নগদ উদ্বৃত্ত রাখার জন্য £৮–৯ মিলিয়ন সংগ্রহের প্রয়োজন হবে বলে জানানো হয়।
sources.notes: This record captures the contemporary 1867 parliamentary financing position without importing the later 1877 retrospective explanation that the Government had decided to raise railway funds directly. The 1867 exchange is therefore evidence of the financing requirement and the absence of newly announced guaranteed railway capital, but not by itself proof of the precise legal instrument or lender used for the £8–9 million.
sources.primary_passage: there would be no capital required, except what had already been mentioned in the Report on these railways
sources.passage_locator: Hansard, House of Commons, 8 July 1867, 'India—Indian Railways.—Question', vol. 188, col. 1192; Sir Stafford Northcote's answer to Mr. Finlay.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — exact contemporary parliamentary wording verified.
sources.source_identity: House of Commons parliamentary debate, 8 July 1867; question on additional guaranteed capital for Indian railway works and answer by Sir Stafford Northcote, Secretary of State for India.
sources.edition: Hansard, House of Commons, 8 July 1867, vol. 188, col. 1192.
sources.what_passage_establishes: The passage establishes that, as of 8 July 1867, the Government did not expect additional guaranteed railway capital beyond amounts already announced; the same answer states that £8–9 million would be raised in 1867–68 for current expenditure, repayment of debt due to Government, and a small balance.
sources.evidence_limits: The passage does not by itself identify the precise borrowing instrument, lender, interest rate, issue terms, or prove that the full £8–9 million was raised specifically for railway construction. It should not be used alone to establish the later policy conclusion that the Indian Government had fully replaced guaranteed-company finance with direct borrowing.
scholarly_references: Hansard, House of Commons, 8 July 1867, vol. 188, col. 1192.
sources.publication_status: A-grade — contemporary parliamentary primary passage locked; suitable as the 1867 financing-transition evidence anchor, with later retrospective sources kept as corroboration only.

sources.title: India Revenue Accounts, 1868: Guaranteed Railway Interest Burden
sources.historical_claim: The 1868 Indian Revenue Accounts recorded a substantial increase in the charge for guaranteed interest on Indian railway capital: for the year ending 31 March 1867 the net guaranteed interest charge, after traffic receipts, was £731,049, while the accounts for 1867–68 showed a further increase in guaranteed-interest charges and the continuing separation of railway guaranteed-interest obligations from ordinary Indian revenue and public-works expenditure.
sources.verification_status: Contemporary parliamentary primary evidence verified from Hansard, House of Commons, 27 July 1868.
sources.bn_title: ভারতের রাজস্ব হিসাব, ১৮৬৮: গ্যারান্টিযুক্ত রেলওয়ে সুদের বোঝা
sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৮৬৮ সালের ভারতের রাজস্ব হিসাবগুলোতে ভারতীয় রেলওয়ে মূলধনের গ্যারান্টিযুক্ত সুদের ব্যয়কে পৃথক আর্থিক বোঝা হিসেবে দেখানো হয়। ১৮৬৭ সালের শেষ হওয়া বছরে ট্রাফিক রসিদ বাদ দেওয়ার পর এই গ্যারান্টিযুক্ত সুদের নিট ব্যয় ছিল £৭৩১,০৪৯; ১৮৬৭–৬৮ হিসাবেও এই খাতে উল্লেখযোগ্য বৃদ্ধি দেখা যায়।
sources.notes: This record is deliberately narrower than the later 1877 retrospective account of the 1867 policy shift. The 1868 contemporary accounts establish the continuing fiscal burden of guaranteed railway capital and its separate accounting treatment; they do not by themselves prove that all new railway borrowing had shifted to direct Government borrowing.
sources.primary_passage: the Guaranteed Interest on the Capital of Railway and other Companies, in India and in England, deducting net Traffic Receipts, was £731,049
sources.passage_locator: Hansard, House of Commons, 27 July 1868, 'India—East India Revenue Accounts—Committee'; resolution covering the year ending 31 March 1867.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — exact contemporary parliamentary wording verified.
sources.source_identity: House of Commons parliamentary financial accounts debate, 27 July 1868, reporting Indian revenue, expenditure, debt interest, public works and guaranteed railway-company interest.
sources.edition: Hansard, House of Commons, 27 July 1868.
sources.what_passage_establishes: The passage establishes the separately reported guaranteed-interest burden on railway and other company capital in the Indian accounts, with £731,049 recorded after deduction of net traffic receipts for the year ending 31 March 1867. The same debate discusses an additional £660,000 increase in guaranteed railway interest in the 1867–68 estimate.
sources.evidence_limits: The passage does not identify individual lenders, loan instruments, issue prices, or prove the exact transition from guaranteed-company borrowing to direct Government borrowing. Those propositions require separate primary evidence.
scholarly_references: Hansard, House of Commons, 27 July 1868, India—East India Revenue Accounts—Committee.
sources.publication_status: A-grade — contemporary parliamentary financial-account evidence with exact passage locked.

sources.title: Indian Railways Finance, 1869: Government Direct-Borrowing Policy
sources.historical_claim: In July 1869 the Duke of Argyll stated that Her Majesty's Government had authorized the Government of India to undertake new railway construction itself, raise the required money on its own credit, and spend it through its own officers.
sources.verification_status: Contemporary parliamentary primary evidence verified from House of Lords Hansard, 23 July 1869.
sources.bn_title: ভারতীয় রেলওয়ে অর্থায়ন, ১৮৬৯: সরকারের সরাসরি ঋণগ্রহণ নীতি
sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৮৬৯ সালের জুলাইয়ে ডিউক অব আর্গাইল জানান যে ভারত সরকারকে নতুন রেলওয়ে নির্মাণ নিজ দায়িত্বে গ্রহণ, নিজস্ব ঋণযোগ্যতার ভিত্তিতে অর্থ সংগ্রহ এবং সরকারি কর্মকর্তাদের মাধ্যমে ব্যয় করার অনুমতি দেওয়া হয়েছে।
sources.notes: This record uses the contemporary 1869 parliamentary financial statement as the primary evidence for the stated policy shift. It does not treat the statement as proof that every later railway loan was immediately raised directly by Government.

sources.evidence_limits: The passage does not by itself identify a particular direct Government loan, lender, issue price, interest rate, or settlement date.

sources.title: Indian Railways Finance, 1870: State Agency and Borrowed Funds for New Works
sources.historical_claim: In March 1870 the Government of India was proceeding with the extension of Indian railways under State agency, and the associated public-works programme proposed about £4–5 million of borrowed funds for new irrigation works and railways.
sources.verification_status: Contemporary parliamentary primary evidence verified from House of Commons Hansard, 18 March 1870 and 4 March 1870.
sources.bn_title: ভারতীয় রেলওয়ে অর্থায়ন, ১৮৭০: সরকারি সংস্থা ও নতুন কাজে ঋণভিত্তিক অর্থায়ন
sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৮৭০ সালের মার্চে ভারত সরকার রাষ্ট্রীয় ব্যবস্থাপনায় ভারতীয় রেলওয়ের সম্প্রসারণ এগিয়ে নিচ্ছিল; একই সময়ে নতুন সেচ ও রেলওয়ে নির্মাণের জন্য প্রায় ৪–৫ মিলিয়ন পাউন্ড ধার করা তহবিল ব্যবহারের প্রস্তাব ছিল।
sources.notes: The 18 March 1870 parliamentary answer records the proposed use of borrowed funds for new irrigation works and railways, while the 4 March 1870 debate records that State agency was being used to extend the railway system under the Secretary of State's instructions. The two passages together provide a direct contemporary implementation-and-finance anchor for the 1869 policy transition.
sources.primary_passage: If to the outlay provided from the revenues we add the sum which it is proposed to lay out from borrowed funds upon new irrigation works and railways, which we may estimate at about £4,000,000 or £5,000,000
sources.passage_locator: Hansard, House of Commons, 18 March 1870, 'India—Public Works—Question', vol. 200, cols. 1208–1209; passage quoted from the Government of India's despatch.

sources.edition: Hansard, House of Commons, 18 March 1870, vol. 200; related implementation statement, 4 March 1870, vol. 199.

sources.title: Indian Government Railways, 1871: State Construction of Lahore–Peshawur Line
sources.historical_claim: In March 1871 the Government of India reported that works had actually commenced on the Lahore–Peshawur line as the first long State railway, while other State lines were being surveyed and prepared for rapid progress.
sources.verification_status: Contemporary parliamentary primary evidence verified from House of Commons Hansard, 24 March 1871.
sources.bn_title: ভারত সরকারের রেলওয়ে, ১৮৭১: লাহোর–পেশাওয়ার লাইনে সরকারি নির্মাণ
sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৮৭১ সালের মার্চে ভারত সরকার জানায় যে লাহোর–পেশাওয়ার লাইনে বাস্তব নির্মাণকাজ শুরু হয়েছে—এটি ছিল প্রথম দীর্ঘ সরকারি রেললাইন; অন্যান্য সরকারি লাইনও জরিপ ও প্রস্তুতির পর্যায়ে ছিল।
sources.notes: This record is deliberately limited to implementation evidence. It shows the post-1869 State-agency policy being put into practice on a named long State line; it does not by itself identify the financing instrument, lender, interest rate, or loan issue terms.
sources.primary_passage: On only one long State line—the Lahore-Peshawur line—have works been actually commenced; but several other lines have been, or are being, now surveyed
sources.passage_locator: Hansard, House of Commons, 24 March 1871, 'India—Railways—Question', vol. 205, col. 573; answer by Mr. Grant Duff.

sources.title: Indian State Railways and Public Works, 1872: £2.5 Million of Loan-Funded Works
sources.historical_claim: In August 1872 the Indian Government reported that about £2.5 million was money raised by loan and intended for public works funded from loans, and separately stated that State railways and canals were being advanced as rapidly as conditions permitted; by the same accounting, £2.75 million had been spent on State railways up to the end of the period covered.
sources.verification_status: Contemporary parliamentary primary evidence verified from House of Commons Hansard, 6 August 1872.
sources.bn_title: ভারতের সরকারি রেলওয়ে ও জনপূর্ত, ১৮৭২: ঋণভিত্তিক ২৫ লক্ষ পাউন্ডের অর্থায়ন
sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৮৭২ সালের আগস্টে ভারত সরকার জানায় যে প্রায় ২৫ লক্ষ পাউন্ড ঋণ নিয়ে জনপূর্তে ব্যয় করার জন্য তোলা হয়েছিল; একই সময়ে সরকারি রেলওয়ে ও খাল দ্রুত এগিয়ে নেওয়া হচ্ছিল এবং সংশ্লিষ্ট হিসাবে সরকারি রেলওয়েতে ২৭.৫ লক্ষ পাউন্ড ব্যয়ের কথা উল্লেখ করা হয়।
sources.notes: This record uses a contemporary parliamentary financial statement to connect loan-raised funds with India's public-works programme and State railways. The passage does not isolate the £2.5 million exclusively for railways, and it does not identify a particular loan issue, lender, rate, or maturity.
sources.primary_passage: About £2,500,000 is money raised by loan, and intended to be laid out on that class of public works for which we pay out of loans, but which has not yet been paid away.
sources.passage_locator: Hansard, House of Commons, 6 August 1872, 'Committee', vol. 212, cols. 566–567; financial statement concerning Indian public works and cash balances.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — exact contemporary parliamentary wording verified.
sources.source_identity: House of Commons committee debate on Indian finances, 6 August 1872; statement by Sir Richard Temple concerning loan-raised funds and public works.
sources.edition: Hansard, House of Commons, 6 August 1872, vol. 212, cols. 566–567.
sources.what_passage_establishes: The passage establishes that about £2.5 million had been raised by loan for public works ordinarily funded from loans but had not yet been disbursed; the same statement says the Government was proceeding with State railways and canals and records £2.75 million of State-railway expenditure.
sources.evidence_limits: The £2.5 million is for the wider class of loan-funded public works, not railways alone. The passage does not identify a particular loan issue, lender, issue price, interest rate, maturity, or settlement date.
scholarly_references: Hansard, House of Commons, 6 August 1872, vol. 212, cols. 566–567.

sources.title: India Public Works Extraordinary, 1873: Five-Year Reproductive Works Programme
sources.historical_claim: In July 1873 the Government of India resolved to devote £4.5 million annually for five years to Public Works Extraordinary, with the works to be reproductive in character; contemporary parliamentary discussion tied the programme to State railway and canal construction and to the need to manage financing through cash balances and borrowing.
sources.verification_status: Contemporary parliamentary primary evidence verified from House of Commons Hansard, 31 July 1873.
sources.bn_title: ভারতের অসাধারণ জনপূর্ত, ১৮৭৩: পাঁচ বছরের উৎপাদনশীল জনপূর্ত কর্মসূচি
sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৮৭৩ সালের জুলাইয়ে ভারত সরকার পাঁচ বছরের জন্য বছরে ৪৫ লক্ষ পাউন্ড অসাধারণ জনপূর্তে ব্যয়ের সিদ্ধান্ত নেয়, এবং এসব কাজকে উৎপাদনশীল প্রকৃতির হওয়ার কথা বলা হয়; সমসাময়িক সংসদীয় আলোচনায় এই কর্মসূচিকে সরকারি রেলওয়ে ও খাল নির্মাণ এবং নগদ সঞ্চয় ও ঋণের মাধ্যমে অর্থায়নের সঙ্গে যুক্ত করা হয়।
sources.notes: This record captures the 1873 policy commitment and financing framework, not a particular loan issue. The contemporary debate notes that remunerative works could initially be paid from cash balances; it therefore should not be read as proof that the full £4.5 million annual programme was immediately debt-financed.
sources.primary_passage: In July last the Government of India determined to expend, during the four years ending 1877–8, the sum of £17,000,000, of which sum they proposed to expend £4,500,000 during the present year.
sources.passage_locator: Hansard, House of Commons, 3 August 1874, vol. 220, cols. 1185–1186, retrospectively describing the July 1873 Government of India resolution; contemporary 31 July 1873 debate separately records the financing context.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — exact parliamentary wording verified.
sources.source_identity: House of Commons Hansard: 1873 Indian Public Works Extraordinary programme and its financing context; retrospective official statement in 1874 records the July 1873 resolution.
sources.edition: Hansard, House of Commons, 3 August 1874, vol. 220, cols. 1185–1186; see also 31 July 1873, vol. 220, cols. 1408–1410.
sources.what_passage_establishes: The 1873 resolution committed £17 million over four years, including £4.5 million in the first year, for Public Works Extraordinary; the programme was intended to cover reproductive works. The 31 July 1873 debate shows that about £4 million of remunerative works in the current year could be paid from cash balances, while the financing question was explicitly framed around the need to borrow in subsequent years if balances were insufficient.
sources.evidence_limits: The quoted £17 million/£4.5 million passage is a 1874 parliamentary retrospective on the 1873 resolution, not the original resolution text. It does not identify a specific loan issue, lender, issue price, interest rate, or maturity. The £4.5 million was not necessarily all borrowed.
scholarly_references: Hansard, House of Commons, 31 July 1873, vol. 220, cols. 1408–1410.
Hansard, House of Commons, 3 August 1874, vol. 220, cols. 1185–1186.

sources.title: India Finance, 1874: Parliamentary Borrowing Power for the Indian Government
sources.historical_claim: In April 1874 the Secretary of State for India reported that borrowing powers under previous Acts had been exhausted except for a temporary £2 million authority granted by the previous year's Loan Act, demonstrating that Parliament was actively regulating and extending the legal borrowing capacity of the Indian Government.
sources.verification_status: Contemporary parliamentary primary evidence verified from House of Commons Hansard, 23 April 1874.
sources.bn_title: ভারতীয় অর্থব্যবস্থা, ১৮৭৪: ভারত সরকারের ঋণগ্রহণের সংসদীয় ক্ষমতা
sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৮৭৪ সালের এপ্রিল মাসে ভারতের সেক্রেটারি অব স্টেট জানান যে পূর্ববর্তী আইনগুলোর অধীনে ঋণগ্রহণের ক্ষমতা প্রায় সম্পূর্ণ ব্যবহৃত হয়ে গেছে; কেবল আগের বছরের Loan Act-এর অধীনে সর্বোচ্চ ২০ লক্ষ পাউন্ড সাময়িকভাবে ঋণ নেওয়ার ক্ষমতা অবশিষ্ট ছিল।
sources.notes: This is a legal borrowing-authority record, not evidence of a particular loan issue. It establishes the statutory ceiling and exhaustion of earlier borrowing powers. A separate March 1874 parliamentary record proposed a new £10 million borrowing authority in response to the Bengal famine.
sources.primary_passage: the borrowing powers of the Secretary of State under all Acts previous to the Loan Act of the present Session had been exhausted, with the single exception of the power contained in the Loan Act of last Session, by which he was enabled to borrow temporarily a sum not exceeding £2,000,000.
sources.passage_locator: Hansard, House of Commons, 23 April 1874, vol. 218, col. 985.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — exact contemporary parliamentary wording verified.
sources.source_identity: House of Commons Hansard, Finance of India—Borrowing Powers, 23 April 1874; answer by Lord George Hamilton.
sources.edition: Hansard, House of Commons, 23 April 1874, vol. 218, col. 985.
sources.what_passage_establishes: Parliamentary borrowing authority for the Secretary of State for India had been exhausted under earlier Acts except for a temporary £2 million authority from the previous year's Loan Act; the 1874 Session was therefore operating within a newly legislated borrowing framework.
sources.evidence_limits: The passage does not itself establish that the £2 million temporary authority was drawn, nor does it identify lender, issue price, interest rate, maturity, or settlement date. It establishes legal borrowing capacity only.
scholarly_references: Hansard, House of Commons, 23 April 1874, vol. 218, col. 985.
Hansard, House of Commons, 20 March 1874, vol. 218, cols. 174–189.

sources.title: India Public Works Finance, 1875: Borrowing Shifted Toward India
sources.historical_claim: In August 1875 the Indian Government stated that public works were being planned on the basis that required borrowing should be raised in India, with only remunerative works eligible for borrowed funds and unproductive works charged to ordinary revenue; the Government also reported a June 1875 Indian loan of 2.5 crore rupees whose tenders were heavily oversubscribed.
sources.verification_status: Contemporary parliamentary primary evidence verified from House of Commons Hansard, 9 August 1875.
sources.bn_title: ভারতের জনপূর্ত অর্থায়ন, ১৮৭৫: ঋণগ্রহণ ভারতে স্থানান্তরের নীতি
sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৮৭৫ সালের আগস্টে ভারত সরকার জানায় যে জনপূর্তের প্রয়োজনীয় ঋণ ভারতে তোলার নীতি গ্রহণ করা হয়েছে; ঋণ থেকে কেবল উৎপাদনশীল কাজ এবং অনুৎপাদনশীল কাজ সাধারণ রাজস্ব থেকে বহন করার কথা বলা হয়। একই সময়ে জুন ১৮৭৫-এ ভারতে ২.৫ কোটি রুপির একটি ঋণ তোলা হয়, যার আবেদন নির্ধারিত ন্যূনতমের দ্বিগুণেরও বেশি ছিল।
sources.notes: This record combines the 1875 policy principle with its contemporaneous implementation evidence. The £4.0–£4.9337 million figures in the debate describe the annual public-works financing requirement and ways and means; they should not be treated as a single loan issue.
sources.primary_passage: The principles on which the Secretary of State had determined the Public Works in India should be constructed. They were that only works of a remunerative character should be undertaken; that they should be constructed from money borrowed in India; and that those of an unproductive character should be debited against ordinary Revenue.
sources.passage_locator: Hansard, House of Commons, 9 August 1875, 'Committee', vol. 226, cols. 805–808; Lord George Hamilton's Indian Finance statement.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — exact contemporary parliamentary wording verified.
sources.source_identity: House of Commons Hansard, Committee on Indian Finance, 9 August 1875; statement by Lord George Hamilton.
sources.edition: Hansard, House of Commons, 9 August 1875, vol. 226, cols. 805–808.
sources.what_passage_establishes: The 1875 policy explicitly preferred India as the place to raise borrowing for public works and distinguished remunerative works funded by borrowing from unproductive works charged to ordinary revenue. The same debate records a June 1875 Indian loan of 2.5 crore rupees with 5.45 crore 47.5 lakh rupees applied for at or above the minimum.
sources.evidence_limits: The policy passage does not itself specify a particular sterling loan, lender, maturity, or issue price. The rupee loan details establish an Indian-market borrowing event but do not by themselves establish the identity of every subscriber or the ultimate use of every rupee.
scholarly_references: Hansard, House of Commons, 9 August 1875, vol. 226, cols. 805–808.
sources.publication_status: A-grade — contemporary parliamentary primary policy statement plus implementation evidence.

sources.title: India Public Works and State Railways, 1876: Borrowing, Reproductive Capital, and State Railway Returns
sources.historical_claim: In August 1876 the Indian Government reaffirmed that remunerative public works were to be financed from money borrowed in India, while State railways were being constructed more cheaply than the guaranteed system; the debate reported £14 million already spent on State railways and £17 million on irrigation works, within £125 million of Government-connected public-works capital, with State railways beginning to earn a return on borrowed capital.
sources.verification_status: Contemporary parliamentary primary evidence verified from House of Commons Hansard, 10 August 1876.
sources.bn_title: ভারতের জনপূর্ত ও সরকারি রেলওয়ে, ১৮৭৬: ঋণ, উৎপাদনশীল মূলধন ও সরকারি রেলওয়ের আয়
sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৮৭৬ সালের আগস্টে ভারত সরকার পুনরায় নিশ্চিত করে যে উৎপাদনশীল জনপূর্ত ভারতে তোলা ঋণের অর্থে করা হবে; একই সময়ে সরকারি রেলওয়ে গ্যারান্টিযুক্ত ব্যবস্থার তুলনায় কম ব্যয়ে নির্মিত হচ্ছিল এবং সরকারি রেলওয়ে ও সেচকাজে বিপুল মূলধন বিনিয়োগের হিসাব সংসদে উপস্থাপিত হয়।
sources.notes: This record is distinct from the 1875 policy record because it documents the 1876 operating results and capital scale of the State-works system, including State-railway returns and the contemporaneous decision to raise a £4 million home loan for ways-and-means reasons. It does not claim that all public-works capital was debt-financed in India.
sources.primary_passage: the Secretary of State the first year he was in office laid down three principles as to public works; none were to be undertaken but those which would pay interest on borrowed capital; those that would not be remunerative were to be constructed out of Revenue, and loans were to be raised in India for public works.
sources.passage_locator: Hansard, House of Commons, 10 August 1876, 'Committee', vol. 231, cols. 990–992.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — exact contemporary parliamentary wording verified.
sources.source_identity: House of Commons Hansard, Committee on Indian Finance, 10 August 1876; statement by Lord George Hamilton.
sources.edition: Hansard, House of Commons, 10 August 1876, vol. 231, cols. 990–992.
sources.what_passage_establishes: The 1876 debate reaffirmed the India-borrowing principle for remunerative public works and described the financial performance and capital scale of State works. State railways had cost about £4,300 per mile without the Agra Bridge and £5,300 with it, versus £16,000 per mile under the earlier comparison; a 4% capital cost could be covered by a £200-per-mile return. The debate also reported £125 million of Government-connected public-works capital, including £14 million on State railways and £17 million on irrigation works, producing £4.296 million in net working receipts.
sources.evidence_limits: The return figures are aggregate financial-performance evidence and do not identify a particular loan issue, lender, maturity, or issue price. The £4 million home loan mentioned in the same debate was raised for ways-and-means reasons and should not be treated as a State-railway loan.
scholarly_references: Hansard, House of Commons, 10 August 1876, vol. 231, cols. 990–992.
sources.publication_status: A-grade — contemporary parliamentary primary passage locked; distinct State-works performance and financing evidence.

sources.title: India Finance, 1877: Famine Loan and Direct Government Borrowing
sources.historical_claim: In June 1877 the Indian Government sought parliamentary authority to raise £5,000,000 on the credit of Indian revenues to meet famine-related expenditure and other financing needs; the same statement explicitly described the post-1867 shift from borrowing through guaranteed railway companies to the Indian Government borrowing directly in the money market.
sources.verification_status: Contemporary parliamentary primary evidence verified from House of Commons Hansard, 21 June 1877.
sources.bn_title: ভারতীয় অর্থব্যবস্থা, ১৮৭৭: দুর্ভিক্ষ ঋণ ও সরকারের প্রত্যক্ষ ঋণগ্রহণ
sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৮৭৭ সালের জুনে ভারত সরকার দুর্ভিক্ষজনিত ব্যয় ও সংশ্লিষ্ট অর্থায়নের প্রয়োজনে ভারতীয় রাজস্বের জামানতে £৫,০০০,০০০ পর্যন্ত ঋণ তোলার সংসদীয় ক্ষমতা চায়; একই আর্থিক বিবৃতিতে ১৮৬৭-পরবর্তী গ্যারান্টিযুক্ত রেলওয়ে কোম্পানির মাধ্যমে ঋণ নেওয়ার বদলে ভারত সরকারের নিজে বাজারে গিয়ে ঋণ নেওয়ার পরিবর্তন স্পষ্টভাবে বর্ণিত হয়।
sources.notes: This record is distinct from the 1876 State-works performance record: it documents a specific 1877 borrowing-authority request and directly explains the institutional transition from indirect borrowing through guaranteed railway companies to Government borrowing on its own account. The £5 million authority was principally connected to famine and associated financing needs; it should not be treated as a single railway loan.
sources.primary_passage: The Indian Government adopted instead the simpler plan of going into the money-market themselves, borrowing money at a lower rate of interest, and expending it themselves.
sources.passage_locator: Hansard, House of Commons, 21 June 1877, 'Committee', vol. 235, cols. 92–144; statement by Lord George Hamilton, especially p. 105 of the digital report/col. 105 section.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — exact contemporary parliamentary wording verified.
sources.source_identity: House of Commons Hansard, Indian Financial Statement, 21 June 1877; statement by Lord George Hamilton.
sources.edition: Hansard, House of Commons, 21 June 1877, vol. 235, cols. 92–144.
sources.what_passage_establishes: The debate records that the earlier guaranteed-company system borrowed indirectly through railway companies and that from 1867 the Indian Government instead went into the money market itself, borrowing at a lower rate and expending the funds itself. The same financial statement records that the Government had raised £5,000,000 in Britain in 1874 and the Indian Government £2,500,000 in that year for Bengal famine needs, and in 1877 sought authority to borrow up to £5,000,000 on the credit of Indian revenues.
sources.evidence_limits: The transition passage establishes the institutional financing change but does not identify a particular 1877 lender, issue price, maturity, or settlement date. The £5,000,000 requested in 1877 was a borrowing authority for Government service and famine-related needs, not evidence that the entire amount was immediately issued or that it financed railway construction.
scholarly_references: Hansard, House of Commons, 21 June 1877, vol. 235, cols. 92–144.
sources.publication_status: A-grade — contemporary parliamentary primary passage locked; distinct 1877 borrowing-authority and institutional-transition evidence.

book_1_integration.part_label: Book 1 — Part II: National banking and nineteenth-century state finance

sources.title: India Public Works, 1878: Parliamentary Inquiry into Loan-Financed Works
sources.historical_claim: In January 1878 Parliament formally moved for a Select Committee to examine the expediency of constructing Indian public works with money raised by loan, amid a stated concern over the financial burden of public-works expenditure and the post-Mutiny shift from guaranteed companies toward State borrowing.
sources.verification_status: Contemporary parliamentary primary evidence verified from House of Commons Hansard, 22 January 1878.
sources.bn_title: ভারতের জনপূর্ত, ১৮৭৮: ঋণ-অর্থায়িত জনপূর্ত নিয়ে সংসদীয় তদন্ত
sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৮৭৮ সালের জানুয়ারিতে ভারতীয় জনপূর্ত ঋণের অর্থে নির্মাণের যৌক্তিকতা পরীক্ষা করতে সংসদে একটি সিলেক্ট কমিটি গঠনের প্রস্তাব ওঠে; একই বিতর্কে গ্যারান্টিযুক্ত কোম্পানি থেকে সরকারি ঋণগ্রহণে রূপান্তর এবং এর আর্থিক বোঝা নিয়ে আলোচনা হয়।
sources.notes: This record is distinct from the 1877 borrowing-authority record: it captures the 1878 parliamentary institutional response and proposed scrutiny of loan-financed public works. The debate also gives a retrospective explanation of the transition from guaranteed railway companies to State borrowing.
sources.primary_passage: That was the origin of guaranteeing railways in India.
sources.passage_locator: Hansard, House of Commons, 22 January 1878, 'Motion for a Select Committee', vol. 237, cols. 323–356; Lord George Hamilton's opening statement, especially cols. 323–325.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — contemporary parliamentary text verified.
sources.source_identity: House of Commons Hansard, Motion for a Select Committee on East India (Public Works), 22 January 1878; motion by Lord George Hamilton.
sources.edition: Hansard, House of Commons, 22 January 1878, vol. 237, cols. 323–356.
sources.what_passage_establishes: The debate records the historical origin of India's railway guarantee system and explains that the post-Mutiny public-works system drew on two sources of capital: guaranteed-company capital and loans raised in the market by the State. It also records the formal motion to inquire into the expediency of constructing public works in India with money raised on loan.
sources.evidence_limits: The quoted sentence alone establishes only the stated origin of the guarantee system; the broader institutional and financing claims depend on the surrounding Hansard passage. It does not establish a particular 1878 loan issue, lender, interest rate, price, or settlement date, and the Select Committee motion itself is not evidence that all proposed borrowing was actually undertaken.
scholarly_references: Hansard, House of Commons, 22 January 1878, vol. 237, cols. 323–356.
sources.publication_status: A-grade — contemporary parliamentary primary evidence; documents the 1878 parliamentary scrutiny of loan-financed Indian public works and the institutional history of State borrowing.

sources.title: India Finance, 1879: £5 Million Indian Loan Issued at 94¾
sources.historical_claim: The Government of India issued a £5,000,000 loan in India in 1879; £4,000,000 of that issue was accepted at 94¾, while the remaining £1,000,000 had not yet been secured at the time of the statement.
sources.verification_status: Primary contemporary parliamentary record verified in Hansard, including the reported amount issued and the accepted issue price.
sources.bn_title: ভারতীয় অর্থব্যবস্থা, ১৮৭৯: ৫০ লক্ষ পাউন্ডের ভারতীয় ঋণ ৯৪¾ দরে ইস্যু
sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৮৭৯ সালে ভারত সরকার ভারতে ৫০ লক্ষ পাউন্ডের একটি ঋণ ইস্যু করে; এর ৪০ লক্ষ পাউন্ড ৯৪¾ দরে গৃহীত হয়, আর বিবৃতির সময় অবশিষ্ট ১০ লক্ষ পাউন্ডের ব্যবস্থা এখনো সম্পন্ন হয়নি।
sources.notes: This record is distinct from the 1878 parliamentary inquiry/policy record because it documents an actual 1879 Indian loan issue and gives a specific accepted issue price. The statement also distinguishes the £5,000,000 Indian borrowing from the separate proposed £2,000,000 temporary advance from England.
sources.primary_passage: Accordingly, the amount to be borrowed in India was £5,000,000, and a loan was issued to that amount; £4,000,000 of that loan was accepted at 94¾.
sources.passage_locator: Hansard, House of Commons, 22 May 1879, vol. 246, col. 1067, within the East India Revenue Accounts—Financial Statement debate.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — exact contemporary parliamentary statement records the Indian loan issue and the accepted amount/price.
sources.source_identity: East India Revenue Accounts—Financial Statement, statement by Mr. E. Stanhope, House of Commons, 22 May 1879; contemporary parliamentary record reporting the 1879 Government of India loan issued in India.
sources.edition: Hansard, House of Commons Debates, 22 May 1879, vol. 246, cols. 1040–1093.
sources.what_passage_establishes: The passage establishes that the Government of India actually issued a £5,000,000 loan in India in 1879 and that £4,000,000 of that loan was accepted at an issue price of 94¾. The surrounding statement also says the remaining £1,000,000 was not yet known to have been obtained.
sources.evidence_limits: The passage establishes the reported issue amount and accepted price but does not identify individual lenders or subscribers, allotment details, maturity, coupon rate, or the complete final disposition of the remaining £1,000,000. It should not be used to infer a particular private banking house's role without separate primary evidence.
scholarly_references: Hansard, House of Commons Debates, 22 May 1879, vol. 246, cols. 1040–1093.
John Strachey and Sir Richard Temple, financial discussions on Indian public finance and borrowing in the late nineteenth century.
sources.publication_status: A-grade — contemporary parliamentary evidence directly records the 1879 Indian loan issue and accepted issue price; lender-level attribution remains outside the passage.

sources.title: United Kingdom Loan to India, 1880: £2.049 Million Funded as Repayable Debt
sources.historical_claim: By March 1880, the United Kingdom had created £2,049,000 of Funded Debt to finance the £2,000,000 loan advanced to India, and the parliamentary statement classified that advance as repayable debt.
sources.verification_status: Primary contemporary parliamentary financial statement verified in Hansard.
sources.bn_title: ভারতকে যুক্তরাজ্যের ঋণ, ১৮৮০: ২০.৪৯ লক্ষ পাউন্ডের তহবিলভুক্ত পুনঃপরিশোধযোগ্য ঋণ
sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৮৮০ সালের মার্চে যুক্তরাজ্য ভারতকে দেওয়া ২০ লক্ষ পাউন্ডের ঋণের অর্থায়নের জন্য ২০.৪৯ লক্ষ পাউন্ডের Funded Debt সৃষ্টি করেছিল এবং সংসদীয় বিবৃতিতে এই অগ্রিমকে পুনঃপরিশোধযোগ্য ঋণ হিসেবে শ্রেণিবদ্ধ করা হয়।
sources.notes: This is distinct from the 1879 Indian-market loan issue: it documents the British-side financing structure of the separate interest-free advance to India and its treatment in the UK public debt accounts.
sources.primary_passage: The Funded Debt, of course, includes £2,049,000 of Stock created for the purpose of the loan of £2,000,000 to India.
sources.passage_locator: Hansard, House of Commons, 11 March 1880, vol. 251, cols. 827–828, Ways and Means—Financial Statement.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — contemporary parliamentary statement explicitly identifies the Stock created to finance the £2,000,000 loan to India.
sources.source_identity: UK Ways and Means—Financial Statement, House of Commons, 11 March 1880; statement on Funded and Unfunded Debt and the £2,000,000 loan to India.
sources.edition: Hansard, House of Commons Debates, 11 March 1880, vol. 251, cols. 817–837.
sources.what_passage_establishes: The passage establishes that £2,049,000 of UK Funded Debt had been created specifically to finance the £2,000,000 loan to India. The same financial statement classifies the £2,000,000 as repayable debt and distinguishes it from non-recoverable war expenditure.
sources.evidence_limits: The passage establishes the UK-side debt financing and accounting treatment, not the identity of subscribers to the UK Stock, the Indian use of every pound, or the final repayment history. It also does not establish that this UK financing replaced Indian-market borrowing generally.
scholarly_references: Hansard, House of Commons Debates, 11 March 1880, vol. 251, cols. 817–837.
sources.publication_status: A-grade — direct contemporary parliamentary financial statement; precise UK debt amount and purpose locked.

sources.title: India Finance, 1881: 300-Lakh Public Works Loan Raised in India at 4 Per Cent
sources.historical_claim: In July 1881 the Government of India raised a 300-lakh loan in India for Public Works at 4 per cent interest, at an issue price of 105 3–16.
sources.verification_status: Contemporary parliamentary financial statement records the July 1881 loan, its purpose, interest rate, and issue price.
sources.bn_title: ভারতের অর্থব্যবস্থা, ১৮৮১: ভারতে ৪ শতাংশে ৩০০ লাখের পাবলিক ওয়ার্কস ঋণ
sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৮৮১ সালের জুলাইয়ে ভারত সরকার ভারতে পাবলিক ওয়ার্কসের জন্য ৪ শতাংশ সুদে ৩০০ লাখের ঋণ গ্রহণ করে, যার ইস্যু মূল্য ছিল ১০৫ ৩/১৬।
sources.notes: The Annual Financial Statement delivered on 22 August 1881 records three loans issued during the preceding 15 months and specifically states that in July 1881 a 300-lakh loan for Public Works was raised in India at 4 per cent, at 105 3–16. This record isolates the distinct July 1881 Indian Public Works borrowing event.
sources.primary_passage: In July, 1881, again, a loan of 300 lakhs for Public Works was raised in India; and, although it was reduced to 4 per cent interest, the price at which it was raised was 105 3–16, as against 103 3–16 last year.
sources.passage_locator: Hansard, House of Commons, 22 August 1881, vol. 265, cols. 628–698; Annual Financial Statement.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — contemporary parliamentary financial statement gives amount, purpose, market/location, interest rate, and issue price.
sources.source_identity: House of Commons, Annual Financial Statement, 22 August 1881; statement by the Marquess of Hartington concerning India Finance and East India Revenue Accounts.
sources.edition: Hansard, House of Commons, 22 August 1881, vol. 265, cols. 628–698.
sources.publisher: Parliament of the United Kingdom; Hansard

sources.evidence_limits: The passage does not identify individual subscribers or underwriting houses, does not give maturity or coupon terms beyond the stated interest rate, and does not by itself establish the full allocation of proceeds among particular public-works projects. It also does not establish that all Indian borrowing was conducted on these terms.
scholarly_references: Hansard, House of Commons, Annual Financial Statement, 22 August 1881, vol. 265, cols. 628–698.

sources.title: Bank of Japan, 1882
sources.historical_claim: The Bank of Japan was established under the Bank of Japan Act of 1882 and began operations on 10 October 1882 as Japan's central bank.
sources.verification_status: Primary-source / contemporary official record verified
sources.bn_title: ব্যাংক অব জাপান, ১৮৮২
sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৮৮২ সালের ব্যাংক অব জাপান আইনের অধীনে ব্যাংক অব জাপান প্রতিষ্ঠিত হয় এবং ১০ অক্টোবর ১৮৮২ তারিখে জাপানের কেন্দ্রীয় ব্যাংক হিসেবে কার্যক্রম শুরু করে।

sources.title: Southern Maratta Railway, 1882: Private Capital Substituted for Direct Government Borrowing
sources.historical_claim: In May 1882 the Government of India approved an exceptional Southern Maratta Railway financing arrangement in which a private company would raise the capital and construct and operate the line, instead of the Government borrowing directly; the company was promised at least 4 per cent for its first five years, with a 3½ per cent base rate plus one-fourth of net receipts thereafter.
sources.verification_status: Contemporary parliamentary statement by the Secretary of State for India records the financing arrangement, its rationale, and the Government's limited guarantee terms.
sources.bn_title: সাউদার্ন মারাঠা রেলওয়ে, ১৮৮২: সরাসরি সরকারি ঋণের বদলে বেসরকারি মূলধন
sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৮৮২ সালের মে মাসে ভারত সরকার সাউদার্ন মারাঠা রেলওয়ের জন্য একটি ব্যতিক্রমী অর্থায়ন ব্যবস্থা অনুমোদন করে, যেখানে সরকার সরাসরি ঋণ নেওয়ার বদলে একটি বেসরকারি কোম্পানিকে মূলধন সংগ্রহ, রেলপথ নির্মাণ ও পরিচালনার দায়িত্ব দেয়; প্রথম পাঁচ বছরে কোম্পানিকে অন্তত ৪ শতাংশ রিটার্নের নিশ্চয়তা দেওয়া হয়।
sources.notes: The Secretary of State stated that the line could not be constructed under the usual rule allowing borrowing for works likely to be remunerative because it would absorb the provision for protective works. The Government therefore accepted an offer for a company to raise the money and construct and work the line. The company was promised a 3½ per cent rate, with one-fourth of net receipts, but was given assurance of at least 4 per cent during the first five years to attract investors. The statement expressly contrasts this with State Railways normally financed by direct Government agency.
sources.primary_passage: the effect of the arrangement is that the money is raised by private capitalists instead of by the direct agency of the Government
sources.passage_locator: Hansard, House of Commons, 25 May 1882, vol. 269, cols. 1596–1599; Southern Maratta Railway Company question and answer.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — contemporary Secretary of State statement directly records the substitution of private capital for direct Government agency and the associated limited guarantee terms.
sources.source_identity: House of Commons, statement by the Marquess of Hartington, Secretary of State for India, concerning the Southern Maratta Railway concession, 25 May 1882.
sources.edition: Hansard, House of Commons, 25 May 1882, vol. 269, cols. 1596–1599.
sources.publisher: Parliament of the United Kingdom; Hansard
sources.what_passage_establishes: The passage establishes that, for this exceptional railway case, capital was to be raised by private investors rather than through the direct borrowing agency of the Government, while the Government accepted a limited return guarantee and retained ownership of the line.
sources.evidence_limits: The passage does not identify individual investors, banks, underwriters, total subscribed capital, issue price, or a completed loan transaction. It establishes a financing/concession structure and contingent Government obligation, not a conventional sovereign loan. The Secretary of State expressly stated that the arrangement was exceptional and was not intended as a general guarantee policy.
scholarly_references: Hansard, House of Commons, 25 May 1882, vol. 269, cols. 1596–1599.
sources.publication_status: A-grade — contemporary parliamentary statement directly records the exceptional private-capital financing structure and limited Government guarantee; individual investor and underwriting identities remain unestablished.

sources.title: India Public Works Loan, 1883: 2½ Crore Rupee Loan to Be Issued in India
sources.historical_claim: In April 1883 the Government of India announced that a 2½-crore-rupee public-works loan would be issued in India, following the established policy against contracting gold debt dischargeable from silver assets; the works were railways expected to earn enough return to cover the loan interest.
sources.verification_status: Contemporary parliamentary statement by the Under Secretary of State for India records the proposed amount, Indian issue location, policy rationale, and intended railway purpose.
sources.bn_title: ভারতের পাবলিক ওয়ার্কস ঋণ, ১৮৮৩: ভারতে ২.৫ কোটি রুপির ঋণ ইস্যু
sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৮৮৩ সালের এপ্রিল মাসে ভারত সরকার ঘোষণা করে যে পাবলিক ওয়ার্কসের জন্য ২.৫ কোটি রুপির ঋণ ভারতে ইস্যু করা হবে; এই সিদ্ধান্ত ছিল রৌপ্য সম্পদ দিয়ে পরিশোধযোগ্য ঋণকে সোনাভিত্তিক ঋণে রূপান্তর না করার প্রতিষ্ঠিত নীতির সঙ্গে সামঞ্জস্যপূর্ণ।
sources.notes: On 13 April 1883 the Under Secretary of State for India stated that the Indian Government had announced a proposed 2½-crore-rupee public-works loan would be issued in India. He linked the decision to the policy of successive Secretaries of State and the 1878–9 Select Committee principle that it was undesirable to contract gold debts dischargeable from silver assets. In response to a question about the works, he stated they were railways expected to produce returns more than sufficient to pay the interest charged on the loan.
sources.primary_passage: the proposed loan of 2½ crores of rupees for public works will be issued in India
sources.passage_locator: Hansard, House of Commons, 13 April 1883, vol. 278, cols. 195–196; 'Indian Public Works—The Loan.'
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — contemporary parliamentary statement gives the proposed loan amount, issue location, policy rationale, and railway purpose.
sources.source_identity: House of Commons, statement by Mr. J. K. Cross, Under Secretary of State for India, 13 April 1883, concerning the proposed Indian Public Works loan.
sources.edition: Hansard, House of Commons, 13 April 1883, vol. 278, cols. 195–196.
sources.publisher: Parliament of the United Kingdom; Hansard
sources.what_passage_establishes: The passage establishes that the proposed 2½-crore-rupee public-works loan was to be issued in India and that this followed a deliberate policy against creating gold debt dischargeable from silver assets. The same exchange identifies the works as railways expected to generate returns sufficient to cover the loan interest.
sources.evidence_limits: The passage records an announced/proposed loan rather than independently proving final subscription, allotment, issue price, coupon, maturity, or subscriber identities. It does not establish that every public-works loan followed this policy or that the proposed amount was ultimately issued in exactly the stated form.
scholarly_references: Hansard, House of Commons, 13 April 1883, vol. 278, cols. 195–196.
sources.publication_status: A-grade — contemporary parliamentary statement directly records the announced Indian rupee loan and its financing-policy rationale; final issue terms remain a separate verification target.

sources.title: India Paper Currency, 1884: Reserve Rule and Government Securities Backing
sources.historical_claim: In July 1884 the Under Secretary of State for India described India's paper-currency reserve regime: Government was required to retain coin or bullion equal to the notes issued, except that up to six crores of rupees could be invested in Government of India securities; gold was not required as the reserve because the rupee was legal tender.
sources.verification_status: Contemporary parliamentary statement by the Under Secretary of State for India records the reserve rule and the statutory basis then governing Indian paper currency.
sources.bn_title: ভারতের কাগুজে মুদ্রা, ১৮৮৪: রিজার্ভ বিধি ও সরকারি সিকিউরিটিতে সমর্থন
sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৮৮৪ সালের জুলাইয়ে ভারতের কাগুজে মুদ্রার রিজার্ভ ব্যবস্থার বর্ণনায় বলা হয় যে সরকারকে ইস্যুকৃত নোটের পূর্ণ মূল্যের সমপরিমাণ মুদ্রা বা বুলিয়ন ধরে রাখতে হতো; তবে সর্বোচ্চ ৬ কোটি রুপি ভারত সরকারের সিকিউরিটিতে বিনিয়োগ করা যেত।
sources.notes: On 8 July 1884 the Under Secretary of State for India, J. K. Cross, described the Indian paper-currency reserve arrangement in Parliament. He stated that coin or bullion had to be retained to the full value of notes issued, subject to an exception allowing up to six crores of rupees to be invested in Government of India securities. He also stated that the reserve was not necessarily gold because the rupee was legal tender in India, and identified the Government of India Act 20 of 1882 as containing the conditions of guarantee.
sources.primary_passage: Government must retain coin or bullion as a reserve to the full value of the notes issued; except a sum of six crores of rupees, or nominally £6,000,000 sterling, which may be invested in securities of the Government of India.
sources.passage_locator: Hansard, House of Commons, 8 July 1884, vol. 290, col. 505; 'India (Finance, &c.)—The Paper Currency.'
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — contemporary parliamentary statement records the reserve requirement and six-crore exception.
sources.source_identity: House of Commons, statement by Mr. J. K. Cross, Under Secretary of State for India, 8 July 1884, answering questions on the Indian paper currency.
sources.edition: Hansard, House of Commons, 8 July 1884, vol. 290, col. 505.
sources.publisher: Parliament of the United Kingdom; Hansard
sources.what_passage_establishes: The passage establishes the contemporary official description of India's paper-currency backing rule: full-value coin or bullion reserve, with up to six crores of rupees permitted in Government of India securities. The same answer states that gold was not mandatory because the rupee was legal tender and identifies the Government of India Act 20 of 1882 as the source of the guarantee conditions.
sources.evidence_limits: The passage is a contemporary parliamentary statement describing the operating/legal framework; it is not itself the 1882 Act text. It does not establish actual reserve composition on a particular date, note circulation beyond the figures separately stated in the answer, or the subsequent development of the currency system.
scholarly_references: Hansard, House of Commons, 8 July 1884, vol. 290, col. 505.
sources.publication_status: A-grade — direct contemporary parliamentary statement locks the reserve rule and six-crore securities exception; the underlying 1882 statutory text remains the preferred supplementary primary-law check.

sources.title: Rothschild Loan to the Egyptian Government, 1884
sources.historical_claim: Messrs. Rothschild arranged a substantial temporary loan for the Egyptian Government in early 1884, with the British Government informed of and expressing approval for the transaction.
sources.verification_status: Contemporary House of Commons record reproduces Government correspondence with Sir Nathaniel Rothschild concerning the proposed £1,000,000 loan and records the Government's knowledge and favorable view.
sources.bn_title: মিশরীয় সরকারকে রথসচাইল্ড ঋণ, ১৮৮৪
sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৮৮৪ সালের শুরুতে রথসচাইল্ডরা মিশরীয় সরকারকে একটি উল্লেখযোগ্য অস্থায়ী ঋণের ব্যবস্থা করে; সমকালীন সংসদীয় নথিতে ব্রিটিশ সরকারের অবগত থাকা ও অনুকূল মতামত নথিভুক্ত হয়েছে।
sources.notes: Hansard records Lord Granville's 22 and 28 January 1884 letters to Sir Nathaniel Rothschild. The first states that Mr. Vincent had approached Rothschild for a £1,000,000 loan to be repaid in six months and that the Cabinet was favorable to Rothschild proceeding if terms could be agreed. The second thanks Rothschild for information on negotiations and treats repayment conditions as a business detail. The record does not establish the final contractual terms.
sources.primary_passage: the Cabinet expressed itself in favour of Sir Evelyn Baring's having done so, and we are glad at your agreeing to the request if you find that you will be able to come to terms with the Egyptian Government.
sources.passage_locator: House of Commons, 8 February 1884, Egypt (Finance, &c.)—Loan by Messrs. Rothschild, Hansard vol. 284, cols. 309–313; Government letters of 22 and 28 January 1884 read into the debate.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — contemporary parliamentary reproduction of Government correspondence.
sources.source_identity: House of Commons debate, 8 February 1884, Egypt (Finance, &c.)—Loan by Messrs. Rothschild.
sources.edition: Hansard, House of Commons, 8 February 1884, vol. 284, cols. 309–313.
sources.what_passage_establishes: The passage establishes Cabinet awareness and favorable disposition toward Rothschild advancing a £1,000,000 six-month loan to the Egyptian Government, subject to terms being agreed.
sources.evidence_limits: It does not establish that the Cabinet guaranteed repayment, the final contractual terms, or broader British control over Egyptian finance.
scholarly_references: Hansard, House of Commons, 8 February 1884, Egypt (Finance, &c.)—Loan by Messrs. Rothschild.
sources.publication_status: A-grade — direct contemporary parliamentary evidence; final contract remains a useful supplementary archival target.
