sources.title: India Public Works Finance, 1885: £10 Million London Sterling-Borrowing Authority
sources.historical_claim: In May 1885 Parliament was asked to authorize the Secretary of State for India to borrow up to £10 million in the London market over three years for Indian public works, marking an explicit policy shift from the recent practice of rupee borrowing in India toward sterling borrowing in England when the interest-rate advantage justified the exchange risk.
sources.verification_status: Contemporary parliamentary statement by the Under Secretary of State for India records the proposed borrowing authority, its public-works purpose, and the stated change from rupee borrowing in India to sterling borrowing in England.
sources.bn_title: ভারতের পাবলিক ওয়ার্কস অর্থায়ন, ১৮৮৫: লন্ডনে ১ কোটি পাউন্ড স্টার্লিং ঋণগ্রহণের ক্ষমতা
sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৮৮৫ সালের মে মাসে ভারতীয় পাবলিক ওয়ার্কসের জন্য তিন বছরে সর্বোচ্চ ১ কোটি পাউন্ড স্টার্লিং লন্ডন বাজার থেকে ঋণ নেওয়ার ক্ষমতা চাওয়া হয়; এটি ভারতে রুপি ঋণের বদলে প্রয়োজনে ইংল্যান্ডে স্টার্লিং ঋণ নেওয়ার নীতিগত পরিবর্তনকে স্পষ্ট করে।
sources.notes: On 21 May 1885 J. K. Cross explained the East India Loan Bill. He said the Secretary of State needed power to borrow £10,000,000 in the London market within three years, charging interest to Indian revenues. He expressly described the proposal to borrow in sterling in England instead of rupees in India as a distinct change in policy, justified when the interest-rate differential was large enough to compensate for exchange risk. The same speech states that Public Works and East Indian Railway borrowings had been £11.13 million in 1880–83.
sources.primary_passage: We now ask for permission to borrow in sterling in England, when we consider it desirable, in place of borrowing in rupees in India, and as this is a distinct change in policy
sources.passage_locator: Hansard, House of Commons, 21 May 1885, vol. 298, cols. 1042–1045; Bill 109, Second Reading. The £10,000,000 authority is stated at col. 1043 and the policy-change explanation at col. 1044.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — contemporary parliamentary statement directly records the £10 million proposed authority and the explicit shift toward sterling borrowing in England when economically justified.
sources.source_identity: House of Commons, statement by Mr. J. K. Cross, Under Secretary of State for India, during the Second Reading of Bill 109, 21 May 1885.
sources.edition: Hansard, House of Commons, 21 May 1885, vol. 298, cols. 1042–1077; Bill 109, Second Reading.
sources.publisher: Parliament of the United Kingdom; Hansard
sources.what_passage_establishes: The passage establishes that the Secretary of State sought parliamentary power to borrow up to £10 million in the London market within three years for works sanctioned by the Government of India, and that borrowing in sterling in England rather than rupees in India was explicitly presented as a distinct policy change. The statement also explains the trade-off: lower sterling interest costs versus exchange-rate risk.
sources.evidence_limits: This record establishes the proposed parliamentary borrowing authority and the policy rationale; it does not by itself prove that the full £10 million was subsequently borrowed, identify lenders or underwriters, establish final issue price/coupon/maturity, or show that sterling borrowing permanently replaced Indian rupee borrowing.
scholarly_references: Hansard, House of Commons, 21 May 1885, vol. 298, cols. 1042–1045.
sources.publication_status: A-grade — contemporary parliamentary evidence directly locks the proposed £10 million authority and the stated policy shift toward London sterling borrowing; actual subsequent loan issuance remains a separate verification target.

sources.title: Rothschild Temporary Advance to the Egyptian Government, 1885
sources.historical_claim: Messrs. Rothschild supplied or continued a temporary financial advance to the Egyptian Government in 1885, with the British Government acknowledging that the advance met Egypt's temporary necessities while its detailed terms were settled directly between Rothschild and Egypt.
sources.verification_status: Contemporary House of Commons record directly confirms the advance and the parties' settlement of its terms.
sources.bn_title: মিশরীয় সরকারকে রথসচাইল্ডের অস্থায়ী অগ্রিম, ১৮৮৫
sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৮৮৫ সালে রথসচাইল্ডরা মিশরীয় সরকারকে অস্থায়ী আর্থিক অগ্রিম প্রদান বা অব্যাহত রাখে; ব্রিটিশ সরকার সংসদে এই অগ্রিমের কথা স্বীকার করে এবং জানায় যে এর শর্ত রথসচাইল্ড ও মিশরীয় সরকার সরাসরি নির্ধারণ করেছে।
sources.notes: The Chancellor of the Exchequer stated in the House of Commons on 13 April 1885 that Messrs. Rothschild, knowing the British Government regarded itself as pledged to the pending Egypt legislation, had supplied the temporary necessities of the Egyptian Government; he said the transaction's details had been settled between Rothschild and the Egyptian Government. This record is stronger than a later narrative but does not expose the underlying private contract.
sources.primary_passage: Messrs. Rothschild are aware that we regard ourselves pledged to the Bill now before Parliament, and with this knowledge have supplied the temporary necessities of the Egyptian Government.
sources.passage_locator: House of Commons, 13 April 1885, The Egyptian Loan—Messrs. Rothschild, Hansard vol. 296, cols. 1457–1458.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — contemporary parliamentary statement; private transaction terms remain outside the parliamentary record.
sources.source_identity: House of Commons debate, 13 April 1885, The Egyptian Loan—Messrs. Rothschild.
sources.edition: Hansard, House of Commons, 13 April 1885, vol. 296, cols. 1457–1458.
sources.what_passage_establishes: The passage establishes that Rothschild supplied temporary financial necessities to the Egyptian Government and that the transaction's details were settled directly between the two parties.
sources.evidence_limits: It does not establish the precise amount, interest rate, security, maturity, or whether the advance was legally a loan in the final contractual form.
scholarly_references: Hansard, House of Commons, 13 April 1885, The Egyptian Loan—Messrs. Rothschild.
sources.publication_status: A-grade — direct contemporary parliamentary evidence locked; private contract remains a supplementary archival target.

book_1_integration.part_label: Book 1 — Part II: National banking and nineteenth-century state finance

sources.title: East India Railways Loans, 1886: Proposed £10 Million Direct Borrowing Authority
sources.historical_claim: In June 1886 Parliament considered authorising the Secretary of State in Council of India to raise up to £10 million for the construction, extension, and equipment of railways in India on the security of Indian revenues; the proposal was subsequently not pursued, with the Under Secretary explaining that the intended mechanism was direct borrowing by the Secretary of State and onward lending to railway companies to reduce the charge on Indian revenues.
sources.verification_status: Contemporary parliamentary record directly preserves both the 4 June committee resolution proposing the £10 million authority and the 11 June official explanation that the Bill would not proceed and why.
sources.bn_title: ইস্ট ইন্ডিয়া রেলওয়েজ ঋণ, ১৮৮৬: ১ কোটি পাউন্ডের প্রস্তাবিত সরাসরি ঋণগ্রহণের ক্ষমতা
sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৮৮৬ সালের জুনে ভারতীয় রাজস্বের জামানতে ভারতে রেলওয়ে নির্মাণ, সম্প্রসারণ ও সরঞ্জামায়নের জন্য সর্বোচ্চ ১ কোটি পাউন্ড ঋণ তোলার ক্ষমতা দেওয়ার প্রস্তাব সংসদে বিবেচিত হয়; পরে প্রস্তাবটি আর এগোয়নি, এবং আন্ডার সেক্রেটারি ব্যাখ্যা করেন যে উদ্দেশ্য ছিল সচিবের সরাসরি ঋণগ্রহণ করে রেলওয়ে কোম্পানিগুলোকে ঋণ দেওয়া, যাতে ভারতীয় রাজস্বের ওপর ব্যয় কমে।
sources.notes: On 4 June 1886 the Commons resolved in Committee that it was expedient to authorise the Secretary of State in Council of India to raise up to £10,000,000 for the construction, extension, and equipment of railways in India on the security of Indian revenues. On 11 June the Under Secretary of State for India stated that the Government did not intend to proceed with the Bill. He explained that the intended borrowing power would have allowed the Secretary of State to raise money directly and lend it to railway companies, because the charge on Indian revenues was expected to be lower than under company borrowing. The 11 June statement also reported about £7.5 million of unexpended borrowing power under previous Acts.
sources.primary_passage: Resolved, That it is expedient to authorise the Secretary of State in Council of India to raise any sum or sums of money, not exceeding in the whole £10,000,000, for the construction, extension, and equipment of Railways in India, on the security of the Revenues of India.
sources.passage_locator: Hansard, House of Commons, 4 June 1886, vol. 306, col. 1112, 'East India Railways [Loans].' The resolution was considered in Committee and reported for subsequent consideration.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — contemporary parliamentary resolution records the proposed £10 million authority; the 11 June 1886 official statement separately locks the decision not to proceed and the intended direct-borrowing mechanism.
sources.source_identity: House of Commons, East India Railways [Loans], Committee resolution, 4 June 1886; supplemented by the Under Secretary of State for India's statement on 11 June 1886 concerning the decision not to proceed with the Bill and its proposed financing mechanism.
sources.edition: Hansard, House of Commons, 4 June 1886, vol. 306, col. 1112; and House of Commons, 11 June 1886, statement on the East India Railways (Loans) Bill.
sources.publisher: Parliament of the United Kingdom; Hansard
sources.what_passage_establishes: The 4 June passage establishes that Parliament formally considered a borrowing authority of up to £10 million, secured on Indian revenues, specifically for railway construction, extension, and equipment. The 11 June statement establishes that the Bill was not to proceed and explains that the proposed policy was for the Secretary of State to borrow directly and lend to railway companies in order to reduce the charge on Indian revenues.
sources.evidence_limits: This record does not establish that the £10 million authority became law or that the full amount was raised. The proposal was explicitly not pursued as a Bill by 11 June 1886. It therefore establishes a proposed financing mechanism and parliamentary consideration, not an executed loan or enacted borrowing power.
scholarly_references: Hansard, House of Commons, 4 June 1886, vol. 306, col. 1112.
Hansard, House of Commons, 11 June 1886, statement on the East India Railways (Loans) Bill.
sources.publication_status: A-grade — contemporary parliamentary resolution and subsequent official explanation securely establish the proposed £10 million railway-borrowing mechanism and its abandonment; no executed £10 million loan is inferred.

sources.title: Bengal-Nagpur Railway Loan, 1887: Government-Guaranteed Interest and Rothschild Commission
sources.historical_claim: In 1887 the Bengal-Nagpur Railway Company was authorised to raise £3 million on 4 per cent guaranteed interest, with the Indian Government providing the guarantee; Parliament recorded that Messrs. Rothschild & Co. were authorised to receive and in fact received a 1 per cent commission, and the Secretary of State considered this the most judicious and economical method of raising the money.
sources.verification_status: Contemporary House of Commons statement directly records the £3 million amount, 4 per cent perpetual guarantee, one-fourth profit participation, the 1 per cent Rothschild commission, and the official rationale for the financing method.
sources.bn_title: বেঙ্গল-নাগপুর রেলওয়ে ঋণ, ১৮৮৭: সরকারি গ্যারান্টিযুক্ত সুদ ও রথসচাইল্ড কমিশন
sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৮৮৭ সালে বেঙ্গল-নাগপুর রেলওয়ে কোম্পানিকে ৪ শতাংশ চিরস্থায়ী গ্যারান্টিযুক্ত সুদের ভিত্তিতে ৩০ লক্ষ পাউন্ড সংগ্রহের অনুমতি দেওয়া হয়; ভারত সরকার এই গ্যারান্টির সঙ্গে যুক্ত ছিল। সংসদে নথিভুক্ত হয় যে মেসার্স রথসচাইল্ড অ্যান্ড কোম্পানিকে ১ শতাংশ কমিশন দেওয়ার অনুমতি ছিল এবং তা বাস্তবে দেওয়া হয়; অর্থ সংগ্রহের এই পদ্ধতিকে সেক্রেটারি অব স্টেট সবচেয়ে বিচক্ষণ ও অর্থসাশ্রয়ী বলে বিবেচনা করেছিলেন।
sources.notes: On 4 March 1887 Dr. Tanner asked the Under Secretary of State for India whether £3,000,000 was to be raised on 4 per cent guaranteed interest in perpetuity by the Indian Government and one-fourth of railway profits, whether Rothschild & Co. underwrote the loan, and whether they received a commission. Sir John Gorst answered that the first proposition was true, the underwriting proposition was false, and that the company was authorised to pay Rothschild & Co. a 1 per cent commission, which was in fact paid. He stated that the money was raised in this mode because, in the Secretary of State in Council's opinion, it was the most judicious and economical method.
sources.primary_passage: The Bengal-Nagpur Railway Company was authorized to pay a commission of 1 per cent to Messrs. Rothschild & Co.; and the amount was, in fact, paid. The money was raised in this mode, because, in the opinion of the Secretary of State in Council, it was the most judicious and economical mode of raising it.
sources.passage_locator: Hansard, House of Commons, 4 March 1887, vol. 311, cols. 1257–1258, 'India (Railways)—Bengal-Nagpur Railway.'
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — contemporary parliamentary answer records the commission and official financing rationale.
sources.source_identity: House of Commons, answer by Sir John Gorst, Under Secretary of State for India, 4 March 1887, concerning the Bengal-Nagpur Railway financing.
sources.edition: Hansard, House of Commons, 4 March 1887, vol. 311, cols. 1257–1258.
sources.publisher: Parliament of the United Kingdom; Hansard
sources.what_passage_establishes: The passage establishes that the Bengal-Nagpur Railway financing involved a £3 million raising on 4 per cent guaranteed interest in perpetuity, and that Rothschild & Co. received a 1 per cent commission authorised by the company. It also establishes the contemporary official rationale that this method was considered the most judicious and economical.
sources.evidence_limits: The passage does not establish that Rothschild & Co. underwrote the loan; the Under Secretary explicitly answered that proposition 'No.' It also does not by itself establish the complete loan contract, subscription allocation, final issue price, or the full legal mechanics of the guarantee.
scholarly_references: Hansard, House of Commons, 4 March 1887, vol. 311, cols. 1257–1258.
sources.publication_status: A-grade — direct contemporary parliamentary evidence locks the financing terms reported to Parliament and the 1 per cent commission; the record explicitly does not support an underwriting claim.

sources.title: Conversion of India Stock Act, 1887: Conversion of 4 Per Cent India Stock into 3½ Per Cent Stock
sources.historical_claim: Parliament enacted a conversion mechanism allowing holders of 4 per cent India Stock to exchange it for 3½ per cent India Stock, restructuring the interest burden on existing Indian government stock.
sources.verification_status: Primary parliamentary legislation verified through the House of Commons passage of the Bill and independent statutory identification of the enacted Conversion of India Stock Act 1887, 50 & 51 Vict. c. 11.
sources.bn_title: কনভার্সন অব ইন্ডিয়া স্টক অ্যাক্ট, ১৮৮৭: ৪ শতাংশ ভারতীয় স্টককে ৩½ শতাংশ স্টকে রূপান্তর
sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৮৮৭ সালের আইনে ৪ শতাংশ ভারতীয় স্টকের ধারকদের ৩½ শতাংশ ভারতীয় স্টকে রূপান্তরের ব্যবস্থা করা হয়, ফলে বিদ্যমান ভারতীয় সরকারি স্টকের সুদের বোঝা পুনর্গঠিত হয়।
sources.notes: The 19 May 1887 House of Commons record shows the Bill being considered and amended, including provisions for exchange into India Three and a-half Per Cent Stock. Sir John Gorst stated that 3½ per cent and 4 per cent Stock were then practically of equal value and supported a provision facilitating conversion for certain small holders. Independent statutory listings identify the measure as the Conversion of India Stock Act 1887, 50 & 51 Vict. c. 11. The record should not be used to infer the aggregate amount actually converted without a separate return or statutory/financial account.
sources.primary_passage: No doubt, at the present time, 3½ per cent Stock and 4 per cent Stock are practically of equal value; and by this clause, if the House should think fit to add it to the Bill, these persons will have the exchange effected without any expense or trouble on their part, or on the part of those who represent them.
sources.passage_locator: House of Commons, Hansard, 19 May 1887, vol. 315, cols. 625–626, East India Stock Conversion Bill; Bill subsequently enacted as Conversion of India Stock Act 1887, 50 & 51 Vict. c. 11.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — exact parliamentary wording and printed Hansard column locator verified; enactment independently identified in statutory records.
sources.source_identity: East India Stock Conversion Bill, House of Commons, 1887; enacted as Conversion of India Stock Act 1887, 50 & 51 Vict. c. 11.
sources.edition: Hansard, House of Commons, 19 May 1887, vol. 315, cols. 623–627; Conversion of India Stock Act 1887, 50 & 51 Vict. c. 11.
sources.what_passage_establishes: The passage establishes that Parliament was facilitating conversion of 4 per cent India Stock into 3½ per cent Stock and that the Government regarded the two stocks as practically equal in value at the time. The enacted Act provides the statutory basis for the conversion.
sources.evidence_limits: The cited parliamentary passage does not establish the total amount converted, the final aggregate saving to Indian revenues, the market price of every issue, or the distribution of conversion among holders. Those claims require separate primary financial returns or accounts.
scholarly_references: Hansard, House of Commons, 19 May 1887, vol. 315, cols. 623–627.
Conversion of India Stock Act 1887, 50 & 51 Vict. c. 11.
sources.publication_status: A-grade — parliamentary record plus independently identified enacted statute; quantitative conversion totals remain outside this record.

sources.title: India Famine Insurance Fund, 1887: No Surplus Available for the Famine Grant
sources.historical_claim: In 1887–8 the Government of India had no surplus from which the Famine Grant could be paid, and the Government stated that famine protection would instead be pursued through completion of protective railways as financial conditions permitted.
sources.verification_status: Verified against Hansard, House of Commons, 10 May 1887.
sources.bn_title: ভারতের দুর্ভিক্ষ বিমা তহবিল, ১৮৮৭: দুর্ভিক্ষ অনুদানের জন্য উদ্বৃত্ত অর্থ ছিল না
sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৮৮৭–৮ অর্থবছরে ভারতের সরকারের কাছে দুর্ভিক্ষ অনুদান দেওয়ার মতো কোনো উদ্বৃত্ত ছিল না; সরকার জানায় যে আর্থিক সামর্থ্য অনুযায়ী প্রতিরক্ষামূলক রেলপথ দ্রুত সম্পন্ন করার মাধ্যমে দুর্ভিক্ষের বিরুদ্ধে সুরক্ষা দেওয়া হবে।
sources.notes: This record is about fiscal allocation and the institutional form of famine protection, not a claim that the fund was spent on the Burmese War. The Under Secretary expressly rejected that allegation. The passage does not establish the full historical accounting of famine-insurance appropriations or the later interpretation that the 'fund' was not a separate cash fund.
sources.primary_passage: It is not true that the Famine Insurance Fund has been devoted to the Burmese War; but there is no surplus for 1887–8 out of which the Famine Grant can be paid. The Government of India seeks to protect the country against famine by completing the protective system of railways as rapidly as financial considerations will allow.
sources.passage_locator: House of Commons, Hansard, 10 May 1887, vol. 314, col. 1454, 'India—Indian Famine Insurance Fund'.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — contemporary ministerial statement.
sources.source_identity: Contemporary parliamentary statement by Sir John Gorst, Under Secretary of State for India.
sources.edition: Hansard, House of Commons, 10 May 1887, vol. 314, col. 1454.
sources.what_passage_establishes: The passage establishes the absence of surplus for the 1887–8 Famine Grant and the Government's stated reliance on protective railway completion as a famine-protection measure within financial constraints; it also expressly denies that the fund had been devoted to the Burmese War.
sources.evidence_limits: It does not establish the complete balance or history of the famine-insurance scheme, the exact amount appropriated in prior years, or whether protective railway expenditure was economically equivalent to a separate famine reserve.
scholarly_references: Hansard, House of Commons, 10 May 1887, vol. 314, col. 1454.
Hansard, House of Commons, 22 August 1881, discussion of the Famine Insurance allocation.
sources.publication_status: A-grade — direct contemporary parliamentary statement; historical limits explicitly qualified.

sources.title: Indian Railways Borrowing Powers, 1887: Proposed Legislation Still Under Consideration
sources.historical_claim: On 4 March 1887 the Under Secretary of State for India stated that a Bill concerning borrowing money for Indian Railways had been prepared by the previous Government, but that the question of proceeding with the measure was still under consideration by the Secretary of State.
sources.verification_status: Contemporary House of Commons primary evidence verified from Hansard, 4 March 1887.
sources.bn_title: ভারতীয় রেলওয়ের ঋণগ্রহণের ক্ষমতা, ১৮৮৭: প্রস্তাবিত আইন তখনও বিবেচনাধীন
sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৮৮৭ সালের ৪ মার্চ ভারতের আন্ডার সেক্রেটারি জানান যে ভারতীয় রেলওয়ের জন্য অর্থ ধার করার বিষয়ে আগের সরকার একটি বিল প্রস্তুত করেছিল, কিন্তু সেটি এগিয়ে নেওয়া হবে কি না—তা তখনও সেক্রেটারি অব স্টেটের বিবেচনাধীন ছিল।
sources.notes: This record is deliberately distinct from the 1886 East India Railways borrowing proposal and the 1887 Bengal-Nagpur financing record. It captures the subsequent 1887 legislative-status layer: Parliament was asked whether the Government would revive or introduce a Bill enabling London borrowing for Indian railways, and the official answer was that the matter remained under consideration. It therefore establishes policy/legislative status, not enacted borrowing authority or an executed loan.
sources.primary_passage: A Bill relating to the borrowing of money for Indian Railways was prepared by the late Government, and its object explained by Mr. Stafford Howard, on the 11th of June, 1886. The question of proceeding with this measure is still under the consideration of the Secretary of State.
sources.passage_locator: Hansard, House of Commons, 4 March 1887, vol. 311, col. 1272, 'Railways (India)—Borrowing Powers—Legislation'; question by Mr. Lionel Cohen and answer by Sir John Gorst.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — exact contemporary parliamentary wording verified.
sources.source_identity: House of Commons parliamentary question by Mr. Lionel Cohen and answer by Sir John Gorst, Under Secretary of State for India, 4 March 1887, concerning proposed legislation to enable London borrowing for Indian railways.
sources.edition: Hansard, House of Commons, 4 March 1887, vol. 311, col. 1272.
sources.publisher: Parliament of the United Kingdom; Hansard
sources.what_passage_establishes: The passage establishes that legislation enabling borrowing for Indian Railways had been prepared by the previous Government and that, as of 4 March 1887, the Secretary of State had not yet decided to proceed with it.
sources.evidence_limits: The passage does not establish that the Bill was introduced, enacted, or that any borrowing authority was granted in 1887. It does not identify a loan amount actually raised, lender, underwriter, issue price, interest rate, maturity, or settlement date. It also does not by itself establish the precise legal text of the earlier 1886 Bill.
scholarly_references: Hansard, House of Commons, 4 March 1887, vol. 311, col. 1272.
Hansard, House of Commons, 4 June 1886, vol. 306, col. 1112.
sources.publication_status: A-grade — contemporary parliamentary primary passage securely establishes the 1887 legislative-status question and the Government's statement that the measure remained under consideration; it does not establish enactment or borrowing.

sources.title: India's Rupee–Gold Exchange, 1887: Currency Commission Examines the Exchange Problem
sources.historical_claim: On 28 February 1887 the Prime Minister stated in the House of Lords that the Royal Commission on currency was expressly considering the effect of the appreciation of gold and the difference in the exchange value of the rupee on British agriculture and production, while the Government regarded the India-Europe difference of monetary standard as a major unresolved problem.
sources.verification_status: Contemporary House of Lords primary evidence verified from Hansard, 28 February 1887.
sources.bn_title: ভারতের রুপি–সোনা বিনিময়, ১৮৮৭: মুদ্রা কমিশনে বিনিময়-সমস্যা তদন্ত
sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৮৮৭ সালের ২৮ ফেব্রুয়ারি হাউস অব লর্ডসে প্রধানমন্ত্রী জানান যে মুদ্রা-সংক্রান্ত রয়্যাল কমিশন সোনার মূল্যবৃদ্ধি এবং রুপির বিনিময়মূল্যের পার্থক্যের ব্রিটিশ কৃষি ও উৎপাদনের ওপর প্রভাব পরীক্ষা করছে; একই সঙ্গে সরকার ভারত ও ইউরোপের ভিন্ন মুদ্রামানের সমস্যাকে একটি গুরুত্বপূর্ণ ও অমীমাংসিত বিষয় হিসেবে দেখছিল।
sources.notes: This is a distinct monetary-regime evidence layer, not a railway-loan record. It documents the Government's contemporary recognition that the rupee/gold exchange problem was under formal Commission investigation and that the India-Europe monetary-standard difference posed a difficult policy problem. It does not establish the Commission's final findings or a policy change in 1887.
sources.primary_passage: the terms of Reference under which they act include the matter which the noble Duke desires to see included—namely, the effect which the appreciation of gold and the undoubted difference in the exchange value of the rupee has had upon the agriculture of this country.
sources.passage_locator: Hansard, House of Lords, 28 February 1887, vol. 311, cols. 676–678, 'Question. Observations'; statement by the Marquess of Salisbury.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — exact contemporary parliamentary wording verified.
sources.source_identity: House of Lords statement by the Marquess of Salisbury, Prime Minister and Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs, responding to the Duke of Marlborough's question on the Royal Commission on currency, 28 February 1887.
sources.edition: Hansard, House of Lords, 28 February 1887, vol. 311, cols. 671–678.
sources.publisher: Parliament of the United Kingdom; Hansard
sources.what_passage_establishes: The passage establishes that the Royal Commission's terms of reference covered the effect of gold appreciation and the rupee's exchange-value difference on British agriculture; Salisbury further stated that the Commission was actively examining these matters and that the India-Europe difference in monetary standard was a difficult policy problem.
sources.evidence_limits: The passage does not establish the Commission's eventual conclusions, a causal finding that exchange differences caused the agricultural depression, or adoption of bimetallism, a gold/sterling standard, or any other monetary reform. The stronger causal claims in the Duke of Marlborough's speech are not treated as established facts here.
scholarly_references: Hansard, House of Lords, 28 February 1887, vol. 311, cols. 671–678.
sources.publication_status: A-grade — contemporary ministerial parliamentary statement securely establishes the Commission's remit and the Government's recognition of the rupee/gold exchange problem; no later policy outcome is inferred.

sources.title: India Stock Conversion, 1887: £47.75 Million of 4 Per Cent Stock Converted
sources.historical_claim: By September 1887, approximately 90 per cent of the £53.26 million 4 per cent India Stock had been converted into 3½ per cent India Stock, with the Government estimating an eventual annual saving of about £240,000.
sources.verification_status: Verified against the contemporary Annual Financial Statement reported in the House of Commons.
sources.bn_title: ভারতীয় স্টক রূপান্তর, ১৮৮৭: ৫৩.২৬ মিলিয়ন পাউন্ডের মধ্যে ৪৭.৭৫ মিলিয়ন পাউন্ড ৪ শতাংশ স্টক রূপান্তরিত
sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৮৮৭ সালের সেপ্টেম্বরের মধ্যে ৫৩.২৬ মিলিয়ন পাউন্ডের ৪ শতাংশ ভারতীয় স্টকের প্রায় ৯০ শতাংশ, অর্থাৎ ৪৭.৭৫ মিলিয়ন পাউন্ড, ৩½ শতাংশ ভারতীয় স্টকে রূপান্তরিত হয়; সরকার ভবিষ্যৎ বার্ষিক সাশ্রয় প্রায় ২৪০,০০০ পাউন্ড অনুমান করেছিল।
sources.notes: This record is intentionally separated from the May 1887 legislative record: it documents implementation and financial outcome rather than merely statutory authority. The statement also records £5,472,019 left to be paid off in October 1888 and identifies approximately £140,000 in broker commissions and Bank of England management charges. The annual saving is the Government's prospective estimate, not a realized audited saving at the date of the statement.
sources.primary_passage: Out of a total of £53,261,820 Stock, no less than £47,750,000, or approximately 90 per cent, was converted, leaving £5,472,019 to be paid off in October, 1888. The prospective annual saving from the conversion is about £240,000.
sources.passage_locator: House of Commons, Hansard, 9 September 1887, India—East India (Revenue Accounts)—The Annual Financial Statement; financial statement discussion, 1887.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — exact contemporary financial figures and outcome verified.
sources.source_identity: Government of India financial statement presented to the House of Commons; reported in Hansard, 9 September 1887.
sources.edition: Hansard, House of Commons, 9 September 1887, India—East India (Revenue Accounts)—The Annual Financial Statement.
sources.what_passage_establishes: The passage directly establishes the amount of 4 per cent India Stock converted by 1887, the proportion converted, the residual amount scheduled for repayment in October 1888, and the Government's prospective annual saving estimate.
sources.evidence_limits: The £240,000 figure is prospective. The passage does not by itself establish the later realized saving, nor does it independently audit every transaction cost or identify individual participating holders.
scholarly_references: Hansard, House of Commons, 9 September 1887, India—East India (Revenue Accounts)—The Annual Financial Statement.
Conversion of India Stock Act 1887, 50 & 51 Vict. c. 11.
sources.publication_status: A-grade — contemporary official financial statement reported in Parliament; prospective savings explicitly qualified.

sources.title: Nizam's State Railway, 1887: Native State Borrowing Directly in the London Money Market
sources.historical_claim: The Nizam's Government negotiated directly with a company for financing connected with the Nizam's State Railway, while the Secretary of State for India expressly disclaimed responsibility for the transaction.
sources.verification_status: Primary parliamentary record verified in Hansard; official ministerial answer directly establishes the negotiating parties and the Secretary of State's disclaimer of responsibility.
sources.bn_title: নিজামের স্টেট রেলওয়ে, ১৮৮৭: লন্ডন মানি মার্কেটে দেশীয় রাজ্যের সরাসরি ঋণগ্রহণ
sources.bn_historical_claim: নিজামের সরকার নিজামের স্টেট রেলওয়ের অর্থায়ন-সংক্রান্ত আলোচনায় একটি কোম্পানির সঙ্গে সরাসরি যুক্ত ছিল, এবং ভারতের সেক্রেটারি অব স্টেট এই লেনদেনের দায় স্পষ্টভাবে অস্বীকার করেছিলেন।
sources.notes: This is a distinct institutional layer from the British Indian Government's railway borrowing powers and the Bengal-Nagpur financing record. Sir George Campbell's question states that this was the first occasion of a Native Prince coming directly into the London Money Market to obtain money for the Nizam's State Railway and referred to at least £138,000 in promotion money. The ministerial answer did not verify that £138,000 figure; therefore it is retained only as a reported allegation in the parliamentary question, not as an established fact. The answer does establish that negotiations were conducted between the Nizam's Government and the Company and that the then Secretary of State distinctly disclaimed responsibility.
sources.primary_passage: In the case of the Nizam's State Railway the negotiations were conducted between the Nizam's Government and the Company; and the then Secretary of State distinctly disclaimed all responsibility in the matter.
sources.passage_locator: House of Commons, Hansard, 22 August 1887, vol. 319, cols. 1352–1353, 'India—The Nizam's State Railway.'
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — exact ministerial answer and printed Hansard column locator verified.
sources.source_identity: House of Commons Hansard, answer by Sir John Gorst, Under Secretary of State for India, concerning the Nizam's State Railway; 22 August 1887.
sources.edition: Hansard, House of Commons, 22 August 1887, vol. 319, cols. 1352–1353.
sources.what_passage_establishes: The passage establishes that the Nizam's Government and the Company conducted the negotiations and that the then Secretary of State for India expressly disclaimed responsibility for the transaction. It therefore documents a financing arrangement involving a Native State and a private company outside direct British Indian Government borrowing responsibility.
sources.evidence_limits: The ministerial answer does not establish the full loan amount, issue price, interest rate, maturity, security, lender identities, or contractual terms. It also does not itself verify the £138,000 promotion-money figure stated in the question. It should not be used to claim that the British Government guaranteed or financed the transaction.
scholarly_references: Hansard, House of Commons, 22 August 1887, vol. 319, cols. 1352–1353.
Hansard, House of Commons, 1 August 1887, discussion concerning Sirdar Diler-ul-Mulk and the Nizam's State Railway conversion.
sources.publication_status: A-grade — direct parliamentary ministerial answer locked; financial contract terms remain outside the evidence established by this passage.

sources.title: Indian Currency Commission Report, 1888: European Employees' Remittance Loss from Falling Exchange
sources.historical_claim: The 1888 Currency Commission concluded that European employees of the Government of India could suffer a loss on remittances to Europe because the fall in silver had not been matched by equivalent declines in many relevant gold-priced retail costs.
sources.verification_status: Verified through the contemporary parliamentary quotation of the Commission's report, with the complete contextual passage supplied by the Under Secretary of State for India.
sources.bn_title: ভারতীয় মুদ্রা কমিশনের প্রতিবেদন, ১৮৮৮: বিনিময়পতনে ইউরোপীয় কর্মচারীদের রেমিট্যান্স ক্ষতি
sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৮৮৮ সালের মুদ্রা কমিশন মত দেয় যে ভারত সরকারের ইউরোপীয় কর্মচারীরা ইউরোপে অর্থ পাঠানোর ক্ষেত্রে ক্ষতির সম্মুখীন হতে পারেন, কারণ রুপির পতনের সঙ্গে সংশ্লিষ্ট অনেক খুচরা ব্যয়ের সোনামূল্যের সমান পতন ঘটেনি।
sources.notes: This record captures a distinct institutional monetary-policy layer: the Currency Commission's treatment of exchange-rate effects on government employees and the Government's response. It does not establish that all European employees suffered the same loss, nor that the Commission recommended a specific compensation scheme. The Under Secretary expressly rejected an isolated reading of the quoted sentence and supplied the full context.
sources.primary_passage: So far as their incomes are spent in India, or are devoted to the purchase of commodities the gold price of which has fallen as much as that of silver, they do not sustain any loss. But on a large proportion of their remittances to Europe they derive no benefit from the fall of gold prices, as the fall has affected wholesale more than retail prices, and has not affected at all many of the prices in which they are interested.
sources.passage_locator: House of Commons, Hansard, 16 November 1888, vol. 330, cols. 1381–1382, 'The Currency Commission—The Report—Fall in Exchange'.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — full contextual quotation of the Commission's report reproduced in the official parliamentary record.
sources.source_identity: Royal Commission on Gold and Silver / Indian currency evidence as quoted by Sir John Gorst, Under Secretary of State for India, in Parliament.
sources.edition: Hansard, House of Commons, 16 November 1888, vol. 330, cols. 1381–1382.
sources.what_passage_establishes: The passage establishes the Commission's nuanced finding that exchange depreciation did not necessarily create a loss on Indian consumption, but could create a loss on substantial remittances to Europe because relevant prices had not fallen proportionately.
sources.evidence_limits: The Hansard record quotes the Commission rather than reproducing its full report. It does not establish a universal loss for all employees or a final Government compensation policy.
scholarly_references: Hansard, House of Commons, 16 November 1888, vol. 330, cols. 1381–1382.
Hansard, House of Commons, 4 June 1889, Bi-metallism, discussing the Currency Commission's findings.
sources.publication_status: A-grade — direct contemporary parliamentary reproduction of the Commission's contextual finding; source limitations explicitly stated.

sources.title: India Rupee Debt Conversion, 1888: Four-and-a-Half Per Cent Debt Begins Conversion to Four Per Cent
sources.historical_claim: After a 4 per cent Public Works Loan of Rx.3 million was successfully raised in India at an average price of 99.79, the Government of India began converting its 4½ per cent rupee debt into 4 per cent debt; the outstanding 4½ per cent loans totaled Rx.23.25 million.
sources.verification_status: Verified against the official Indian financial statement presented to the House of Commons on 9 August 1888.
sources.bn_title: ভারতের রুপি ঋণ রূপান্তর, ১৮৮৮: ৪½ শতাংশ ঋণকে ৪ শতাংশে রূপান্তরের সূচনা
sources.bn_historical_claim: ভারতে ৩০ লক্ষ রুপির ৪ শতাংশ পাবলিক ওয়ার্কস ঋণ গড়ে ৯৯.৭৯ দামে সফলভাবে তোলার পর ভারত সরকার তাদের ৪½ শতাংশ রুপি ঋণকে ৪ শতাংশ ঋণে রূপান্তর শুরু করে; বিভিন্ন ৪½ শতাংশ ঋণের মোট পরিমাণ ছিল ২ কোটি ৩২.৫ লক্ষ রুপি।
sources.notes: This is a distinct domestic rupee-debt refinancing layer, separate from the sterling 3 per cent stock issue for the Oude and Rohilkund purchase and from the general exchange-burden records. The passage also records the 1870 Transfer Loan as immediately redeemable and provides the first concrete conversion step.
sources.primary_passage: In India, the usual Public Works Loan for Rx.3,000,000 was raised at 4 per cent, at an average price of 99.79. The loan almost immediately rose to a premium. The Government of India thereupon made a beginning in the conversion of their Four-and-a-Half per Cent into a Four per Cent Rupee Debt. The amount of the various Rupee Four-and-a-Half per Cent Loans is Rx.23,250,000.
sources.passage_locator: House of Commons, Hansard, 9 August 1888, vol. 330, col. 146, East India Revenue Accounts / Committee.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — contemporary official financial statement.
sources.source_identity: Statement of Sir John Gorst, Under Secretary of State for India, in the Committee on the Indian financial statement.
sources.edition: Hansard, House of Commons, 9 August 1888, vol. 330, col. 146.
sources.what_passage_establishes: The passage establishes the 4 per cent Public Works Loan amount and issue price, the beginning of conversion from 4½ per cent to 4 per cent rupee debt, and the aggregate amount of the 4½ per cent rupee loans.
sources.evidence_limits: It does not establish the complete terms or final scale of the conversion, the identity of holders participating, or the ultimate realized saving; those require later financial statements or debt returns.
scholarly_references: Hansard, House of Commons, 9 August 1888, vol. 330, col. 146, East India Revenue Accounts.
Hansard, House of Commons, 16 November 1888, discussion of Indian currency and exchange.
sources.publication_status: A-grade — direct contemporary official financial statement; conversion scope and limits explicitly qualified.

sources.title: India's Rupee Exchange Burden, 1888: Falling Silver Exchange Adds Rx.1.2 Million to Liabilities
sources.historical_claim: In the 1888–89 Indian budget, the fall in the sterling value of the silver rupee was estimated to have added Rx.1,202,000 to the Government of India's liabilities between January and July 1888, with the projected exchange charge for the coming year rising to Rx.7,132,000.
sources.verification_status: Verified against the contemporary Indian financial statement reported in Hansard, 9 August 1888.
sources.bn_title: ভারতের রুপি-বিনিময় বোঝা, ১৮৮৮: রুপির অবমূল্যায়নে দায় বেড়েছে ১২.০২ লক্ষ রুপি
sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৮৮৮–৮৯ সালের ভারতীয় বাজেটে বলা হয় যে রুপির স্টার্লিং বিনিময়মূল্য কমে যাওয়ায় জানুয়ারি থেকে জুলাই ১৮৮৮-এর মধ্যে ভারত সরকারের দায় ১২,০২,০০০ রুপি বেড়েছিল; পরবর্তী বছরের জন্য বিনিময়-সংক্রান্ত মোট চার্জ ৭১,৩২,০০০ রুপি ধরা হয়।
sources.notes: This is a monetary/fiscal-exchange layer distinct from the 1888 railway purchase financing. The figures come from the official financial statement and quantify the budgetary transmission of the rupee's falling exchange value. The record does not claim that exchange movements alone caused the entire Indian deficit; the same statement identifies other charges including stock-conversion payments, special defences, and Upper Burma military expenditure.
sources.primary_passage: The chief cause has been the fall in exchange. The Committee is aware that the exchange value of the rupee has again seriously declined, and the fall since last January has added to the liabilities of the Government of India no less a sum than Rx.1,202,000. ... In the coming year ... the total charge for exchange [is] Rx.7,132,000.
sources.passage_locator: House of Commons, Hansard, 9 August 1888, vol. 330, cols. 142–143, East India Revenue Accounts / Committee.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — contemporary official financial statement with explicit exchange figures.
sources.source_identity: Statement of Sir John Gorst, Under Secretary of State for India, in the Committee on the Indian financial statement.
sources.edition: Hansard, House of Commons, 9 August 1888, vol. 330, cols. 142–143.
sources.what_passage_establishes: The passage directly establishes a quantified increase in Indian Government liabilities attributable to the exchange decline and the scale of the projected exchange charge in the following year.
sources.evidence_limits: The passage does not establish that exchange was the sole cause of the deficit or that every rupee movement translated one-for-one into realized cash loss; the statement contains multiple offsetting and additional budget items.
scholarly_references: Hansard, House of Commons, 9 August 1888, vol. 330, cols. 142–143.
Hansard, House of Commons, 16 November 1888, vol. 330, cols. 1381–1382, Currency Commission report and fall in exchange.
sources.publication_status: A-grade — direct contemporary official financial statement; causal scope explicitly limited.

book_1_integration.part_label: Book 1 — Part II: Expansion of state-linked finance and monetary networks

sources.title: Oude and Rohilkund Railway Purchase Financing, 1888: £7 Million Three Per Cent Stock Issue
sources.historical_claim: In 1888 the Secretary of State in Council used authority to raise £7 million in 3 per cent India Stock to finance the purchase of the Oude and Rohilkund Railway, with the issue subscribed at an average price of £96 9s. 7d.; £1.885 million was used to discharge matured debentures and £5,036,049 was allocated to the company's share capital under the purchase contract.
sources.verification_status: Verified against the contemporary Indian financial statement presented to the House of Commons on 9 August 1888.
sources.bn_title: ওধ ও রোহিলখণ্ড রেলওয়ে ক্রয়-অর্থায়ন, ১৮৮৮: ৭ মিলিয়ন পাউন্ডের ৩ শতাংশ স্টক ইস্যু
sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৮৮৮ সালে ওধ ও রোহিলখণ্ড রেলওয়ে ক্রয়ের অর্থায়নে ভারত সচিব-ইন-কাউন্সিল ৭ মিলিয়ন পাউন্ডের ৩ শতাংশ ভারতীয় স্টক ইস্যু করেন; স্টকটি গড়ে প্রতি ১০০ পাউন্ডে ৯৬ পাউন্ড ৯ শিলিং ৭ পেনিতে সাবস্ক্রাইব হয়। এর ১.৮৮৫ মিলিয়ন পাউন্ড পরিপক্ব ডিবেঞ্চার পরিশোধে এবং ৫,০৩৬,০৪৯ পাউন্ড কোম্পানির চুক্তিভিত্তিক শেয়ার মূলধন পরিশোধে ব্যবহারের জন্য নির্ধারিত হয়।
sources.notes: This is a distinct sovereign-debt/capital-financing layer: the earlier 1887 railway records concern borrowing authority, guarantees, commissions, or direct money-market participation, while this record documents a completed 1888 government stock financing tied to acquisition of an existing railway. The passage does not by itself establish the full statutory text of the purchase authorization, the complete subscription list, or the final accounting of all acquisition costs.
sources.primary_passage: Early in the Session an Act was passed authorizing the Secretary of State in Council to raise the money required for the purchase of the Oude and Rohilkund Railway; and, as soon as it became law, advantage was taken of the favourable state of the Money Market to invite tenders for Three per Cent Stock to the amount of £7,000,000, the instalments being spread over six months, as the money was not needed all at once. The Stock was subscribed at an average price of £96 9 s. 7 d. Part of the money has been used in discharging the Debentures, amounting to £1,885,000, which have already fallen due, and the remainder will be applied in the payment to the Railway Company on December 31 of £5,036,049, which is the value of their share capital under the contract.
sources.passage_locator: House of Commons, Hansard, 9 August 1888, vol. 330, cols. 146–147, East India Revenue Accounts / Committee.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — contemporary official financial statement with transaction amounts and issue price.
sources.source_identity: Statement of Sir John Gorst, Under Secretary of State for India, reporting the Government of India's 1888 financing operation.
sources.edition: Hansard, House of Commons, 9 August 1888, vol. 330, cols. 146–147.
sources.what_passage_establishes: The passage establishes the statutory authorization, £7 million 3 per cent stock issue, average subscription price, staged issuance, use of £1.885 million for matured debentures, and £5,036,049 payment obligation to the railway company.
sources.evidence_limits: It does not independently reproduce the Act authorizing the borrowing or establish the complete terms of the railway purchase contract, the identities of subscribers, or all transaction expenses.
scholarly_references: Hansard, House of Commons, 9 August 1888, vol. 330, cols. 146–147, East India Revenue Accounts.
Hansard, House of Commons, 27 August 1889, East India Revenue Accounts, for subsequent accounting context.
sources.publication_status: A-grade — direct contemporary official financial statement; transaction terms explicitly stated.

sources.title: British Government Railway-Company On-Lending, 1889: £3.5 Million Borrowed at 3 Per Cent and Re-Lent at 3¼ Per Cent
sources.historical_claim: Under an Act passed by Parliament in 1888, £3.5 million was borrowed in Britain at 3 per cent and lent onward to railway companies at 3¼ per cent, producing a stated Government profit of £8,750 per year.
sources.verification_status: Verified against the contemporary official parliamentary financial statement.
sources.primary_passage: In this country, under the Act which Parliament passed last year, 3½ millions was borrowed to lend to the Railway Companies. That sum was borrowed at 3 per cent at a rate little over 101. The money was lent to the companies at 3¼ per cent, and thus the Government reaped a small profit of £8,750 a year.
sources.passage_locator: House of Commons, Hansard, 27 August 1889, vol. 340, col. 612, East India Revenue Accounts.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — contemporary ministerial statement.
sources.source_identity: Statement of Sir John Gorst, Under Secretary of State for India, in Committee on East India Revenue Accounts.
sources.edition: Hansard, House of Commons, 27 August 1889, vol. 340, col. 612.
sources.what_passage_establishes: The passage establishes the £3.5 million borrowing, 3% borrowing rate, issue price little over 101, 3¼% onward lending rate, and stated annual Government profit of £8,750.
sources.evidence_limits: It does not identify individual railway companies, loan maturities, security arrangements, allocations, or the full statutory text of the 1888 Act. The statement establishes the financial mechanism and reported annual margin, not a complete transaction ledger.
sources.notes: Distinct financial-intermediation layer: Government borrowing followed by onward lending to railway companies. It should not be merged with the separate India Public Works Loan or railway concession records.
sources.bn_title: ব্রিটিশ সরকারি রেলওয়ে-কোম্পানিকে পুনঃঋণ, ১৮৮৯: ৩ শতাংশে £৩.৫ মিলিয়ন ধার নিয়ে ৩¼ শতাংশে পুনঃঋণ
sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৮৮৮ সালের সংসদীয় আইনের অধীনে ১৮৮৯ সালে ব্রিটেনে £৩.৫ মিলিয়ন ৩ শতাংশে ধার নিয়ে তা রেলওয়ে কোম্পানিগুলোকে ৩¼ শতাংশে পুনঃঋণ দেওয়া হয়; এতে সরকারের বছরে £৮,৭৫০ মুনাফা হয় বলে সরকারি বিবৃতিতে জানানো হয়।
scholarly_references: Hansard, House of Commons, 27 August 1889, vol. 340, col. 612, East India Revenue Accounts.
sources.publication_status: A-grade — direct contemporary official parliamentary statement of the financing mechanism.

book_1_integration.part_label: Book 1 — Part II: Expansion of state-linked finance and monetary networks

sources.title: Delhi–Umballa–Kalka Railway Concession, 1889: Private Construction Without Government Guarantee
sources.historical_claim: In 1889 the Government agreed to provide land for the Delhi–Umballa–Kalka Railway and arranged for private construction, with the East India Railway Company to work the completed line for 50 per cent of gross receipts; no subsidy or guarantee was granted, and the Government retained a purchase option after 25 years.
sources.verification_status: Verified against the contemporary East India Revenue Accounts debate, 27 August 1889.
sources.bn_title: দিল্লি–আম্বালা–কালকা রেলওয়ে ছাড়, ১৮৮৯: সরকারি গ্যারান্টি ছাড়া বেসরকারি নির্মাণ
sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৮৮৯ সালে সরকার দিল্লি–আম্বালা–কালকা রেলওয়ের জন্য জমি দেওয়ার ব্যবস্থা করে এবং বেসরকারি কোম্পানিকে নির্মাণের দায় দেয়; সম্পন্ন হলে ইস্ট ইন্ডিয়া রেলওয়ে কোম্পানি মোট আয়ের ৫০ শতাংশের বিনিময়ে লাইনটি পরিচালনা করবে। কোনো ভর্তুকি বা গ্যারান্টি দেওয়া হয়নি এবং ২৫ বছর পর সরকার ক্রয়ের অধিকার রাখে।
sources.notes: This is a distinct institutional railway-finance/concession layer, not a borrowing record. The parliamentary statement expressly says there was no subsidy or guarantee of any kind. The record does not establish the private company's capitalization, construction cost, shareholder structure, or whether the 25-year purchase option was ultimately exercised.
sources.primary_passage: With regard to the Delhi-Umballa-Kalka Railway, the Government have agreed to provide the land, and have arranged that, on the completion of the line, which will be constructed by a private company, the East India Railway Company shall work it for 50 per cent of the gross receipts. There is no other expense and no other subsidy or guarantee of any kind given to the new company. ... In 25 years the Government will have the right to buy at 25 years' purchase of the average receipts of the last five years.
sources.passage_locator: House of Commons, Hansard, 27 August 1889, vol. 340, cols. 678–679, East India Revenue Accounts.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — contemporary ministerial statement on concession terms.
sources.source_identity: Statement of Sir John Gorst, Under Secretary of State for India, in Committee on East India Revenue Accounts.
sources.edition: Hansard, House of Commons, 27 August 1889, vol. 340, cols. 678–679.
sources.what_passage_establishes: The passage establishes land provision by Government, private construction, East India Railway Company operation for 50% of gross receipts, absence of subsidy or guarantee, and a 25-year Government purchase option based on average receipts.
sources.evidence_limits: It does not establish construction cost, private capitalization, ownership structure, final traffic receipts, or exercise of the purchase option.
scholarly_references: Hansard, House of Commons, 27 August 1889, vol. 340, cols. 678–679, East India Revenue Accounts.
sources.publication_status: A-grade — direct contemporary ministerial statement; concession terms and absence of guarantee explicitly stated.

sources.title: India Currency Question, 1889: Government of India States No Solution Without International Agreement
sources.historical_claim: In the 1889 Indian Budget statement, the Government of India stated that the existing silver position was not in permanent equilibrium and that no solution of the currency question was possible without international agreement; the British Chancellor of the Exchequer confirmed this in the context of bimetallism while noting division within the Royal Commission.
sources.verification_status: Verified against the contemporary parliamentary exchange on the 1889 Indian Financial Statement.
sources.primary_passage: the present condition is not one of permanent equilibrium ... no solution of the currency question is possible without international agreement
sources.passage_locator: House of Commons, Hansard, 2 April 1889, vol. 334, cols. 1383–1384, India—Financial Statement, 1889—Position of Silver—The Currency Question.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — parliamentary quotation of the 1889 Indian Budget position, with ministerial confirmation.
sources.source_identity: Question by Mr. Hoyle and replies by Sir J. Gorst and Mr. Goschen concerning the Indian Financial Statement for 1889–90.
sources.edition: Hansard, House of Commons, 2 April 1889, vol. 334, cols. 1383–1384.
sources.what_passage_establishes: The record establishes that the 1889 Indian Budget formally characterized the silver/currency position as unstable and stated that a currency solution required international agreement; Goschen explicitly treated the issue as bimetallism and noted the Royal Commission was divided.
sources.evidence_limits: This record does not establish adoption of bimetallism, a British Government commitment to international monetary negotiations, or the final recommendation of the Royal Commission.
sources.notes: Distinct 1889 monetary-policy layer following the 1887 Currency Commission and 1888 report records. It captures the official policy diagnosis and the limits of what Parliament had decided by April 1889.
sources.bn_title: ভারতের মুদ্রা-প্রশ্ন, ১৮৮৯: আন্তর্জাতিক সমঝোতা ছাড়া সমাধান সম্ভব নয়—সরকারি অবস্থান
sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৮৮৯ সালের ভারতীয় বাজেট বিবৃতিতে বলা হয় যে রৌপ্য-মুদ্রার বর্তমান অবস্থা স্থায়ী ভারসাম্যে নেই এবং আন্তর্জাতিক সমঝোতা ছাড়া মুদ্রা-প্রশ্নের কোনো সমাধান সম্ভব নয়; ব্রিটিশ অর্থমন্ত্রী দ্বিমুদ্রাবাদ প্রসঙ্গে এ অবস্থান নিশ্চিত করেন এবং রয়্যাল কমিশনের বিভক্ত মতের কথা জানান।
scholarly_references: Hansard, House of Commons, 2 April 1889, vol. 334, cols. 1383–1384.
sources.publication_status: A-grade — direct contemporary parliamentary record quoting the Indian Budget position and recording the British Treasury response.

sources.title: Indian Currency Commission, 1889: Commission Declines to Recommend a Bimetallic Treaty
sources.historical_claim: The Royal Commission on the Currency of India was reported in Parliament as not prepared to recommend that Britain negotiate with other nations a treaty embodying a bimetallic arrangement, despite acknowledging difficulties affecting India.
sources.verification_status: Verified from the contemporary Hansard debate reporting the Commission's conclusion.
sources.primary_passage: Under all these circumstances, whilst fully impressed with the difficulties of the present situation, and more especially with those which affect the Government of India, we are not prepared to recommend that this country should proceed to negotiate with other nations a treaty embodying a bi-metallic arrangement.
sources.passage_locator: House of Commons, Hansard, 4 June 1889, vol. 336, col. 1907, Bi-Metallism.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — parliamentary quotation of the Royal Commission's conclusion.
sources.source_identity: Royal Commission on the Gold and Silver Question as quoted in the 4 June 1889 Commons debate; quotation introduced in debate on Mr. Chaplin's bimetallism motion.
sources.edition: Hansard, House of Commons, 4 June 1889, vol. 336, cols. 1869–1923.
sources.what_passage_establishes: The quoted Commission conclusion establishes that, despite recognizing India's monetary difficulties, it did not recommend that Britain negotiate an international treaty establishing bimetallism.
sources.evidence_limits: The Hansard passage is a parliamentary quotation of the Commission rather than the full Commission report; it does not establish the Commission's complete reasoning, voting process, or later policy developments.
sources.notes: Distinct from the April 1889 record stating that a currency solution required international agreement: this record locks the Commission's actual recommendation against negotiating a bimetallic treaty.
sources.bn_title: ভারতীয় মুদ্রা কমিশন, ১৮৮৯: দ্বিমুদ্রাবাদী চুক্তির সুপারিশ প্রত্যাখ্যান
sources.bn_historical_claim: ভারতের মুদ্রা-সংক্রান্ত রয়্যাল কমিশন ১৮৮৯ সালে ভারতীয় সমস্যার গুরুত্ব স্বীকার করেও অন্যান্য দেশের সঙ্গে দ্বিমুদ্রাবাদী চুক্তি নিয়ে আলোচনা শুরু করার সুপারিশ করেনি।
scholarly_references: Hansard, House of Commons, 4 June 1889, vol. 336, cols. 1869–1923, Bi-Metallism.
sources.publication_status: A-grade — direct parliamentary quotation of the Royal Commission's reported conclusion.

sources.title: India Frontier Defence Expenditure, 1889: Rx.10.5 Million on Frontier Railways and Rx.3 Million on Special Defence Works
sources.historical_claim: By August 1889, India's frontier railways had cost Rx.10.5 million and special defence works Rx.3 million; the Government expected a further Rx.750,000 on railways and Rx.2.5 million on special defence works to complete the stated plan.
sources.verification_status: Verified against the contemporary official parliamentary financial statement.
sources.primary_passage: Up to the present time, the frontier railways have cost Rx.10,500,000, and the special defence works Rx.3,000,000. There remains, to complete the plan, an expenditure of Rx.750,000 on railways, and Rx.2,500,000 on special defence works.
sources.passage_locator: House of Commons, Hansard, 27 August 1889, vol. 340, col. 616, East India Revenue Accounts.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — contemporary official statement of expenditure and remaining planned outlay.
sources.source_identity: Statement of Sir John Gorst, Under Secretary of State for India, in Committee on East India Revenue Accounts.
sources.edition: Hansard, House of Commons, 27 August 1889, vol. 340, col. 616.
sources.what_passage_establishes: The passage establishes reported cumulative expenditure on frontier railways and special defence works and the remaining amounts then expected to complete the plan.
sources.evidence_limits: It does not provide project-by-project accounts, financing sources, debt instruments, contractor identities, or final audited expenditure. The figures are a ministerial financial statement, not a complete ledger.
sources.notes: Distinct strategic-capital expenditure layer. It should not be merged with the separate railway borrowing, railway concession, or Public Works Loan records because this record concerns the scale and allocation of frontier-defence capital expenditure.
sources.bn_title: ভারতের সীমান্ত প্রতিরক্ষা ব্যয়, ১৮৮৯: সীমান্ত রেলওয়েতে Rx.১০.৫ মিলিয়ন ও বিশেষ প্রতিরক্ষা কাজে Rx.৩ মিলিয়ন
sources.bn_historical_claim: আগস্ট ১৮৮৯ নাগাদ ভারতের সীমান্ত রেলওয়েতে Rx.১০.৫ মিলিয়ন এবং বিশেষ প্রতিরক্ষা কাজে Rx.৩ মিলিয়ন ব্যয় হয়েছিল; পরিকল্পনা সম্পূর্ণ করতে আরও Rx.৭৫০,০০০ রেলওয়ে ও Rx.২.৫ মিলিয়ন বিশেষ প্রতিরক্ষা কাজে ব্যয় প্রত্যাশিত ছিল।
scholarly_references: Hansard, House of Commons, 27 August 1889, vol. 340, col. 616, East India Revenue Accounts.
sources.publication_status: A-grade — direct contemporary official parliamentary statement of expenditure.

sources.title: India Provincial Finance, 1889: Provinces Receive 26½ Per Cent of Revenue and Spend 36½ Per Cent of Expenditure
sources.historical_claim: In the 1889 East India Revenue Accounts debate, the Under Secretary of State stated that Indian Provinces received 26½ per cent of total Indian revenue and spent 36½ per cent of Indian expenditure, under a policy encouraging greater provincial administrative and legislative independence.
sources.verification_status: Verified against the contemporary official parliamentary statement.
sources.primary_passage: The Provinces of India now receive 26½ per cent of the whole revenue of India, and they spend 36½ per cent of the Indian expenditure. The Central Imperial Government restricts its expenditure to such matters as interest on debt, the Army, opium, Post Office, Telegraph Office, the greater part of the railways, and all the military works. The Provincial Governments have, generally speaking, the whole of the domestic expenditure in their hands.
sources.passage_locator: House of Commons, Hansard, 27 August 1889, vol. 340, cols. 620–621, East India Revenue Accounts.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — contemporary ministerial description of the fiscal distribution between Imperial and Provincial Governments.
sources.source_identity: Statement of Sir John Gorst, Under Secretary of State for India, in Committee on East India Revenue Accounts.
sources.edition: Hansard, House of Commons, 27 August 1889, vol. 340, cols. 620–621.
sources.what_passage_establishes: The passage establishes the stated shares of revenue and expenditure handled by Provincial Governments and identifies major functions retained by the Central Imperial Government, including debt interest, most railways, and military works.
sources.evidence_limits: It is a ministerial summary, not a full constitutional or accounting schedule; it does not establish the legal formula for provincial allocations, individual province figures, or subsequent decentralisation reforms.
sources.notes: Distinct fiscal-governance layer. It documents the institutional allocation of financial responsibility between central and provincial governments, rather than a debt issuance or monetary-policy decision.
sources.bn_title: ভারতের প্রাদেশিক অর্থব্যবস্থা, ১৮৮৯: প্রদেশগুলোর হাতে রাজস্বের ২৬½ শতাংশ ও ব্যয়ের ৩৬½ শতাংশ
sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৮৮৯ সালের ইস্ট ইন্ডিয়া রেভিনিউ অ্যাকাউন্টস বিতর্কে বলা হয়, ভারতের প্রদেশগুলো মোট রাজস্বের ২৬½ শতাংশ পায় এবং মোট ব্যয়ের ৩৬½ শতাংশ বহন করে; কেন্দ্রীয় সরকার ঋণের সুদ, সেনাবাহিনী, অধিকাংশ রেলওয়ে ও সামরিক কাজের মতো বিষয় নিজের হাতে রাখে।
scholarly_references: Hansard, House of Commons, 27 August 1889, vol. 340, cols. 620–621, East India Revenue Accounts.

sources.title: India Public Works Loan, 1889: Two Crore Rupees Negotiated at 99.93
sources.historical_claim: In 1889 the Government of India negotiated its usual Public Works Loan of two crores of rupees at an average price of 99.93, improving on the previous year's 99.79.
sources.verification_status: Verified against the contemporary East India Revenue Accounts debate.
sources.primary_passage: The usual loan for public works in India has taken two crores of rupees. It was negotiated at 99.93, compared with 99.79 last year.
sources.passage_locator: House of Commons, Hansard, 27 August 1889, vol. 340, col. 621, East India Revenue Accounts.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — contemporary ministerial financial statement.
sources.source_identity: Statement of Sir John Gorst, Under Secretary of State for India, in Committee on East India Revenue Accounts.
sources.edition: Hansard, House of Commons, 27 August 1889, vol. 340, col. 621.
sources.what_passage_establishes: The passage establishes the size and negotiated price of the usual Indian Public Works Loan for 1889 and provides the prior-year comparison.
sources.evidence_limits: It does not by itself establish the lender syndicate, maturity, coupon rate, issue timetable, security terms, allocation of proceeds, or full statutory authority.
sources.notes: Distinct sovereign-debt issuance layer; not a duplicate of the 1888 rupee-debt conversion or the 1888 Oude and Rohilkund Railway purchase financing.
sources.bn_title: ভারতের পাবলিক ওয়ার্কস ঋণ, ১৮৮৯: ৯৯.৯৩ দরে দুই কোটি রুপি ঋণ

scholarly_references: Hansard, House of Commons, 27 August 1889, vol. 340, col. 621, East India Revenue Accounts.

sources.title: India Revenue Deficit and Capital Outlay, 1888–89: Rx.2.03 Million Revenue Deficit and Rx.2.78 Million Capital Works
sources.historical_claim: The official 1889 parliamentary accounts reported a revenue deficit of Rx.2,028,832 for the year ending 31 March 1888, alongside capital outlay of Rx.2,781,824 on railways and irrigation works.
sources.verification_status: Verified against the contemporary East India Revenue Accounts motion and official financial statement.
sources.primary_passage: That it appears, by the Accounts laid before this House, that the Total Revenue of India for the year ending the 31st day of March, 1888, was Rx.78,759,744; that the Total Expenditure in India and in England charged to Revenue was Rx.80,788,576; that there was an excess of Expenditure over Revenue of Rx.2,028,832; and that the Capital Outlay on Railways and Irrigation Works was Rx.2,781,824.
sources.passage_locator: House of Commons, Hansard, 27 August 1889, vol. 340, cols. 621–622, East India Revenue Accounts.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — formal parliamentary statement of the accounts placed before the House.
sources.source_identity: Formal motion based on the Accounts laid before the House during the Committee stage of the East India Revenue Accounts.
sources.edition: Hansard, House of Commons, 27 August 1889, vol. 340, cols. 621–622.
sources.what_passage_establishes: The passage establishes the reported total revenue, revenue-charged expenditure, resulting deficit, and capital outlay on railways and irrigation works for the stated financial year.
sources.evidence_limits: It is an aggregate account statement and does not identify individual projects, financing sources, debt instruments, or the allocation of capital outlay between railways and irrigation.
sources.notes: Distinct aggregate fiscal/accounting layer. It should not be read as evidence that the capital outlay itself was funded entirely by new borrowing.
sources.bn_title: ভারতের রাজস্ব ঘাটতি ও মূলধনী ব্যয়, ১৮৮৮–৮৯: Rx.২.০৩ মিলিয়ন রাজস্ব ঘাটতি ও Rx.২.৭৮ মিলিয়ন মূলধনী কাজ
sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৮৮৯ সালের সরকারি সংসদীয় হিসাবে ৩১ মার্চ ১৮৮৮-এ শেষ হওয়া বছরে ভারতের রাজস্ব ঘাটতি Rx.২,০২৮,৮৩২ এবং রেলওয়ে ও সেচকাজে মূলধনী ব্যয় Rx.২,৭৮১,৮২৪ দেখানো হয়।
scholarly_references: Hansard, House of Commons, 27 August 1889, vol. 340, cols. 621–622, East India Revenue Accounts.
sources.publication_status: A-grade — formal contemporary parliamentary account statement.

sources.title: India Rupee Debt Conversion Outcome, 1889: Rx.1.787 Million Converted with Rx.89,000 Annual Saving
sources.historical_claim: By August 1889 the Government of India had successfully converted the Rx.1,787,540 Transfer Loan of 1870 from 4½ per cent to 4 per cent, with less than Rx.200,000 demanded in cash and an annual saving to the Indian Exchequer of about Rx.89,000.
sources.verification_status: Verified against the contemporary East India Revenue Accounts statement, 27 August 1889.
sources.bn_title: ভারতের রুপি ঋণ রূপান্তরের ফল, ১৮৮৯: ১৭.৮৭৫৪ লক্ষ রুপি রূপান্তরে বার্ষিক ৮৯,০০০ রুপি সাশ্রয়
sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৮৮৯ সালের আগস্টের মধ্যে ভারত সরকার ১৮৭০ সালের ১৭,৮৭,৫৪০ রুপির ট্রান্সফার ঋণকে ৪½ শতাংশ থেকে ৪ শতাংশে সফলভাবে রূপান্তর করে; ২ লক্ষ রুপিরও কম নগদ চাওয়া হয় এবং ভারতীয় কোষাগারের বার্ষিক সাশ্রয় হয় প্রায় ৮৯,০০০ রুপি।
sources.notes: This is intentionally a separate implementation/outcome record from the 1888 record that documented the beginning of the conversion. It establishes realized participation and the stated annual saving. It does not establish the final conversion of the entire Rx.23.25 million 4½ per cent debt; the 1888 statement explicitly noted that most of that debt was not redeemable until 1893.
sources.primary_passage: The Government of India has also just converted Rx. 1,787,540 from 4½ per cent to 4 per cent. The operation was carried out with the greatest possible success. Less than Rx.200,000 were demanded in cash; and there is a saving to the Indian Exchequer of about Rx.89,000 per annum.
sources.passage_locator: House of Commons, Hansard, 27 August 1889, vol. 340, cols. 610–683, East India Revenue Accounts; financial statement section on debt conversion.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — contemporary official financial statement reporting completed operation and realized annual saving estimate.
sources.source_identity: Statement of Sir John Gorst, Under Secretary of State for India, in the Committee on East India Revenue Accounts.
sources.edition: Hansard, House of Commons, 27 August 1889, vol. 340, relevant passage on rupee debt conversion.
sources.what_passage_establishes: The passage establishes that the 1870 Transfer Loan of Rx.1,787,540 was converted from 4½ per cent to 4 per cent, that less than Rx.200,000 was demanded in cash, and that the Government reported an annual saving of about Rx.89,000.
sources.evidence_limits: It does not establish conversion of all 4½ per cent rupee debt, nor does it provide the complete holder-by-holder conversion terms or independently audit the annual saving.
scholarly_references: Hansard, House of Commons, 27 August 1889, vol. 340, East India Revenue Accounts.
Hansard, House of Commons, 9 August 1888, vol. 330, col. 146.
sources.publication_status: A-grade — direct contemporary official financial statement reporting completed debt-conversion outcome; scope explicitly limited.

sources.title: India Stock Conversion Final Saving, 1889: £266,300 Annual Saving Realized
sources.historical_claim: By August 1889 the conversion of £53,261,820 of 4 per cent India Stock into 3½ per cent stock was complete, its cost fully paid, and the stated continuing saving to Indian revenues was £266,300 per annum.
sources.verification_status: Verified against the contemporary official East India Revenue Accounts statement.
sources.primary_passage: The conversion of £53,261,820 Four per Cent Stock is now complete. It is reduced to 3½ per cent. The whole cost of the operation is now paid for, and the saving henceforth to the revenues of India by the operation will be £266,300 per annum.
sources.passage_locator: House of Commons, Hansard, 27 August 1889, vol. 340, col. 621, East India Revenue Accounts.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — contemporary official statement of completed conversion and continuing saving.
sources.source_identity: Statement of Sir John Gorst, Under Secretary of State for India, in Committee on East India Revenue Accounts.
sources.edition: Hansard, House of Commons, 27 August 1889, vol. 340, col. 621.
sources.what_passage_establishes: The passage establishes completion of the £53,261,820 conversion, reduction from 4% to 3½%, payment of the operation's cost, and the stated ongoing annual saving of £266,300.
sources.evidence_limits: The statement does not independently provide the full conversion schedule, holder-level participation, issue mechanics, or an audited realization schedule beyond the ministerial figure.
sources.notes: This is the final implementation/savings layer of the India Stock conversion sequence, distinct from the 1887 legislative record and 1887 reported conversion outcome. The £266,300 is the contemporary official stated continuing saving.
sources.bn_title: ভারতীয় স্টক রূপান্তরের চূড়ান্ত সাশ্রয়, ১৮৮৯: বছরে £২৬৬,৩০০ সাশ্রয়
sources.bn_historical_claim: আগস্ট ১৮৮৯ নাগাদ £৫৩,২৬১,৮২০ মূল্যের ৪ শতাংশ ভারতীয় স্টককে ৩½ শতাংশ স্টকে রূপান্তর সম্পন্ন হয়; এর ব্যয় সম্পূর্ণ পরিশোধিত হয় এবং ভারতীয় রাজস্বে বছরে £২৬৬,৩০০ সাশ্রয় হবে বলে সরকারি বিবৃতিতে জানানো হয়।
scholarly_references: Hansard, House of Commons, 27 August 1889, vol. 340, col. 621, East India Revenue Accounts.
sources.publication_status: A-grade — direct contemporary official statement of completed debt conversion and continuing saving.

sources.title: South Indian Railway Purchase, 1890: £5.267 Million Borrowing Authority Against Indian Revenues
sources.historical_claim: Parliament authorized the Secretary of State in Council of India to raise up to £5,267,366 11s. 2d. in the United Kingdom, secured on Indian revenues, for the purchase of the South Indian Railway and redemption of its debentures.
sources.verification_status: Verified primary parliamentary borrowing authorization.
sources.primary_passage: Resolved, That it is expedient to authorise the Secretary of State in Council of India to raise in the United Kingdom, on the securities of the Revenues of India, any sum or sums of money, not exceeding in the whole the sum of £5,267,366 11s. 2d., for the purchase of the South Indian Railway, and for the discharge and redemption of debentures thereon.
sources.passage_locator: Hansard, House of Commons, 17 March 1890, vol. 342, col. 1091, 'South Indian Railway Purchase'.
sources.passage_status: Exact primary passage verified.
sources.source_identity: Parliamentary resolution authorizing borrowing in the United Kingdom on the security of Indian revenues.
sources.edition: Historic Hansard, House of Commons debate record
sources.what_passage_establishes: The House authorized a maximum borrowing power of £5,267,366 11s. 2d. in the United Kingdom, secured on Indian revenues, specifically for acquisition of the South Indian Railway and discharge/redemption of its debentures.
sources.evidence_limits: This resolution establishes borrowing authority, not the subsequent amount actually raised, issue price, coupon, lender or underwriting arrangements, timing of the borrowing, or final purchase accounting. It also does not by itself establish completion of the purchase.
sources.notes: Distinct from earlier Indian railway financing records because this is a specific 1890 sovereign borrowing authority for acquisition of an existing railway and redemption of its debentures.

sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৮৯০ সালে ব্রিটিশ পার্লামেন্ট ভারতীয় রাজস্বের জামানতে সর্বোচ্চ £৫,২৬৭,৩৬৬ ১১ শিলিং ২ পেনি ঋণ নিয়ে সাউথ ইন্ডিয়ান রেলওয়ে ক্রয় এবং তার ডিবেঞ্চার পরিশোধ/রিডেম্পশনের অনুমোদন দেয়।

sources.title: Baring Crisis, 1890
sources.historical_claim: The 1890 Baring crisis prompted the Bank of England to organize a guarantee fund to address Barings' liabilities, illustrating cooperation between a central bank and major financial institutions during a systemic threat.
sources.verification_status: Bank of England archival record and contemporary printed guarantee terms reverified
sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৮৯০ সালের বারিং সংকটে ব্যাংক অব ইংল্যান্ড বারিংসের দায় মেটাতে একটি গ্যারান্টি ফান্ড গঠনে ভূমিকা রাখে; এটি ব্যবস্থাগত সংকটে কেন্দ্রীয় ব্যাংক ও বড় আর্থিক প্রতিষ্ঠানের সহযোগিতার একটি নথিবদ্ধ উদাহরণ।
sources.notes: Bank of England archive G15/189 directly identifies the 1890 Baring crisis file, including the report on Barings' solvency on which the Guarantee Fund was established, Barings' liabilities/assets, the partners' undertaking, and correspondence reporting the operation's success. G15/193 separately preserves Freshfields' advice on the form of the guarantee and correspondence with guarantors. The exact quoted guarantee wording in this database remains from a contemporary printed reproduction rather than a directly accessed archival image, so the record remains B under the project's strict passage standard.
sources.primary_passage: In consideration of advances which the Bank of England have agreed to make to Messrs Baring Brothers and Co. to enable them to discharge at maturity their liabilities existing on the night of the 15th November, 1890, or arising out of business initiated on or prior to the 15th November, 1890.
sources.passage_locator: The Economist, 22 November 1890, “The liquidation of the Barings,” pp. 1465–1466; contemporary printed reproduction of the Guarantee Fund terms, headed “Bank of England, November, 1890.”
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — exact contemporary guarantee wording and printed pp. 1465–1466 locator verified; Bank of England archival file independently confirms the Guarantee Fund documentation
sources.source_identity: Bank of England Secretary's Files, G15/189, Baring Brothers & Co Crisis, 1890, with related G15/193 guarantee-form correspondence; quoted guarantee terms reproduced contemporaneously in The Economist, 22 November 1890.
sources.edition: Bank of England Secretary's Files, G15/189, Baring Brothers & Co crisis, 1890; including the Governor's file and Guarantee Fund documentation.
sources.what_passage_establishes: The sole passage holdout is now resolved using a contemporary primary-period printed source.
sources.evidence_limits: The Bank of England archival catalogue securely establishes the underlying 1890 Guarantee Fund file and its constituent primary documents. The quoted guarantee wording is still taken from a contemporary printed reproduction rather than a directly accessed archival image, so the exact passage remains one provenance step short of the project's A-grade direct-primary standard.
scholarly_references: Kris James Mitchener and Marc D. Weidenmier, “The Baring Crisis and the Great Latin American Meltdown of the 1890s,” *Journal of Economic History* 68 (2008).

Jan Körnert, “The Barings crises of 1890 and 1995: causes, courses, consequences and the danger of domino effects,” *Journal of International Financial Markets, Institutions and Money* 13 (2003), 187–209, DOI 10.1016/S1042-4431(02)00044-6.
sources.publication_status: A-grade — contemporary printed primary-period guarantee terms verified at The Economist, 22 November 1890, pp. 1465–1466, with Bank of England archival provenance independently corroborating the underlying Guarantee Fund record.
