sources.title: India Council Bills, 1890: Government Rejects Delaying Necessary Bill Sales for a Higher Silver Exchange
sources.historical_claim: The Secretary of State for India stated that Council-bill sales had not been increased because of anticipated United States silver legislation, that no surplus sale had occurred and therefore no loss had resulted, and that necessary bill sales could not be delayed merely in expectation of a future rise in silver.
sources.verification_status: Verified direct official parliamentary answer.
sources.primary_passage: India Council Bills have not been sold for some time past much beyond the average monthly rate. The expectation of legislation in the United States has not influenced the amount of the sales. ... There has been no surplus sale, and consequently no loss. As regards the last paragraph, the Secretary of State cannot delay such sale of bills as is necessary to meet the wants of the Service on the chance of a future rise in the value of silver.
sources.passage_locator: Hansard, House of Commons, 21 July 1890, vol. 347, col. 331, 'India Council Bills'.
sources.passage_status: Exact primary passage verified.
sources.source_identity: Official parliamentary answer by the Under Secretary of State for India concerning Council-bill sale policy and silver-exchange expectations.
sources.edition: Historic Hansard, House of Commons debate record
sources.what_passage_establishes: It establishes the Government's stated Council-bill sale policy: sales were not being deliberately increased in anticipation of U.S. silver legislation; no surplus sale had occurred; and necessary sales to meet service requirements could not be postponed in hope of a future rise in silver.
sources.evidence_limits: This passage does not quantify the full annual sales program, identify purchasers or intermediaries, or establish whether the policy maximized revenue. It records the Government's official answer rather than an independent assessment of the policy.
sources.notes: Distinct from the 1890 Council-bill volume and exchange-sensitivity records: this record captures the stated institutional decision rule governing when bill sales could be made or deferred.
sources.bn_title: ভারতের কাউন্সিল বিল, ১৮৯০: রূপার বিনিময় হার বাড়ার আশায় প্রয়োজনীয় বিল বিক্রি স্থগিত করা হয়নি
sources.bn_historical_claim: ভারত সরকারের বক্তব্য ছিল, মার্কিন রূপা-সংক্রান্ত আইন প্রত্যাশা করে কাউন্সিল বিলের বিক্রি বাড়ানো হয়নি; কোনো অতিরিক্ত বিক্রিও হয়নি, ফলে এমন বিক্রয়জনিত ক্ষতি ঘটেনি; এবং ভবিষ্যতে রূপার মূল্য বাড়তে পারে—এই আশায় পরিষেবার প্রয়োজনীয় বিল বিক্রি স্থগিত করা যায় না।

sources.title: India Official Exchange Rate, 1890: Fixed at 1s. 5d. for Nearly £1 Million of Transactions
sources.historical_claim: The Secretary of State for India stated that the official exchange rate fixed in March 1890 at 1s. 5d. per rupee could not be altered during the financial year because it applied to transactions amounting to nearly £1,000,000.
sources.verification_status: Verified direct official parliamentary answer.
sources.primary_passage: The Secretary has no information of the matter. In reply to the question of the hon. Member for Hull (Mr. King), I have to say that the Secretary of State cannot alter the official rate of exchange after it has been once fixed. It is applied to very large transactions, amounting nearly to £1,000,000.
sources.passage_locator: Hansard, House of Commons, 22 July 1890, vol. 347, cols. 498–499, 'Rate of Exchange in India'.
sources.passage_status: Exact primary passage verified.
sources.source_identity: Official parliamentary answer by the Under Secretary of State for India concerning the fixed official exchange rate used for large Government transactions.
sources.edition: Historic Hansard, House of Commons debate record
sources.what_passage_establishes: It establishes that the official rupee exchange rate had been fixed at 1s. 5d. in March 1890, could not be altered after fixation for that financial year, and applied to transactions totaling nearly £1,000,000.
sources.evidence_limits: The answer does not identify every transaction covered, explain the full administrative rule governing the fixed rate, or quantify the Government's net gain or loss from applying it. The questioner's claims about pensions and exchange gains are not treated as established facts here.
sources.notes: Distinct institutional monetary layer from the July and December 1890 exchange records: it documents the administrative use of a fixed official exchange rate for a substantial volume of Government transactions.
sources.bn_title: ভারতের সরকারি বিনিময় হার, ১৮৯০: প্রায় £১ মিলিয়ন লেনদেনে ১ শিলিং ৫ পেনি হার স্থির
sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৮৯০ সালের মার্চে প্রতি রুপিতে ১ শিলিং ৫ পেনি সরকারি বিনিময় হার নির্ধারিত হয় এবং তা পরিবর্তন করা যায়নি; এই হার প্রায় £১,০০০,০০০ মূল্যের বৃহৎ সরকারি লেনদেনে প্রয়োগ করা হতো।

sources.title: South Indian Railway Guarantee, 1890: Government Purchase Ends Guarantee and Saves £36,000
sources.historical_claim: The Government stated that its 1890 purchase of the South Indian Railway exercised a power reserved under the 1873 guarantee to terminate the guarantee and purchase the railway, producing an estimated annual economy of £36,000.
sources.verification_status: Verified direct official parliamentary statement.
sources.primary_passage: The policy of the Government is to construct railways in the cheapest possible manner for the people of India. No fresh guarantee is proposed under this Bill. The proposal is to carry out an arrangement by which an economy of, £36,000 will be effected in the interest of the people of India. Under the conditions of the guarantee entered into in 1873, power was reserved to the Secretary of State for India to terminate the guarantee in 1890, and purchase on terms there specified. ... It is to give effect to that power reserved to the Government, and, to effect the economy I have mentioned, we ask the House to sanction the purchase.
sources.passage_locator: Hansard, House of Commons, 24 March 1890, vol. 342, cols. 1796–1797, 'South Indian Railway Purchase Bill.—(No. 105.)'
sources.passage_status: Exact primary passage verified.
sources.source_identity: Official statement by the First Lord of the Treasury during debate on the South Indian Railway Purchase Bill.
sources.edition: Historic Hansard, House of Commons debate record
sources.what_passage_establishes: The Government explicitly linked the 1890 purchase to a termination-and-purchase power reserved in the 1873 guarantee and stated that the arrangement would effect an economy of £36,000.
sources.evidence_limits: The £36,000 is the Government's stated expected economy, not an independently audited realized saving. The passage does not give the full 1873 guarantee terms, purchase price, or subsequent financial results.
sources.notes: This is a distinct contractual/guarantee layer within the South Indian Railway transaction: the March 17 record establishes borrowing authority, while this record establishes the legal mechanism and stated fiscal rationale for terminating the guarantee and purchasing the railway.
sources.bn_title: সাউথ ইন্ডিয়ান রেলওয়ে গ্যারান্টি, ১৮৯০: সরকারি ক্রয়ে গ্যারান্টি সমাপ্ত ও £৩৬,০০০ সাশ্রয়
sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৮৯০ সালে সরকার জানায় যে ১৮৭৩ সালের গ্যারান্টিতে সংরক্ষিত ক্ষমতা ব্যবহার করে সাউথ ইন্ডিয়ান রেলওয়ের গ্যারান্টি সমাপ্ত করে রেলওয়েটি কেনা হবে এবং এতে বছরে আনুমানিক £৩৬,০০০ সাশ্রয় হবে।
sources.publication_status: Deployed

sources.title: India Council Bills, 1890: March–May Sales Rose to Rs.8.29 Crore
sources.historical_claim: Official parliamentary figures show Indian Council bill and telegraphic-transfer sales of Rs.8,29,00,000 in March–May 1890, versus Rs.6,55,48,015 in the corresponding months of 1889.
sources.verification_status: Verified direct official parliamentary answer.
sources.primary_passage: The sales of bills and transfers during March, April, and May this year were Rs.8,29,00,000, against Rs.6,55,48,015 in the corresponding months of 1889.
sources.passage_locator: Hansard, House of Commons, 25 July 1890, vol. 347, col. 903, 'Sale of Bills and Telegraph Transfers in India'.
sources.passage_status: Exact primary passage verified.
sources.source_identity: Official parliamentary answer reporting India Council bill and telegraphic-transfer sales for March–May 1890 and the comparable 1889 period.
sources.edition: Historic Hansard, House of Commons debate record
sources.what_passage_establishes: It establishes the official volume of Council bill and telegraphic-transfer sales during March–May 1890 and provides the directly comparable 1889 figure.
sources.evidence_limits: The passage does not identify purchasers, individual maturities, prices, discount rates, allocation by bill versus transfer, or the full annual volume. It therefore does not by itself establish the identities or concentration of the financial intermediaries involved.
sources.notes: Distinct from the 1890 exchange-rate records: this record captures the scale of the India Office's bill/transfer sales mechanism itself, rather than the exchange rate or its fiscal sensitivity.
sources.bn_title: ভারতের কাউন্সিল বিল, ১৮৯০: মার্চ–মে বিক্রি বেড়ে Rs.৮.২৯ কোটি
sources.bn_historical_claim: সরকারি সংসদীয় তথ্য অনুযায়ী ১৮৯০ সালের মার্চ–মে মাসে ভারতীয় কাউন্সিল বিল ও টেলিগ্রাফিক ট্রান্সফারের বিক্রি ছিল Rs.৮,২৯,০০,০০০; ১৮৮৯ সালের একই সময়ে ছিল Rs.৬,৫৫,৪৮,০১৫।

sources.title: India Council Bills, 1890: One Penny Rise in Exchange Produces Rx.1.1 Million Gain
sources.historical_claim: The India Office reported that a rise in the exchange rate from 1s. 6d. to 1s. 7d. per rupee produced a gain of Rx.1,100,000, and that Council bills were then fetching 3d. per rupee more than when silver was at 3s. 6d. per ounce.
sources.verification_status: Verified direct official parliamentary answer.
sources.primary_passage: The gain produced by the rise of 1d. varies with the rate of exchange. The gain by a rise from 1s. 6d. to 1s. 7d. is Rx.1,100,000. Council bills are fetching 3d. per rupee more than when silver was at 3s. 6d. per ounce.
sources.passage_locator: Hansard, House of Commons, 25 July 1890, vol. 347, cols. 903–904, 'Indian Exchequer and the Rate of Exchange'.
sources.passage_status: Exact primary passage verified.
sources.source_identity: Official parliamentary answer by the Under Secretary of State for India on the fiscal effect of exchange movements and the price of Council bills.
sources.edition: Historic Hansard, House of Commons debate record
sources.what_passage_establishes: It establishes an official contemporary calculation of the Indian Exchequer's gain from a one-penny exchange-rate rise at a specified rate, and records the then-current premium on Council bills relative to the stated silver-price benchmark.
sources.evidence_limits: The answer gives an illustrative exchange-rate gain rather than a full-year audited result. It does not establish the aggregate annual gain from all exchange movements, the complete Council-bill pricing mechanism, or causation between silver prices and the quoted bill premium.
sources.notes: Distinct from the December 1890 exchange-budget variance record: this passage quantifies the marginal fiscal sensitivity of the Indian Exchequer to exchange-rate movement and explicitly connects the contemporary Council-bill rate to the silver-price benchmark.
sources.bn_title: ভারতের কাউন্সিল বিল, ১৮৯০: বিনিময় হারে এক পেনি বৃদ্ধি থেকে Rx.১.১ মিলিয়ন লাভ
sources.bn_historical_claim: ভারতীয় এক্সচেকার জানায়, বিনিময় হার ১ শিলিং ৬ পেনি থেকে ১ শিলিং ৭ পেনিতে উঠলে Rx.১,১০০,০০০ লাভ হয়; একই সময়ে কাউন্সিল বিল রুপিপ্রতি ৩ পেনি বেশি দামে বিক্রি হচ্ছিল, যখন রূপার দাম ছিল প্রতি আউন্স ৩ শিলিং ৬ পেনি।

sources.title: India Rate of Exchange, 1890: Exchange Gains Put £995,063 Above the Budget Estimate
sources.historical_claim: The Government of India reported that the 1890–91 estimated exchange rate was 16.552 pence per rupee; actual rates had ranged from 17 1/16d. to 20 15/16d., producing £995,063 in excess of the estimate by 8 December 1890.
sources.verification_status: Verified direct official parliamentary answer.
sources.primary_passage: The estimated rate of exchange for 1890–91 was 16.552 pence per rupee. The lowest rate realised during the year has been 17 1–16d.; the highest 20 15–16d. The excess over the estimate is £995,063.
sources.passage_locator: Hansard, House of Commons, 8 December 1890, vol. 349, col. 695, 'Rate of Exchange in India'.
sources.passage_status: Exact primary passage verified.
sources.source_identity: Official parliamentary answer by the Under Secretary of State for India reporting the Indian Finance Minister's exchange estimate and realized range.
sources.edition: Historic Hansard, House of Commons debate record
sources.what_passage_establishes: It establishes the official budget exchange assumption for 1890–91, the lowest and highest realized rates reported to Parliament by 8 December, and an excess of £995,063 over the estimate.
sources.evidence_limits: The answer does not establish the full mechanism producing the excess, the precise accounting treatment of the £995,063, or the final full-year realized exchange result. It also does not by itself establish a causal attribution to silver-market movements or any later currency-policy decision.
sources.notes: Distinct monetary-regime/fiscal-exchange layer from the earlier 1887–1889 records: this is a contemporaneous 1890 official measurement of exchange performance against the budget assumption.
sources.bn_title: ভারতের বিনিময় হার, ১৮৯০: বিনিময়-লাভ বাজেট-অনুমানের চেয়ে £৯৯৫,০৬৩ বেশি
sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৮৯০–৯১ সালের জন্য নির্ধারিত রুপি-বিনিময় হার ছিল প্রতি রুপিতে ১৬.৫৫২ পেনি; ৮ ডিসেম্বর ১৮৯০ পর্যন্ত বাস্তব হার ১৭ ১/১৬d. থেকে ২০ ১৫/১৬d. পর্যন্ত ছিল এবং এতে বাজেট-অনুমানের তুলনায় £৯৯৫,০৬৩ অতিরিক্ত প্রাপ্তি দেখা যায়।

sources.title: Tirhoot State Railway, 1890: Government-Owned Railway Put Under Private Company Management
sources.historical_claim: The Government of India confirmed that the state-owned Tirhoot State Railway was being handed over to the Bengal and North Western Railway for management, with profits divided in proportion to Government and company capital, while the Government had first supported and later opposed the arrangement.
sources.verification_status: Verified direct official parliamentary answer.
sources.primary_passage: The answer to the first paragraph is in the affirmative, but for management only, and for the purpose of securing economy and efficiency. ... The division of profit between the Government and the company will be in proportion to their respective capitals. ... It was at first in favour of, and afterwards against, the arrangement.
sources.passage_locator: Hansard, House of Commons, 8 July 1890, vol. 346, cols. 1108–1109, 'Indian Railways'.
sources.passage_status: Exact primary passage verified.
sources.source_identity: Official parliamentary answer by the Under Secretary of State for India concerning management of the Government-owned Tirhoot State Railway.
sources.edition: Historic Hansard, House of Commons debate record
sources.what_passage_establishes: It establishes a Government-owned state railway being placed under private-company management for economy and efficiency, with profit division linked to respective capital contributions, and confirms that the Government of India changed its position on the arrangement.
sources.evidence_limits: The passage does not establish the complete management contract, duration, fee structure, detailed capital amounts, or subsequent financial performance. The questioner's claim that the state railway yielded 7% and the private company 2½% was explicitly corrected by Government to 4.62% and 4.18%, respectively.
sources.notes: Distinct institutional railway-finance layer from the South Indian Railway purchase: this concerns operational control and profit-sharing of an existing Government-owned railway rather than acquisition financing.

sources.title: Indian Bank Rates, 1891: Calcutta 4% and Bombay 5%
sources.historical_claim: The official parliamentary account stated that bank rates never rose above 4% in Calcutta and 5% in Bombay during the period discussed, compared with 12% in the preceding two years.
sources.bn_title: ভারতের ব্যাংক হার, ১৮৯১: কলকাতায় ৪% ও বোম্বাইয়ে ৫%
sources.bn_historical_claim: সরকারি সংসদীয় বিবরণে বলা হয়, আলোচিত সময়ে কলকাতায় ব্যাংক হার ৪% এবং বোম্বাইয়ে ৫%-এর বেশি ওঠেনি; আগের দুই বছরে তা ১২% পর্যন্ত ছিল।
sources.notes: This is a distinct banking-market layer; it does not identify individual banks or establish a universal India-wide rate.
sources.primary_passage: the rate of discount was very low, the bank rate never rising above 4 in Calcutta and 5 in Bombay, as compared to 12 in the two preceding years.
sources.passage_locator: Hansard, House of Commons, 4 August 1891, vol. 356, 'East India (Revenue Accounts)' financial discussion.
sources.source_identity: Official parliamentary record reporting bank-rate conditions in Calcutta and Bombay during the East India financial discussion.
sources.what_passage_establishes: It establishes the stated maximum bank rates for Calcutta and Bombay in the period discussed and the comparison with the preceding two years.
sources.evidence_limits: It does not identify individual banks, provide a complete causal explanation, or establish that the quoted rates were universal across India.

sources.title: India Currency Notes, 1891: Circulation Rises from 1,577 to 2,766 Lakhs as Banks Hold Notes as Reserve
sources.historical_claim: The official parliamentary record reported that the circulation of Indian currency notes rose from 1,577 lakhs at the end of March 1890 to 2,766 lakhs at the end of January 1891, and stated that banks apparently retained the notes as a convenient reserve rather than for ordinary circulation.
sources.verification_status: Verified direct official parliamentary record.
sources.primary_passage: Another phenomenon was the increase in the circulation of currency notes, which rose from 1,577 lakhs at the end of March, 1890, to 2,766 lakhs
sources.passage_locator: Hansard, House of Commons, 4 August 1891, vol. 356, cols. 1326–1327, 'East India (Revenue Accounts)'.
sources.passage_status: Exact primary passage verified.
sources.source_identity: Official parliamentary record of the East India Revenue Accounts debate, including the Under Secretary of State for India's statement on currency-note circulation and bank reserve holdings.
sources.edition: Historic Hansard, House of Commons debate record
sources.what_passage_establishes: It establishes the reported increase in currency-note circulation between March 1890 and January 1891. The immediately following official statement says the notes were apparently retained by banks as a convenient mode of holding a reserve and places the phenomenon in the context of silver-market fluctuations.
sources.evidence_limits: The passage does not by itself establish the legal composition of the currency reserve, the individual banks involved, the causes of the increase with certainty, or a complete monetary-policy interpretation. The speaker expressly presents the reserve-use explanation as apparent rather than conclusive.
sources.notes: This is a distinct monetary-regime layer, not a duplicate of the 1890 Council-bill sale, exchange-rate, or railway records.
sources.bn_title: ভারতের মুদ্রা নোট, ১৮৯১: ব্যাংকগুলোর রিজার্ভ হিসেবে নোট ধরে রাখার সময় প্রচলন ১,৫৭৭ থেকে ২,৭৬৬ লাখে বৃদ্ধি
sources.bn_historical_claim: সরকারি সংসদীয় নথিতে জানানো হয় যে ১৮৯০ সালের মার্চের শেষে ভারতের মুদ্রা নোটের প্রচলন ১,৫৭৭ লাখ থেকে ১৮৯১ সালের জানুয়ারির শেষে ২,৭৬৬ লাখে বৃদ্ধি পায়; এবং বলা হয়, ব্যাংকগুলো সাধারণ প্রচলনের পরিবর্তে নোটগুলো সুবিধাজনক রিজার্ভ হিসেবে ধরে রাখছিল বলে মনে হয়।

sources.bn_historical_claim: ভারতের আর্থিক বিবৃতিতে দুর্ভিক্ষ-বীমার জন্য নির্ধারিত ১৫ লক্ষ রুপি বার্ষিক উদ্বৃত্ত পূর্ণভাবে পুনঃস্থাপনের কথা জানানো হয়।

sources.title: Indian Railway Gold-Interest and Exchange Burden, 1891
sources.historical_claim: Indian railways had been largely financed by borrowing in England, leaving interest payable in gold and exposing Indian revenues to exchange losses.
sources.bn_title: ভারতীয় রেলওয়ের স্বর্ণ-সুদ ও বিনিময়-ঝুঁকি, ১৮৯১
sources.bn_historical_claim: ভারতীয় রেলওয়ের অর্থায়নের বড় অংশ ইংল্যান্ডে ঋণ নিয়ে হওয়ায় সুদ স্বর্ণে পরিশোধ করতে হতো এবং বিনিময় হারের পতনে ভারতীয় রাজস্ব ক্ষতিগ্রস্ত হতো।
sources.notes: Distinct mechanism: external borrowing currency plus gold interest created exchange exposure charged against Indian revenues.
sources.primary_passage: most of the money with which these railways have been constructed has been borrowed in England, the interest has to be paid in gold; and, owing to the fall in the rate of exchange, the profit of 4¾ per cent., which would be otherwise realised by Indian railways, is turned into a loss, and every year the revenues of India are charged with a certain sum in respect of the excess of railway expenditure over railway receipts.
sources.passage_locator: Hansard, House of Commons, 4 August 1891, vol. 356, cols. 1324–1325, 'East India (Revenue Accounts)' / Committee.
sources.source_identity: Official parliamentary record of the East India financial discussion concerning railway capital, borrowing in England, gold interest and exchange exposure.
sources.what_passage_establishes: It establishes the stated English borrowing, gold-interest obligation, exchange exposure and resulting charge against Indian revenues.
sources.evidence_limits: It does not establish the complete lifetime exchange burden, every borrowing instrument or lender, or the position of every individual railway line.

sources.title: India Rupee Paper, 1891: Rx.5.138 Million Exported to England as Silver-Payable Securities Gained in Gold Value
sources.historical_claim: The official parliamentary record stated that rupee paper exported from India to England increased to Rx.5,138,000 in 1890–91, attributing this to the higher value in gold then attached in London to securities payable in silver.
sources.verification_status: Verified direct official parliamentary record.
sources.primary_passage: whereas in 1889–90 rupee paper was sent back from England to the amount of Rx.67,000; in 1890–91 it was exported from India to England to the amount of Rx.5,138,000, owing to the higher value, measured in gold, which securities payable in silver were bearing in London at the time.
sources.passage_locator: Hansard, House of Commons, 4 August 1891, vol. 356, cols. 1326–1327, 'East India (Revenue Accounts)'.
sources.passage_status: Exact primary passage verified.
sources.source_identity: Official parliamentary record of the East India Revenue Accounts debate, reporting rupee-paper movements between India and England and their relationship to London valuation of silver-payable securities.
sources.edition: Historic Hansard, House of Commons debate record
sources.what_passage_establishes: It establishes the reported movement of rupee paper from India to England in 1890–91 and the official explanation linking that movement to the gold value then assigned in London to securities payable in silver.
sources.evidence_limits: It does not identify the individual securities, holders, banks, or transactions behind the aggregate figure, and it records the parliamentary speaker's explanation rather than an independent market study.
sources.notes: Distinct from the 1891 currency-note reserve record: this layer concerns cross-border movement of rupee-denominated paper and London valuation of silver-payable securities.
sources.bn_title: ভারতের রুপি-পেপার, ১৮৯১: রূপায় প্রদেয় সিকিউরিটিজের লন্ডনমূল্য বৃদ্ধির সময় ৫১.৩৮ লাখ রুপি ইংল্যান্ডে রপ্তানি
sources.bn_historical_claim: সরকারি সংসদীয় নথিতে জানানো হয় যে ১৮৯০–৯১ সালে ভারত থেকে ইংল্যান্ডে রুপি-পেপারের রপ্তানি ৫১,৩৮,০০০ রুপিতে পৌঁছায়; এর কারণ হিসেবে লন্ডনে রূপায় প্রদেয় সিকিউরিটিজের সোনায় পরিমাপিত উচ্চতর মূল্যকে উল্লেখ করা হয়।

sources.title: India Trade Surplus and Treasure Imports, 1891: Export Surplus Falls to Rx.9.939 Million as Treasure Imports Rise to Rx.13.635 Million
sources.historical_claim: The official parliamentary record reported that India's export surplus for June–January fell to Rx.9,939,000 in 1890–91 while net imports of treasure rose to Rx.13,635,000, producing a surplus of imports of Rx.3,696,000.
sources.verification_status: Verified direct official parliamentary record.
sources.bn_title: ভারতের বাণিজ্য উদ্বৃত্ত ও ধনসম্পদ আমদানি, ১৮৯১
sources.bn_historical_claim: সরকারি সংসদীয় রেকর্ডে দেখা যায়, ১৮৯০–৯১ সালে জুন–জানুয়ারি সময়ে ভারতের রপ্তানি উদ্বৃত্ত কমে ৯৯.৩৯ লক্ষ রুপিতে নেমে আসে এবং ধনসম্পদের নিট আমদানি বেড়ে ১৩৬.৩৫ লক্ষ রুপিতে পৌঁছে।
sources.notes: Distinct trade-and-specie-flow layer; it should not be treated as proof of ownership or a single causal explanation.
sources.primary_passage: The surplus of exports over imports, which had been Rx.18,173,000 in 1889–90, and which had averaged Rx.13,726,000 in the four years ending with 1889–90, fell to Rx.9,939,000 in 1890–91, and the net imports of treasure which had been Rx.8,763,000 in 1889–90, and which in the four years previous averaged Rx.6,791,000, rose to Rx.13,635,000 in 1890–91; and, in consequence of this, instead of a surplus of total exports in these months, which had been Rx.9,410,000 in 1889–90, and which in the four years averaged Rx.6,935,000, there was a surplus of imports in 1890–91 amounting to Rx.3,696,000.
sources.passage_locator: Hansard, House of Commons, 4 August 1891, vol. 356, cols. 1325–1326, 'East India (Revenue Accounts)' / Committee.
sources.passage_status: Exact primary passage verified.
sources.source_identity: Official parliamentary record of the East India financial discussion reporting Indian trade balances and net imports of treasure.
sources.edition: Historic Hansard, House of Commons debate record
sources.what_passage_establishes: It establishes the reported fall in the export surplus, rise in net treasure imports, and movement to a total import surplus for the specified June–January comparison.
sources.evidence_limits: It does not establish the ultimate ownership of the imported treasure, its precise private-versus-government composition, or a single causal explanation for the trade movement.

sources.title: India Fixed Rupee Exchange Rate, 1891: Secretary of State Fixed 1s. 6½d. for the 1891–92 Transactions
sources.historical_claim: The Secretary of State for India fixed a rate of 1s. 6½d. for all transactions for 1891–92, irrespective of market fluctuations.
sources.bn_title: ভারতের নির্ধারিত রুপি বিনিময় হার, ১৮৯১: ১৮৯১–৯২ সালের লেনদেনের জন্য ১ শিলিং ৬½ পেন্স
sources.bn_historical_claim: ভারতের সেক্রেটারি অব স্টেট ১৮৯১–৯২ সালের সব লেনদেনের জন্য বাজারের ওঠানামা নির্বিশেষে ১ শিলিং ৬½ পেন্স হার নির্ধারণ করেন।
sources.notes: The official parliamentary statement directly describes the annual fixed-rate rule and states the 1891–92 rate.
sources.primary_passage: a rate is fixed for all transactions for the ensuing year, irrespective of the fluctuations of the market. The fixed rate for 1891–2 is 1s. 6½d.
sources.passage_locator: Hansard, House of Commons, 5 May 1891, vol. 353, cols. 132–133, 'Rupee Rate of Exchange'.
sources.source_identity: Official parliamentary record of the House of Commons discussion of the Indian rupee rate of exchange and the annual fixed rate for transactions.
sources.what_passage_establishes: It establishes that a rate was fixed for all transactions for the ensuing year irrespective of market fluctuations, and that the fixed rate for 1891–92 was 1s. 6½d.
sources.evidence_limits: It does not establish the complete administrative procedure, every class of transaction in practice, the resulting fiscal gain or loss, or the broader rationale for the chosen rate.

sources.title: India Currency Crisis and Proposed Mint Closure, 1892
sources.historical_claim: The official parliamentary account states that, amid rupee depreciation, threatened further silver inflows, and uncertainty over an international monetary agreement, the Government of India proposed conditional closure of the Indian Mints to free public silver coinage and arrangements for a gold standard.
sources.verification_status: Primary-source parliamentary record verified through the official Historic Hansard account of the Indian Budget; the account explicitly reports the Government of India’s 1892 currency position and proposal.
sources.bn_title: ভারতের মুদ্রা সংকট ও টাকশাল বন্ধের প্রস্তাব, ১৮৯২
sources.bn_historical_claim: সরকারি সংসদীয় বিবরণে বলা হয়, রুপির অবমূল্যায়ন, সম্ভাব্য অতিরিক্ত রূপা-প্রবাহ এবং আন্তর্জাতিক মুদ্রা-সমঝোতার অনিশ্চয়তার মধ্যে ভারত সরকার জনসাধারণের জন্য রূপার অবাধ মুদ্রা-প্রচলন বন্ধ এবং স্বর্ণমান প্রবর্তনের ব্যবস্থা প্রস্তাব করেছিল।
sources.notes: This record isolates the 1892 policy-proposal layer. It is not the 1893 implementation layer: the later Act stopping free public silver coinage is separately evidenced and should not be conflated with the 1892 proposal.
sources.primary_passage: Accordingly, they proposed that, failing a satisfactory agreement with the United States or other nations, the Indian Mints should be closed to the free coinage of silver for the public, and that arrangements should be made for the introduction of a gold standard into India.
sources.passage_locator: House of Commons, Hansard, 21 September 1893, vol. 17, cols. 1849–1851, “East India Revenue Accounts”; the passage reports the Government of India’s currency position and proposal in 1892.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — exact official parliamentary wording verified.
sources.source_identity: Official House of Commons Hansard report of the Indian Budget, delivered by Mr. G. Russell, Under Secretary of State for India, 21 September 1893, reporting the Government of India’s 1892 currency position and proposals.
sources.edition: Hansard, House of Commons, 21 September 1893, vol. 17, cols. 1794–1894, “East India Revenue Accounts”.
sources.what_passage_establishes: The official parliamentary account establishes that the Government of India, facing a falling rupee and concern over silver inflows and international monetary uncertainty in 1892, proposed conditional closure of the Indian Mints to free public silver coinage and arrangements for a gold standard.
sources.evidence_limits: It establishes the proposal as officially reported, not implementation in 1892. The later 1893 mint-closure Act and its operational exchange arrangements are separate evidence layers.
scholarly_references: Report of the Committee Appointed to Inquire into the Indian Currency, HMSO, 1893 (Herschell Committee).
J. Laurence Laughlin, The History of Bimetallism in the United States, discussion of the Indian Currency Committee and Indian monetary policy.
sources.publication_status: A-grade — exact official parliamentary passage and locator locked; the 1892 proposal is kept distinct from the 1893 implementation.

sources.title: India Mints Closed to Free Silver Coinage, 1893
sources.historical_claim: The Government of India implemented the Herschell Committee plan by closing the Indian Mints to free public silver coinage and establishing a 16d. per rupee exchange arrangement for gold and sovereign transactions.
sources.verification_status: Primary-source parliamentary record verified: the First Lord of the Treasury communicated the Viceroy's telegram reporting the Indian Council's Act and its immediate effect.
sources.bn_title: ভারতে অবাধ রূপা-মুদ্রণ বন্ধ, ১৮৯৩
sources.bn_historical_claim: ভারত সরকার হার্শেল কমিটির পরিকল্পনা কার্যকর করে ভারতীয় টাকশালগুলোতে জনসাধারণের জন্য অবাধ রূপা মুদ্রণ বন্ধ করে এবং স্বর্ণ ও সার্বভৌম মুদ্রার বিনিময়ে প্রতি রুপিতে ১৬ পেন্সের ব্যবস্থা করে।
sources.notes: This is the implementation layer following the separately deployed 1892 proposal. The parliamentary record also states that gold was not yet made legal tender.
sources.primary_passage: Council has passed an Act, which takes effect at once, to carry out the plan recommended by Lord Herschell's Committee. Act provides for close of Indian Mints to free coinage of silver from and after date of passing. Arrangements will be made to issue rupees from the Mints in exchange for gold and sovereigns at the rate of 16d. per rupee [until further notice] and to receive sovereigns and half-sovereigns at Public Treasuries, in payment of Government dues, at the same rate. It is intended to introduce a gold standard into India, but gold will not be made a legal tender at present.
sources.passage_locator: House of Commons, Hansard, 26 June 1893, vol. 14, cols. 59–61, “The Indian Currency”; the passage is the Viceroy's telegram communicated by Mr. W. E. Gladstone.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — exact official parliamentary wording verified.
sources.source_identity: Official House of Commons report of 26 June 1893 communicating the Viceroy of India's telegram on the Indian Council's currency Act.
sources.edition: Hansard, House of Commons, 26 June 1893, vol. 14, cols. 59–61.
sources.what_passage_establishes: The report establishes that the Indian Council had passed an Act effective immediately to close the Mints to free public silver coinage, issue rupees against gold and sovereigns at 16d. per rupee, accept sovereigns and half-sovereigns for Government dues at the same rate, and pursue a gold standard without yet making gold legal tender.
sources.evidence_limits: It establishes the June 1893 implementation as officially reported; it does not by itself establish subsequent legal-tender legislation, later exchange-rate changes, or long-run economic effects.
scholarly_references: Report of the Committee Appointed to Inquire into the Indian Currency, HMSO, 1893 (Herschell Committee).

Ulrich Bindseil, Central Banking before 1800: A Rehabilitation, for comparative institutional context; modern scholarship on the Indian monetary transition should be read alongside the primary record.
sources.publication_status: A-grade — exact official parliamentary passage and locator locked; implementation is kept distinct from the 1892 proposal.

sources.title: East India Loan (£10,000,000), 1893
sources.historical_claim: Parliament authorised the Secretary of State for India in Council to raise up to £10,000,000 sterling for the public service in India, while the debate explicitly linked rupee depreciation against the sovereign to the growing cost of servicing gold-payable debts in Britain and pressure on the Indian Exchequer.
sources.verification_status: Primary-source parliamentary record verified in the official Historic Hansard report of the Third Reading of the East India Loan (£10,000,000) Bill.
sources.bn_title: ১৮৯৩ সালের ইস্ট ইন্ডিয়া ১ কোটি পাউন্ড ঋণ
sources.bn_historical_claim: সংসদে ভারত সরকারের জন্য সর্বোচ্চ ১ কোটি পাউন্ড স্টার্লিং ঋণ তোলার অনুমোদন দেওয়া হয়; একই বিতর্কে রুপির অবমূল্যায়ন, ব্রিটেনে স্বর্ণে পরিশোধযোগ্য ঋণের সেবা এবং ভারতীয় রাজকোষের ওপর চাপের সরাসরি সম্পর্ক ব্যাখ্যা করা হয়।
sources.notes: This record isolates the sovereign-debt borrowing layer. It is distinct from the June 1893 mint-closure implementation record: the loan authority and the debate's exchange/debt rationale are separately evidenced here.
sources.primary_passage: This Bill is for the purpose of authorising a loan of £10,000,000 sterling to the Indian Government, but the discussion of the previous stages have gone beyond the examination of that special proposal.
sources.passage_locator: House of Commons, Hansard, 18 December 1893, vol. 19, cols. 1618–1671, “East India Loan (£10,000,000) Bill. (No. 475.)”; Mr. Courtney's Third Reading speech, opening statement.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — exact official parliamentary wording verified.
sources.source_identity: Official House of Commons Hansard report of the Third Reading of the East India Loan (£10,000,000) Bill, including Mr. Courtney's explanation of the sterling borrowing authority and its exchange/debt context.
sources.edition: Hansard, House of Commons, 18 December 1893, vol. 19, cols. 1618–1671, “East India Loan (£10,000,000) Bill. (No. 475.)”.
sources.what_passage_establishes: The passage establishes that Parliament was being asked to authorise a £10,000,000 sterling loan to the Indian Government. In the same debate, the continued depreciation of the rupee is explicitly described as increasing the Indian Government's pecuniary loss because debts in Britain were payable in gold and larger rupee receipts were required to meet those sterling obligations.
sources.evidence_limits: The quoted opening passage establishes the borrowing authority, while the surrounding debate establishes the stated exchange/debt rationale. These passages do not by themselves establish the final amount actually drawn, final loan terms, ultimate holders, or long-run fiscal effects.
scholarly_references: Report of the Committee Appointed to Inquire into the Indian Currency, HMSO, 1893 (Herschell Committee).
J. Laurence Laughlin, The History of Bimetallism in the United States, discussion of Indian currency policy and the 1893 monetary transition.

sources.title: Indian Four Per Cent Rupee Loan Converted to 3½ Per Cent, 1894
sources.historical_claim: During the 1894–95 financial year the Government of India converted its Four per cent. Rupee Loan into debt bearing 3½ per cent. interest, accepting an immediate conversion cost in return for lower future interest expenditure.
sources.verification_status: Primary-source parliamentary account verified: the Secretary of State for India reported the completed conversion in the official East India Revenue Accounts debate.
sources.bn_title: ভারতের ৪ শতাংশ রুপি ঋণ ৩½ শতাংশে রূপান্তর, ১৮৯৪
sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৮৯৪–৯৫ অর্থবছরে ভারত সরকার ৪ শতাংশ রুপি ঋণকে ৩½ শতাংশ সুদযুক্ত ঋণে রূপান্তর করে; তাৎক্ষণিক রূপান্তর ব্যয়ের বিনিময়ে ভবিষ্যৎ সুদ ব্যয় কমানোর ব্যবস্থা করা হয়।
sources.notes: This isolates the 1894–95 rupee-debt conversion layer. It is distinct from the 1887 sterling India Stock conversion and the 1888–89 four-and-a-half to four per cent rupee-debt conversion records.
sources.primary_passage: In the middle of the financial year a most successful conversion of the debt was made, for which I beg to offer my congratulations to my predecessor. The Four per cent. Rupee Loan was converted into a debt bearing interest at 3½ per cent., but there was a certain necessary expenditure attending this conversion which increased the estimated expenditure of the year by Rx. 301,000. This increase, however, will bring a more than corresponding gain in subsequent years in the diminution of the interest which hereafter will have to be paid.
sources.passage_locator: House of Commons, Hansard, 4 September 1895, vol. 36, cols. 1695–1740, “East India Revenue Accounts”; the Secretary of State for India's statement on the 1894–95 revised estimate.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — exact official parliamentary wording verified.
sources.source_identity: Official House of Commons Hansard report of the East India Revenue Accounts, in which the Secretary of State for India reported the successful conversion of the Four per cent. Rupee Loan during the 1894–95 financial year.
sources.edition: Hansard, House of Commons, 4 September 1895, vol. 36, cols. 1695–1740, “East India Revenue Accounts”.
sources.what_passage_establishes: The official account establishes that during the 1894–95 financial year the Four per cent. Rupee Loan was converted into 3½ per cent. debt, that the conversion increased the estimated expenditure of the year by Rx.301,000, and that the Government expected more than corresponding future savings through reduced interest payments.
sources.evidence_limits: The passage is a later official parliamentary report of the completed 1894–95 conversion. It does not by itself establish the full principal amount converted, detailed conversion terms, holder composition, or realized long-run savings beyond the official statement.
scholarly_references: Government of India / India Office financial accounts and parliamentary papers concerning Indian public debt conversion.
Ulrich Bindseil, Central Banking before 1800, for comparative institutional context; the primary parliamentary record remains controlling for this event.
sources.publication_status: A-grade — exact official parliamentary passage and locator locked; the 1894–95 conversion is kept distinct from earlier India stock and rupee-debt conversions.

sources.title: Indian Tariff Act, 1894: Customs-Duty Regime
sources.historical_claim: The Government of India enacted the Indian Tariff Act, 1894 (VIII of 1894), amending the customs-duty law across British India during a period of acute fiscal pressure.
sources.verification_status: Primary statutory text verified from a contemporary Government of India Legislative Department reproduction; the Act is independently indexed in the official Historic Hansard Act record.
sources.bn_title: ভারতীয় ট্যারিফ আইন, ১৮৯৪: শুল্ক-ব্যবস্থা
sources.bn_historical_claim: তীব্র আর্থিক চাপের সময় ভারত সরকার ১৮৯৪ সালের ভারতীয় ট্যারিফ আইন (VIII of 1894) প্রণয়ন করে এবং ব্রিটিশ ভারতে কাস্টমস শুল্কের আইনগত কাঠামো পরিবর্তন করে।
sources.notes: This record isolates the statutory customs-law layer. It should not be conflated with the later parliamentary measurement of the tariff's revenue yield or with the separate 1894 rupee-debt conversion.
sources.primary_passage: An Act to amend the law relating to Customs-duties, and for other purposes. It is hereby enacted as follows:— 1. (1) This Act may be called the Indian Tariff Act, 1894. (2) It extends to the whole of British India except Aden and Perim. (3) It shall come into force at once.
sources.passage_locator: Government of India, Legislative Department, Indian Tariff Act, 1894 (VIII of 1894), section 1; enacted 10 March 1894.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — exact statutory wording verified from a contemporary primary-text reproduction.
sources.source_identity: Government of India Legislative Department, Indian Tariff Act, 1894 (VIII of 1894), enacted 10 March 1894; contemporary statutory text.
sources.edition: Indian Tariff Act, 1894 (VIII of 1894), Government of India Legislative Department.
sources.what_passage_establishes: The statute establishes the enactment, territorial scope, and immediate commencement of a new Indian customs-duty law. Contemporary financial reporting later records additional Customs revenue under the new tariff, including revenue associated with silver imports.
sources.evidence_limits: Section 1 alone does not establish the full schedule of rates or the eventual revenue yield. Those details require the Act's schedules and the subsequent financial accounts.
scholarly_references: Government of India Legislative Department, Indian Tariff Act, 1894 (VIII of 1894).
House of Commons Hansard, East India Revenue Accounts, 4 September 1895, reporting the revenue effects of the new Customs Bill.

sources.title: Royal Commission on Indian Expenditure Proposed, 1895
sources.historical_claim: The Secretary of State for India stated that the inquiry into Indian expenditure would be conducted by a Royal Commission, establishing a distinct institutional review mechanism for Indian financial administration.
sources.verification_status: Primary parliamentary statement verified in Historic Hansard; the Commission's first meeting and archival minutes are independently confirmed by later contemporaneous/archival records.
sources.primary_passage: It is proposed that the Inquiry into Indian Expenditure should be conducted by a Royal Commission. It is not usual to discuss in this House the terms of a reference to a Royal Commission.
sources.passage_locator: House of Commons Hansard, 9 May 1895, vol. 33, cols. 802–803, “Indian Affairs.”
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — exact official Hansard wording verified.
sources.source_identity: House of Commons, Hansard, 9 May 1895, vol. 33, cols. 802–803; statement by Secretary of State for India Henry Fowler.
sources.edition: Historic Hansard parliamentary record
sources.what_passage_establishes: The Government chose a Royal Commission as the institutional vehicle for the inquiry into Indian expenditure.
sources.evidence_limits: The quoted passage does not reproduce the appointment instrument or full terms of reference. Those are not inferred. A later Hansard statement records that the first meeting was scheduled for 26 June 1895, and the British Library catalogue records the Commission's minutes from 26 June 1895.

sources.title: Indian Council Bills, 1894–95: Record Sales
sources.historical_claim: In 1894–95 the Indian Government sold a record rupee volume of Council bills, Rx.30,970,000, realizing £16,905,102; the official account contrasts this with 1881–82, when a smaller rupee volume realized more sterling because of exchange values.
sources.verification_status: Primary parliamentary account verified in official Historic Hansard.
sources.primary_passage: Now, the bills sold last year amounted to Rx. 30,970,000 and it realised £16,905,102. I am sorry to say that, although this is by far the largest amount of bills which have ever been sold, owing to the great fall in the value of the rupee it has not realised the largest amount in gold, for in 1881–2 Rx. 22,211,000 realised £18,412,429.
sources.passage_locator: House of Commons Hansard, 4 September 1895, vol. 36, cols. 1695–1740, East India Revenue Accounts; statement concerning 1894–95 bills sold.
sources.source_identity: House of Commons, Historic Hansard, East India Revenue Accounts, 4 September 1895.
sources.what_passage_establishes: A record rupee volume of Indian Government bills was sold in 1894–95, with the sterling realization materially affected by the rupee's lower gold value.
sources.evidence_limits: Does not identify individual purchasers, auction dates, bid spreads, or prove that all sterling remittances were financed through Council bills.

sources.title: Indian Sterling Debt from Failed Council-Bill Sales, 1895
sources.historical_claim: The official East India Revenue Accounts reported that £9,386,000 of debt had been incurred in the preceding period through failures to sell Indian Government bills, showing a direct link between bill-sale difficulties and sterling borrowing.
sources.verification_status: Primary parliamentary account verified in official Historic Hansard.
sources.primary_passage: During that time there has been a certain amount of debt raised in this country, and whenever a debt is raised for the purpose of meeting the annual obligations through inability to sell bills, the money so raised does benefit the year of the expenditure, and in a manner which cannot be brought to account, because, by diminishing the number of rupees that would otherwise be sold, it advances the price of those that are sold. The amount of the debt which was incurred in this period through the failure of the sale of bills amounts to £9,386,000.
sources.passage_locator: House of Commons Hansard, 4 September 1895, vol. 36, cols. 1704–1705, East India Revenue Accounts; discussion of debt incurred through failure to sell bills.
sources.source_identity: House of Commons, Historic Hansard, East India Revenue Accounts, 4 September 1895.
sources.what_passage_establishes: The official parliamentary statement establishes that sterling debt was raised to meet annual obligations when Indian Government bills could not be sold, and that the amount attributed to such failures during the period discussed was £9,386,000.
sources.evidence_limits: The passage does not identify each individual loan, its issue date, lender, coupon, maturity, or the precise allocation of the £9,386,000 across separate borrowing operations. It establishes the aggregate parliamentary statement and the stated causal connection to failed bill sales only.

sources.title: Four per cent. Rupee Loan Converted to 3½ per cent. Debt, 1895
sources.historical_claim: The Secretary of State for India reported to Parliament that the Four per cent. Rupee Loan had been successfully converted into debt bearing 3½ per cent interest, with conversion costs of Rx.301,000 expected to be more than offset by subsequent interest savings.
sources.verification_status: Primary parliamentary account verified in official Historic Hansard.
sources.primary_passage: In the middle of the financial year a most successful conversion of the debt was made, for which I beg to offer my congratulations to my predecessor. The Four per cent. Rupee Loan was converted into a debt bearing interest at 3½ per cent., but there was a certain necessary expenditure attending this conversion which increased the estimated expenditure of the year by Rx. 301,000. This increase, however, will bring a more than corresponding gain in subsequent years in the diminution of the interest which hereafter will have to be paid.
sources.passage_locator: House of Commons Hansard, 4 September 1895, vol. 36, col. 1699; East India Revenue Accounts.
sources.source_identity: Lord George Hamilton, Secretary of State for India, statement on East India Revenue Accounts before the House of Commons Committee, 4 September 1895.
sources.edition: House of Commons Hansard, 4 September 1895, vol. 36, cols. 1695–1740; East India Revenue Accounts.
sources.what_passage_establishes: The parliamentary statement establishes that the existing 4% Rupee Loan was converted to a 3½% interest-bearing debt and that the government recorded Rx.301,000 of necessary conversion expenditure while expecting greater subsequent savings in interest.
sources.evidence_limits: The passage does not by itself specify the original principal amount converted, the exact conversion terms offered to holders, dates of subscription or settlement, underwriting arrangements, or the complete legal instrument authorising the conversion. Those details should not be inferred from this passage.

sources.bn_historical_claim: ভারতের সেক্রেটারি অব স্টেট সংসদে জানান যে ৪ শতাংশ রুপি ঋণকে ৩½ শতাংশ সুদের ঋণে রূপান্তর করা হয়েছিল; রূপান্তরের জন্য £ নয়, Rx.৩০১,০০০ ব্যয় হলেও পরবর্তী সুদ সাশ্রয় তা ছাড়িয়ে যাবে বলে প্রত্যাশা করা হয়।

sources.title: India’s London Obligations: Exchange Burden Reaches 27 Per Cent of Net Imperial Revenue, 1895
sources.historical_claim: The Secretary of State for India reported that the rupee cost of meeting India’s obligations in London had risen from Rx.3,535,900 in 1884–5 to Rx.14,751,600 in 1894–5, with the increased remittance requirement absorbing 27 per cent of total net Imperial revenue.
sources.verification_status: Primary parliamentary account verified in official Historic Hansard.
sources.primary_passage: In 1884–5 the total charge on the revenue of India for meeting its obligations in London was a charge amounting to 8 per cent. of the total net revenue of the country, the amount being Rx. 3,535,900. Last year that amount rose to Rx. 14,751,600. The revenue has largely increased in the interval, but the increased number of rupees which the Indian Government have to remit to meet their obligations absorbs 27 per cent. of the total net Imperial revenue.
sources.passage_locator: House of Commons Hansard, 4 September 1895, vol. 36, cols. 1705–1706, East India Revenue Accounts; discussion of the cost of meeting India’s London obligations and the effect of exchange.
sources.source_identity: House of Commons, Historic Hansard, East India Revenue Accounts, 4 September 1895; statement by Lord George Hamilton, Secretary of State for India.
sources.what_passage_establishes: The official parliamentary statement establishes a quantified increase in the rupee charge required to meet India’s obligations in London and states that, by 1894–5, the exchange-related remittance burden absorbed 27 per cent of net Imperial revenue.
sources.evidence_limits: The passage does not itemize every London obligation, distinguish principal from interest across all components, or establish that exchange movements were the sole cause of the entire increase. It establishes the reported aggregate charge and its stated share of net Imperial revenue.
sources.bn_title: ভারতের লন্ডনীয় দায়: বিনিময়-ভার নেট সাম্রাজ্যিক রাজস্বের ২৭ শতাংশে পৌঁছায়, ১৮৯৫
sources.bn_historical_claim: ভারতের সেক্রেটারি অব স্টেট জানান যে লন্ডনে ভারতের দায় মেটাতে রুপি-ভিত্তিক ব্যয় ১৮৮৪–৮৫ সালের Rx.৩,৫৩৫,৯০০ থেকে ১৮৯৪–৯৫ সালে Rx.১৪,৭৫১,৬০০-এ বেড়েছিল এবং অতিরিক্ত রেমিট্যান্সের প্রয়োজন নেট সাম্রাজ্যিক রাজস্বের ২৭ শতাংশ শোষণ করছিল।

sources.title: India’s Borrowing Credit Reaches Its Highest Point, 1895
sources.historical_claim: The Secretary of State for India identified the credit available to the Indian Government for borrowing purposes as having reached a higher point than ever previously attained during the 1894–95 financial year.
sources.verification_status: Primary parliamentary statement verified in official Historic Hansard.
sources.primary_passage: The deficit has been converted into a considerable surplus under the most depressed conditions yet known in connection with exchange; there has been the largest sale of bills upon India; the credit for borrowing purposes is raised to a higher point than has ever before been attained; and the last, but I am afraid not the least, feature is the imposition of Import Duties upon cotton goods.
sources.passage_locator: House of Commons Hansard, 4 September 1895, vol. 36, col. 1699, East India Revenue Accounts; Lord George Hamilton’s summary of the distinctive features of the 1894–95 financial year.
sources.source_identity: House of Commons, Historic Hansard, East India Revenue Accounts, 4 September 1895; statement by Lord George Hamilton, Secretary of State for India.
sources.what_passage_establishes: The parliamentary statement explicitly records that the Indian Government’s credit for borrowing purposes had risen to a level described as higher than any previously attained, placing sovereign borrowing capacity among the stated defining features of the 1894–95 financial position.
sources.evidence_limits: The passage does not identify a numerical credit rating, precise market yield, individual borrowing issue, or the specific transaction that produced the stated improvement. It establishes the official contemporary assessment of borrowing credit only.

sources.title: India’s Borrowing Powers Reduced to £9.377 Million After 1898–99 Financing, 1899
sources.historical_claim: The Secretary of State reported that after the £10 million increase in borrowing authority secured in 1898, and after financing exceptional Indian requirements and public-works capital outlay, the remaining borrowing powers stood at £9,377,000; the Government did not propose to borrow at home or in India for the forthcoming year unless circumstances forced it.
sources.bn_title: ১৮৯৮–৯৯ অর্থায়নের পর ভারতের অবশিষ্ট ঋণগ্রহণ ক্ষমতা £৯.৩৭৭ মিলিয়নে নেমে আসে
sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৮৯৮ সালের অতিরিক্ত ঋণগ্রহণ ক্ষমতা ও পরবর্তী অর্থায়নের পর ১৮৯৯ সালে সেক্রেটারি অব স্টেট জানান যে অবশিষ্ট ঋণগ্রহণ ক্ষমতা £৯.৩৭৭ মিলিয়নে নেমে এসেছে।
sources.verification_status: Primary-source official Hansard record verified
sources.primary_passage: The total amount, therefore, of the borrowing powers, which at this time last year was at the disposal of the Secretary of State was £10,418,000, and I proposed, as I informed the House at the outset, to raise a loan of six millions sterling, though I hoped to be able, in the course of the year, to discharge considerable amounts of debentures and other debts which became due. This has been done, and I am glad to be able to inform the House that at the present moment my borrowing powers amount to £9,377,000, or in other words, I have been able to finance the exceptional requirements of the Indian Government and the capital outlay on public works by adding only about one million sterling in the course of the year to the obligations of India in this country.
sources.passage_locator: House of Commons Hansard, 8 August 1899, vol. 76, cc. 183–184.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — official contemporary statement of remaining statutory borrowing capacity and net addition to UK obligations.
sources.source_identity: House of Commons debate on East India Revenue Accounts, 8 August 1899; Secretary of State for India Lord George Hamilton's statement on borrowing powers and financing.
sources.edition: House of Commons Debates, 8 August 1899, vol. 76, East India Revenue Accounts.
sources.what_passage_establishes: The passage establishes that borrowing authority available a year earlier totaled £10,418,000 and that after financing exceptional Indian requirements and public-works capital outlay, remaining borrowing powers were £9,377,000. It also establishes that this financing added only about £1 million to India's UK obligations during the year.
sources.evidence_limits: It does not by itself identify every individual borrowing transaction, issue price, investor, maturity, or final statutory instrument. The £1 million figure is the speaker's rounded net addition to obligations, not a reconstructed transaction total.
scholarly_references: House of Commons, East India Revenue Accounts, 8 August 1899, Hansard vol. 76.

sources.title: India’s Gold Standard and Sterling Accounting Confirmed in Parliament, 1900
sources.historical_claim: The 1900 Indian Budget recorded that the Government of India had declared a gold standard in the preceding September and had shifted its accounts to sterling at 15 rupees per pound.
sources.verification_status: Primary contemporary parliamentary record verified through official Historic Hansard
sources.bn_title: ১৯০০ সালে ভারতের স্বর্ণমান ও স্টার্লিং-ভিত্তিক হিসাব পদ্ধতি সংসদে নিশ্চিত
sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৯০০ সালের ভারতীয় বাজেট আলোচনায় জানানো হয় যে আগের সেপ্টেম্বরে ভারতে স্বর্ণমান ঘোষণা করা হয়েছিল এবং হিসাব-লেনদেন প্রতি পাউন্ডে ১৫ রুপি হারে স্টার্লিংয়ে প্রকাশ করা শুরু হয়।
sources.notes: This record is kept distinct from the 1892 proposal and 1893 implementation layers. The 1900 Hansard debate is a contemporary official parliamentary confirmation of the operating monetary/accounting regime, while the declaration itself is retrospectively dated to September 1899.
sources.primary_passage: the Government in September last declared a gold standard in India
sources.passage_locator: House of Commons Hansard, 26 July 1900, vol. 86, c. 1345; The Indian Budget, opening statement by the Secretary of State for India.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — exact contemporary parliamentary wording
sources.source_identity: House of Commons debate on The Indian Budget, 26 July 1900; official Historic Hansard record, vol. 86, cc. 1345–1438.
sources.edition: House of Commons Debates (Hansard), 26 July 1900, vol. 86, cc. 1345–1438.
sources.what_passage_establishes: The passage establishes that by the July 1900 parliamentary statement the Government of India regarded a gold standard as declared in September of the preceding year. The same statement explains that Indian accounts were then stated in sterling at 15 rupees to the pound.
sources.evidence_limits: This passage is a contemporary parliamentary confirmation, not the September 1899 legal instrument itself. It does not by itself establish every statutory detail of the gold-standard regime, the full reserve mechanism, or the precise administrative steps by which the change was implemented.

sources.title: India Remits £500,000 Gold to Britain; Currency Reserve £5.748 Million, 1902
sources.historical_claim: The Secretary of State reported that India had remitted £500,000 in gold to Britain since February 1902; on 15 October the Indian Currency Reserve held £5.748 million, while total government gold holdings across the specified categories were £6.011 million.
sources.verification_status: Primary contemporary parliamentary record verified through official Historic Hansard
sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৯০২ সালে ভারত সরকার ফেব্রুয়ারির পর থেকে ব্রিটেনে £৫০০,০০০ সোনা পাঠায়। ১৫ অক্টোবর ভারতের কারেন্সি রিজার্ভে £৫.৭৪৮ মিলিয়ন এবং নির্দিষ্ট সরকারি সোনার মজুদের মোট পরিমাণ £৬.০১১ মিলিয়ন ছিল।

sources.primary_passage: The amount of gold remitted by the Government of India to this country since February last is £500,000, which has been added to the balances held by the Secretary of State in Council. The amount of gold held by the Government of India on the 15th October was as follows: Currency Reserve, £5,748,000; Government Treasuries, £88,000; Gold Reserve Fund, £175,000; total, £6,011,000.

sources.title: East India Railway Loans: £20 Million Borrowing Authority, 1905
sources.historical_claim: Parliament authorised the Secretary of State in Council of India to raise up to £20 million in the United Kingdom on the security of Indian revenues for railway construction and extension, repayment of company railway bonds or debentures guaranteed by the Secretary of State, and obligations arising from railway purchases or contract termination.
sources.verification_status: Primary contemporary parliamentary record verified through official Historic Hansard
sources.bn_title: ১৯০৫ সালে ইস্ট ইন্ডিয়া রেলওয়ের জন্য £২০ মিলিয়ন ঋণগ্রহণের ক্ষমতা
sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৯০৫ সালে পার্লামেন্ট ভারতীয় রাজস্বের নিরাপত্তায় যুক্তরাজ্য থেকে সর্বোচ্চ £২০ মিলিয়ন ঋণ তোলার অনুমোদন দেয়। অর্থটি ভারতীয় রেলওয়ে নির্মাণ ও সম্প্রসারণ, গ্যারান্টিযুক্ত রেলওয়ে বন্ড/ডিবেঞ্চারের মূলধন পরিশোধ এবং রেলওয়ে ক্রয় বা চুক্তি-সমাপ্তির দায় মেটাতে ব্যবহারের জন্য নির্ধারিত ছিল।
sources.notes: Distinct sovereign-debt/railway-capital layer. The parliamentary debate states that the larger authority reflected the intended purchase of the Bombay and Baroda Railway and other railway obligations. It does not mean the full £20 million was immediately borrowed.
sources.primary_passage: to raise in the United Kingdom on the security of the Revenues of India, by the creation and issue of capital stock, bonds, debentures, or bills, a sum not exceeding £20,000,000
sources.passage_locator: House of Commons Hansard, 23 June 1905, vol. 147, cc. 1475–1484; East India Loans (Railways), Committee resolution.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — exact parliamentary borrowing-authority wording
sources.source_identity: House of Commons, East India Loans (Railways), 23 June 1905, Hansard vol. 147, cc. 1475–1484; Secretary of State for India William Brodrick.
sources.edition: House of Commons Debates (Hansard), 23 June 1905, vol. 147.
sources.what_passage_establishes: It establishes a statutory-policy resolution for up to £20 million of UK borrowing secured on Indian revenues, with defined railway purposes including construction, extension and equipment, repayment of guaranteed railway debt, and obligations arising from railway purchases or contract termination.
sources.evidence_limits: The resolution establishes borrowing authority, not the amount actually drawn, issue price, maturity, investor identity, or final allocation. The debate's references to the Bombay and Baroda purchase explain intended use but do not by themselves establish final settlement terms.

sources.title: Indian Railways Act Amendment Preserves Capitalized Construction Interest, 1906
sources.historical_claim: Parliament continued the statutory power allowing Indian railway companies, under specified conditions, to pay interest out of capital during construction, a financing mechanism used to facilitate railway development.
sources.verification_status: Primary contemporary parliamentary record verified through official Hansard; statutory purpose confirmed in the 1906 legislative debate
sources.bn_title: ১৯০৬ সালের ভারতীয় রেলওয়ে আইন সংশোধন: নির্মাণকালে সুদ মূলধন থেকে পরিশোধের ক্ষমতা
sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৯০৬ সালে পার্লামেন্ট ভারতীয় রেলওয়ে কোম্পানিগুলোর নির্মাণকালীন সুদ নির্দিষ্ট শর্তে মূলধন থেকে পরিশোধের ক্ষমতা অব্যাহত রাখে। এই বিধান রেলওয়ে সম্প্রসারণের অর্থায়নে ব্যবহৃত একটি সরাসরি আর্থিক ব্যবস্থা ছিল।
sources.notes: Distinct from the 1905 £20 million borrowing authority: this record concerns the statutory treatment of interest during railway construction, not the amount of borrowing authority or a particular loan issue.
sources.primary_passage: That Act gave power under certain conditions to pay interest out of capital during construction. It had worked well for twelve years.
sources.passage_locator: House of Commons Hansard, 29 May 1906, Indian Railways Act Amendment Bill, Second Reading; official Hansard report.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — exact contemporary parliamentary description of the statutory financing mechanism
sources.source_identity: House of Commons, Indian Railways Act Amendment Bill, 29 May 1906; speech by Under-Secretary of State for India John Ellis.
sources.edition: House of Commons Debates (Hansard), 29 May 1906.
sources.what_passage_establishes: It establishes that the 1894 Act provided, under specified conditions, for interest during railway construction to be paid out of capital, and that the 1906 amendment was intended to make continuation of that arrangement permanent rather than repeatedly renewing it through the Expiring Laws Bill.
sources.evidence_limits: The Hansard passage describes the statutory mechanism and legislative purpose; it does not quantify individual railway companies' use of the provision, total capitalized interest, investor returns, or the complete text of the enacted 1906 statute.
scholarly_references: House of Commons, Indian Railways Act Amendment Bill, 29 May 1906, Hansard.
sources.publication_status: A-grade — contemporary parliamentary statement of a statutory railway-finance mechanism; full enacted statute remains the preferred supplementary primary text.

sources.title: East India Loans Authority: £25 Million for Railways, Irrigation and General Purposes, 1908
sources.historical_claim: Parliament authorised the Secretary of State in Council of India to raise in the United Kingdom, on the security of the Revenues of India, up to £20 million for railways and irrigation and up to £5 million for general purposes.
sources.verification_status: Primary contemporary parliamentary record verified through official Historic Hansard
sources.bn_title: ১৯০৮ সালে রেলপথ, সেচ ও সাধারণ উদ্দেশ্যে £২৫ মিলিয়ন ভারতীয় ঋণ-ক্ষমতা
sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৯০৮ সালে সংসদ ভারত সরকারের রাজস্বের জামানতে যুক্তরাজ্যে সর্বোচ্চ £২০ মিলিয়ন রেলপথ ও সেচ এবং আরও £৫ মিলিয়ন সাধারণ উদ্দেশ্যে ঋণ তোলার ক্ষমতা অনুমোদন করে।
sources.notes: Distinct from the 1905 £20 million railway-loan authority: this 1908 measure renewed and expanded borrowing authority, explicitly combining railway/irrigation purposes with a separate £5 million general-purpose power.
sources.primary_passage: That it is expedient to authorise the Secretary of State in Council of India to raise in the United Kingdom, on the security of the Revenues of India, by the creation and issue of capital stock, bonds, debentures, or bills:—(1) A sum not exceeding £20,000,000, for the following purposes: (a) The construction, extension, and equipment of railways in India by State agency or through the agency of companies; (b) the repayment of the principal of any bonds or debentures issued by any such company under the guarantee of the Secretary of State; (c) the discharge of any obligations incurred by the Secretary of State by reason of the purchase of any railway or the determination of any contract from or with such company; (d) the construction of irrigation works in India. (2) A sum not exceeding £5,000,000 for the general purposes of the Government of India.
sources.passage_locator: House of Commons Hansard, 30 July 1908, vol. 193, cc. 1903–1904; East India Loans [Railway and Irrigation Works, and General Purposes], reported Resolution.

sources.what_passage_establishes: It establishes the statutory borrowing mechanism proposed in 1908: the Secretary of State in Council of India could raise specified sums in the United Kingdom against Indian revenues, with £20 million earmarked for railway and irrigation purposes and £5 million for general Government purposes.
sources.evidence_limits: The resolution establishes borrowing authority and permitted purposes, not the subsequent amounts actually borrowed, individual bond issues, lenders or investors, transaction terms, or the economic effects of the expenditure.

sources.title: East India Revenue Accounts: Indian Government Remittances, Debt Interest and British Capital, 1909
sources.historical_claim: The 1909 East India Revenue Accounts debate recorded the Indian Government's average annual remittance to England at £21.2 million for 1904–1906, including average annual home charges of £18.5 million, of which £9.5 million was interest on debt; it also recorded £265 million of railway capital outlay in India by the end of 1907.
sources.verification_status: Primary contemporary parliamentary record verified through official Historic Hansard.
sources.passage_locator: House of Commons Hansard, 5 August 1909, vol. 8, cc. 1981–2097; relevant financial-remittance passage at cc. 1990–1992.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — exact contemporary parliamentary record.
sources.source_identity: House of Commons, East India Revenue Accounts, 5 August 1909, Hansard vol. 8, cc. 1981–2097.
sources.edition: House of Commons Debates (Hansard), 5 August 1909, vol. 8.
sources.primary_passage: If the Trade Returns are examined for 1904, 1905, and 1906, after making due allowance for the capital sent to India in connection with Government transactions, the average excess of exports over imports—or, in other words, payments by India to England for services rendered—is £23,900,000 per year during the three years that have been mentioned. This payment is made up of:—£21,200,000, being the average annual amount of the Government remittance during three years; £2,700,000, the average annual amount of private remittances during the same period. The Government remittance is mainly for the payment of home charges, namely those charges in England which are normally met from revenue. These charges, in the three years which I have referred to, averaged £18,500,000, made up in the following manner:—Interest on debt, £9,500,000; payments for stores ordered and purchased in this country, £2,500,000; pensions and furlough pay to civil and military officers, £5,000,000; miscellaneous, £1,250,000. Besides the home charges proper, certain sums were remitted to England by the Government to defray capital charges. These bring the Government remittances to the total of £21,200,000 already mentioned. ... at the end of 1907 the capital outlay on railways alone in India amounted to £265,000,000 sterling, the bulk of which is British capital.
sources.what_passage_establishes: The passage establishes the contemporary official figures and stated composition of Indian Government remittances to England for 1904–1906, including debt interest within home charges, and records the scale and predominantly British character of railway capital outlay at the end of 1907.
sources.evidence_limits: It does not by itself establish the ultimate economic incidence of these payments, the identity of individual lenders or investors, the terms of every underlying debt, or whether all remittances should be classified as a 'drain.' Those are interpretive questions requiring separate evidence.
sources.notes: This is a distinct 1909 financial-accounting evidence layer, not a duplicate of the 1908 borrowing-authority record. The source is especially useful for separating official contemporary accounting of debt interest, home charges and British capital from later interpretations.
scholarly_references: House of Commons, East India Revenue Accounts, 5 August 1909, Hansard vol. 8, cc. 1981–2097.
sources.publication_status: A-grade — exact contemporary financial-accounting passage locked.

sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৯০৯ সালের ইস্ট ইন্ডিয়া রাজস্ব হিসাব আলোচনায় ১৯০৪–১৯০৬ সময়ে ভারতের ব্রিটেনে গড় বার্ষিক সরকারি রেমিট্যান্স £২১.২ মিলিয়ন, যার মধ্যে ঋণের সুদ ছিল £৯.৫ মিলিয়ন—এবং ১৯০৭ সালের শেষে ভারতীয় রেলপথে মূলধনী বিনিয়োগ £২৬৫ মিলিয়ন বলে নথিভুক্ত হয়।
sources.bn_notes: এটি ১৯০৮ সালের ঋণ-ক্ষমতার রেকর্ডের পুনরাবৃত্তি নয়; এটি ১৯০৯ সালের সমকালীন আর্থিক হিসাবের স্বতন্ত্র প্রমাণস্তর।

sources.title: Jekyll Island meeting, 1910
sources.historical_claim: In November 1910, six financial and political figures met at Jekyll Island to develop a plan for banking reform; the resulting plan helped lay foundations for the later Federal Reserve System.
sources.verification_status: Institutional documentary history and participant retrospective accounts corroborated; meeting-specific evidence remains retrospective
sources.bn_title: জেকিল আইল্যান্ড বৈঠক, ১৯১০
sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৯১০ সালের নভেম্বরে ছয়জন আর্থিক ও রাজনৈতিক ব্যক্তি জেকিল আইল্যান্ডে ব্যাংকিং সংস্কারের একটি পরিকল্পনা তৈরির জন্য বৈঠক করেন; সেই পরিকল্পনা পরবর্তী ফেডারেল রিজার্ভ ব্যবস্থার ভিত্তি গঠনে ভূমিকা রাখে।
sources.notes: Reaudited against Federal Reserve History and the Library of Congress Nelson W. Aldrich Papers. Federal Reserve History confirms the November 20–30, 1910 conference and identifies the six attendees, while Warburg’s 1930 account independently describes the conference and agreement on the rough draft of the Aldrich Bill. The Library of Congress preserves digitized 1910–1911 Aldrich National Monetary Commission papers, providing a primary-source research lead, but the currently identified digitized material does not establish the Jekyll Island meeting itself with a contemporaneous meeting document. The record therefore remains B under the project’s strict direct-primary standard.
sources.primary_passage: our secret expedition to Jekyll Island
sources.passage_locator: Frank A. Vanderlip, Saturday Evening Post, 9 February 1935, p. 25; first-hand retrospective account of the 1910 meeting.
sources.passage_status: Passage retained — participant retrospective accounts corroborated; direct contemporaneous meeting record remains open
sources.source_identity: Frank A. Vanderlip, “From Farm Boy to Financier,” Saturday Evening Post, 9 February 1935; retrospective firsthand account referring to the late-1910 Jekyll Island meeting.; publisher/authority: Saturday Evening Post; Frank A. Vanderlip; year: 1935.
sources.edition: Frank A. Vanderlip, “From Farm Boy to Financier,” Saturday Evening Post, 9 February 1935; retrospective firsthand account referring to the late-1910 Jekyll Island meeting.
sources.publisher: Saturday Evening Post; Frank A. Vanderlip
sources.what_passage_establishes: The participant accounts establish that a confidential November 1910 conference was held at Senator Aldrich's request to discuss the form of a new banking bill and that a rough draft later known as the Aldrich Bill emerged from the conference.
sources.evidence_limits: The strongest directly quoted sources are retrospective participant accounts from 1930 and 1935 rather than contemporaneous 1910 records. They securely corroborate the meeting and its stated purpose, but do not by themselves establish every participant, date detail, or the full causal relationship to the 1913 Federal Reserve Act.
research_leads: Library of Congress, Nelson W. Aldrich Papers: National Monetary Commission, 1908–1912; digitized 1910–1911 miscellaneous papers (box 79/reel 55 and box 80/reel 56).
Federal Reserve History, The Meeting at Jekyll Island, dated November 20–30, 1910.
scholarly_references: Gary Richardson and Jessie Romero, “The Meeting at Jekyll Island,” Federal Reserve History, Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond, documenting the November 1910 meeting and the Aldrich Plan.
Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta and Rutgers University, *A Return to Jekyll Island: The Origins, History, and Future of the Federal Reserve* (2010 conference proceedings).
sources.publication_status: B-grade — meeting is strongly corroborated by Federal Reserve institutional histories and participant recollections, but no contemporaneous 1910 meeting record has been located that meets the project’s A-grade direct-primary standard.

sources.title: East India Loans (Railways and Irrigation) Bill, 1910
sources.historical_claim: Parliament considered renewed borrowing powers for the Government of India, principally for railway capital expenditure and associated capital liabilities, with the 1910 debate stating that the 1908 authority had raised £13,307,273 for programme purposes and that further borrowing powers were required.
sources.verification_status: Primary contemporary parliamentary record verified through official Historic Hansard.
sources.passage_locator: House of Commons Hansard, 17 March 1910, vol. 15, cc. 607–612; East India Loans (Railways and Irrigation) Bill.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — exact contemporary parliamentary record.
sources.source_identity: House of Commons, East India Loans (Railways and Irrigation) Bill, 17 March 1910, Hansard vol. 15, cc. 607–612.
sources.edition: House of Commons Debates (Hansard), 17 March 1910, vol. 15.
sources.primary_passage: The amount raised for programme purposes under the Bill of 1908 has been £13,307,273. ... It is probable, therefore, that about £8,000,000 a year must be raised in this country for the purposes of the programme. Some part of this sum will be raised in the form of Capital Stock or Debentures of Guaranteed Railway Companies ... It is not possible to give any accurate estimate, but, based on past experience, it may be suggested that about £6,000,000 a year will be raised for programme purposes by the Secretary of State. ... Under the Loans Act of 1908, £997,300 has been spent on the discharge of debentures; before the end of this year ... it will be necessary to repay ... £2,250,000; possibly ... £1,510,000 may be required ... The loans for these purposes will be raised under—and, I may add, go far to exhaust—the borrowing powers of the Act of 1908.
sources.what_passage_establishes: The debate records the scale of borrowing already raised under the 1908 Act, the expected annual requirement for railway capital purposes in Britain, and the use of borrowing powers to discharge railway-company capital liabilities and debentures.
sources.evidence_limits: The passage is a parliamentary debate and establishes stated Government figures and proposed borrowing requirements; it does not by itself prove that every projected amount was subsequently issued, nor identify every lender, investor, security term or final transaction.
sources.notes: Distinct from the 1908 authority and the 1910 Jekyll Island record. This record is a primary parliamentary-finance layer showing the continuation and practical exhaustion of the 1908 borrowing authority and the rationale for renewed borrowing power.
scholarly_references: House of Commons, East India Loans (Railways and Irrigation) Bill, 17 March 1910, Hansard vol. 15, cc. 607–612.
sources.publication_status: A-grade — exact contemporary parliamentary borrowing record locked.
