sources.title: East India Revenue Accounts (Indian Budget), 1911
sources.historical_claim: The 1911 Indian Budget debate recorded improved railway and irrigation finances, higher earnings of guaranteed railway companies, a reduction of non-productive Indian public debt to £46 million by 31 March 1911, and allocation of £2 million of the surplus toward discharge of floating debt.
sources.verification_status: Primary contemporary parliamentary record verified through official Historic Hansard.
sources.passage_locator: House of Commons Hansard, 26 July 1911, vol. 28, cc. 1664–1783, especially cc. 1667–1669.
sources.source_identity: House of Commons, East India Revenue Accounts (Indian Budget), 26 July 1911, Hansard vol. 28, cc. 1664–1783.
sources.edition: House of Commons Debates (Hansard), 26 July 1911, vol. 28.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — exact contemporary parliamentary financial record.
sources.primary_passage: Railways accounted for £1,272,000 of the surplus; irrigation £91,000, and telegraphs £104,000. The improvement in the profit of railways is the result of the increase in the gross traffic receipts—£674,500—and the decrease of working expenses, interest charges, and miscellaneous charges by £597,700. The guaranteed companies received as surplus profits or net earnings £100,000 more last year than the year before. ... £2,000,000 has been set aside to be used towards the discharge of floating debt. ... the non-productive debt amounted on the 31st March, 1911, to only £46,000,000, as against £71,000,000 ten years previously.
sources.what_passage_establishes: The contemporary Budget debate establishes stated government figures for railway profitability and guaranteed-company earnings, and records a substantial reduction in non-productive debt together with a £2 million allocation toward floating-debt discharge.
sources.evidence_limits: These figures are official budgetary statements in parliamentary debate; they do not by themselves establish the ultimate distribution of railway profits, the identities or returns of individual investors, the economic incidence of debt service, or that debt reduction represented cancellation of all underlying obligations.
scholarly_references: House of Commons, East India Revenue Accounts (Indian Budget), 26 July 1911, Hansard vol. 28, cc. 1664–1783.
sources.notes: Distinct 1911 financial-accounting layer. The separate 13 December 1911 Return of Loans Raised in India was identified but not promoted to an A-grade evidence record because the Hansard entry only records presentation of the Return; the underlying Return itself should be inspected before extracting figures.
sources.publication_status: A-grade — exact contemporary Indian Budget financial passage locked.

sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৯১১ সালের ভারতীয় বাজেট আলোচনায় রেলওয়ে থেকে £১.২৭২ মিলিয়ন উদ্বৃত্ত, গ্যারান্টিযুক্ত রেলওয়ে কোম্পানিগুলোর বাড়তি আয় এবং ৩১ মার্চ ১৯১১-এ অনুৎপাদনশীল ঋণ £৪৬ মিলিয়নে নেমে আসার কথা নথিভুক্ত হয়; উদ্বৃত্তের £২ মিলিয়ন ফ্লোটিং ডেট পরিশোধে রাখা হয়।

sources.title: East India Revenue Accounts (Indian Budget), 1912
sources.historical_claim: The 1912 Indian Budget debate recorded record railway net profit of £3,204,500 for 1911–12 and stated that the surplus would be retained to reduce borrowing for capital expenditure on railways, irrigation works and the construction of New Delhi.
sources.verification_status: Primary contemporary parliamentary record verified through official Historic Hansard.
sources.passage_locator: House of Commons Hansard, 30 July 1912, East India Revenue Accounts (Indian Budget).
sources.source_identity: House of Commons, East India Revenue Accounts (Indian Budget), 30 July 1912, Hansard.
sources.edition: House of Commons Debates (Hansard), 30 July 1912.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — exact contemporary parliamentary financial record.
sources.primary_passage: The net profit on the year's working was therefore the record sum of £3,204,500, an excess over the Budget Estimate of £1,272,800. ... The surplus, therefore, is going to be retained, in order to reduce the amount to be borrowed on capital expenditure, on railways, irrigation works, and the building of the new Delhi.
sources.what_passage_establishes: The contemporary Budget debate establishes the reported railway net profit and the Government's stated decision to use the surplus to reduce the amount that otherwise would have to be borrowed for specified capital expenditure.
sources.evidence_limits: This establishes reported budgetary figures and the stated financing policy; it does not by itself establish the final amount of borrowing avoided, the ultimate incidence of railway profits, or the identity and terms of capital providers.
scholarly_references: House of Commons, East India Revenue Accounts (Indian Budget), 30 July 1912, Hansard.

sources.title: East India Revenue Accounts (Indian Budget), 1913
sources.historical_claim: The 1913 Indian Budget debate recorded a surplus of nearly £8 million over the Budget Estimate, attributed mainly to large railway receipts and high opium prices, with the surplus directed principally toward provincial grants and reduction or avoidance of debt; it also stated that successive Governments had used India's resources and credit to build the railway system.
sources.verification_status: Primary contemporary parliamentary record verified through official Historic Hansard.
sources.passage_locator: House of Commons Hansard, 7 August 1913, vol. 56, cc. 1780–1908; financial discussion at cc. 1783–1784.
sources.source_identity: House of Commons, East India Revenue Accounts (Indian Budget), 7 August 1913, Hansard vol. 56, cc. 1780–1908.
sources.edition: House of Commons Debates (Hansard), 7 August 1913, vol. 56.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — exact contemporary parliamentary financial record.
sources.primary_passage: There was last year, due mainly to the very large railway receipts and the high prices obtained for opium, a surplus of not less than nearly £8,000,000 over the Budget Estimate. This surplus is to be spent mainly on Grants to provincial Governments for education and sanitation and, with the surplus estimated for in the Budget on the reduction and avoidance of debt. ... For the last two generations successive Secretaries of State and Governments of India have used the resources and the credit of India to build up a railway system which has always been closely associated with the State, and has become more closely associated with it during the last generation.
sources.what_passage_establishes: The contemporary Budget debate establishes the reported size and stated causes of the prior-year surplus, its intended allocation partly to debt reduction/avoidance, and the official characterization of railway development as having been built using India's resources and credit under close State association.
sources.evidence_limits: The debate establishes official statements and policy descriptions, not the ultimate economic incidence of railway finance, the identities of capital providers, or whether every planned debt-reduction allocation was subsequently executed exactly as stated.
scholarly_references: House of Commons, East India Revenue Accounts (Indian Budget), 7 August 1913, Hansard vol. 56, cc. 1780–1908.
sources.publication_status: A-grade — exact contemporary Budget passage locked.

sources.title: East India Loans Raised in England: Outstanding Indian-Revenue Loans, 1916

sources.verification_status: Primary parliamentary record verified through official Historic Hansard; the underlying Return is identified by the statutory presentation notice.

sources.source_identity: House of Commons, Return of all Loans raised in England, chargeable on the Revenues of India, outstanding at commencement of half-year ending 30 September 1916, presented 12 October 1916.
sources.edition: House of Commons Papers, 1916; statutory Return presented 12 October 1916.
sources.passage_status: Presentation record locked; underlying Return retained for later loan-level extraction.
sources.primary_passage: Copy presented of Return of all Loans raised in England, chargeable on the Revenues of India, outstanding at the commencement of the half-year ending on the 30th September, 1916, etc. [by Act]; to lie upon the Table, and to be printed.
sources.what_passage_establishes: The parliamentary record establishes the existence and scope of the official Return covering England-raised loans charged on Indian revenues and outstanding as of the beginning of the half-year ending 30 September 1916.

sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৯১৬ সালে সংসদে ভারতের রাজস্বের ওপর ধার্য এবং ইংল্যান্ডে তোলা বকেয়া ঋণের একটি সরকারি রিটার্ন পেশ করা হয়, যা ৩০ সেপ্টেম্বর ১৯১৬-এ শেষ হওয়া অর্ধ-বর্ষের শুরুতে বকেয়া ঋণগুলোকে চিহ্নিত করে।

sources.title: India's £100 Million Contribution to the Cost of the War, 1917
sources.historical_claim: Parliament formally consented to a £100,000,000 contribution charged on the revenues of India toward the cost of the First World War, to be provided partly from a loan raised in India and partly through India's assumption of interest liability on the required amount of British War Loan; Indian taxation and budget provisions were to meet the resulting annual interest and sinking-fund charges.
sources.verification_status: Primary contemporary parliamentary record verified through official Historic Hansard.
sources.passage_locator: House of Commons Hansard, 14 March 1917, vol. 91, cc. 1137–1241; Motion 'Contribution Towards Cost of War'.
sources.source_identity: House of Commons, Mr. Chamberlain's Motion / Contribution Towards Cost of War, 14 March 1917, Hansard vol. 91, cc. 1137–1241.
sources.edition: House of Commons Debates (Hansard), 14 March 1917, vol. 91.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — exact contemporary parliamentary resolution.
sources.primary_passage: That ... the Government of India ... have recommended that a Contribution charged on the Revenues of India should be made towards the expenses of the same, such contribution to consist of the sum of £100,000,000 to be provided in part from the proceeds of a loan to be raised in India and the remainder by assuming liability for interest on British War Loan of the required amount ... the Government of India have now made provision by legislation and in their Revenue and Expenditure Estimates for meeting, by means of increased taxation and otherwise, the annual charge for interest and sinking fund in respect of the Contribution ... this House consents that a Contribution of £100,000,000 charged on the Revenues of India shall be made towards the cost of the War.
sources.what_passage_establishes: The parliamentary resolution establishes the legal/political consent for a £100 million Indian-revenue war contribution and its financing structure: part by an Indian loan and the balance through assumption of British War Loan interest liability, with Indian revenue measures covering annual interest and sinking-fund charges.
sources.evidence_limits: The resolution establishes the authorized contribution and financing mechanism, not the final cash flows, exact amount actually raised in India, final British War Loan instruments assumed, or the incidence of the Indian taxation used to service the obligation. Those require subsequent financial statements and loan records.
scholarly_references: House of Commons, Contribution Towards Cost of War, 14 March 1917, Hansard vol. 91, cc. 1137–1241.
sources.notes: A distinct wartime sovereign-finance layer. A later 1918 debate reports that £35 million was actually raised in India toward the £100 million contribution, which is retained for a separate 1918 verification record rather than imported into this 1917 authorization record.
sources.publication_status: A-grade — exact parliamentary resolution locked.
sources.bn_title: ১৯১৭ সালে ভারতের £১০০ মিলিয়ন যুদ্ধ-অবদান
sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৯১৭ সালে ব্রিটিশ সংসদ ভারতের রাজস্বের ওপর ধার্য £১০০ মিলিয়ন যুদ্ধ-অবদানে সম্মতি দেয়; এর একটি অংশ ভারতে ঋণ তুলে এবং বাকি অংশ ব্রিটিশ যুদ্ধঋণের সুদের দায় গ্রহণের মাধ্যমে দেওয়ার কথা ছিল, আর ভারতীয় রাজস্ব ও করব্যবস্থা সুদ ও সিঙ্কিং ফান্ডের বার্ষিক ব্যয় মেটাবে।

book_1_integration.part_label: Book 1 — Part II: Expansion of state-backed monetary and financial systems

sources.title: India's War Contribution: £35 Million Raised in India, 1918
sources.historical_claim: In August 1918 the Secretary of State for India reported that the £100 million Indian contribution toward the war had produced £35 million from an Indian loan, transferred to the Imperial Government, while a further £30 million was raised through Treasury Bills for India's own wartime expenditure; a second war loan had already realized £16.5 million.
sources.verification_status: Primary contemporary parliamentary record verified through official Historic Hansard.
sources.passage_locator: House of Commons Hansard, 6 August 1918, Mr. Montagu's Statement, vol. 109, cc. 1138–1142.
sources.source_identity: House of Commons, Mr. Montagu's Statement on Indian finance and war effort, 6 August 1918, Hansard vol. 109, cc. 1138–1142.
sources.edition: House of Commons Debates (Hansard), 6 August 1918, vol. 109.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — exact contemporary parliamentary financial statement.
sources.primary_passage: The contribution of £100,000,000 towards the cost of the War ... The loan last year realised £35,000,000, which was in due course transferred to the Imperial Government, and at a later date in the same year the Government of India succeeded in raising for its own needs £30,000,000 in the form of Treasury Bills for the purpose of financing war expenditure in India. ... This year a new War Loan has been issued ... Already £16,500,000 has been realised, and therefore it is obvious that of the £100,000,000 promised well over £50,000,000 has already been raised in India itself.
sources.what_passage_establishes: The statement establishes actual reported proceeds and transfer of the first Indian war loan, a separate £30 million Treasury-bill financing operation for Indian wartime expenditure, and at least £16.5 million already realized from the subsequent war loan by August 1918.
sources.evidence_limits: The statement does not provide the full terms, maturities, subscriber composition, or final total of all Indian war loans, nor does it by itself establish the ultimate incidence of taxation or purchasing power used to service them.
scholarly_references: House of Commons, Mr. Montagu's Statement, 6 August 1918, Hansard vol. 109, cc. 1138–1142.
sources.publication_status: A-grade — exact contemporary realization figures locked.
sources.bn_title: ১৯১৮ সালে ভারতের যুদ্ধ-অবদান: ভারতে £৩৫ মিলিয়ন ঋণ সংগ্রহ ও অতিরিক্ত ট্রেজারি বিল
sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৯১৮ সালের আগস্টে ভারতের জন্য জানানো হয় যে £১০০ মিলিয়ন যুদ্ধ-অবদানের মধ্যে ভারতে তোলা ঋণ থেকে £৩৫ মিলিয়ন সংগ্রহ করে ইম্পেরিয়াল সরকারের কাছে হস্তান্তর করা হয়েছে; একই সময়ে ভারতের নিজস্ব যুদ্ধব্যয় মেটাতে আরও £৩০ মিলিয়ন ট্রেজারি বিলের মাধ্যমে সংগ্রহ করা হয় এবং নতুন যুদ্ধঋণ থেকে £১৬.৫ মিলিয়ন ইতিমধ্যে পাওয়া গিয়েছিল।

book_1_integration.part_label: Book 1 — Part II: Expansion of state-backed monetary and financial systems

sources.title: Indian War Expenditure: £127.8 Million by 31 March 1919
sources.historical_claim: The British Government reported in Parliament that India's war expenditure up to 31 March 1919 was approximately £127.8 million, including the £100 million contribution toward His Majesty's Government's war outlay.
sources.verification_status: Primary contemporary parliamentary record verified through official Historic Hansard.
sources.passage_locator: House of Commons Hansard, 19 May 1919, vol. 116, cc. 14–15.
sources.source_identity: House of Commons, War Expenditure, 19 May 1919, Hansard vol. 116, cc. 14–15.
sources.edition: House of Commons Debates (Hansard), 19 May 1919, vol. 116.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — exact contemporary parliamentary answer.
sources.primary_passage: Including a contribution of £100,000,000 towards the war outlay of His Majesty's Government, the war expenditure of the Government of India up to the 31st March, 1919, may be taken at about £127,800,000. A further contribution has been proposed by the Government of India, and is at present under consideration.
sources.what_passage_establishes: The parliamentary answer establishes the Government's reported aggregate Indian war expenditure through 31 March 1919 and explicitly states that the £100 million Imperial contribution was included within that figure.
sources.evidence_limits: The answer does not provide the full expenditure ledger, distinguish all borrowing from taxation or other financing, or establish the final amount of any further contribution then under consideration.
scholarly_references: House of Commons, War Expenditure, 19 May 1919, Hansard vol. 116, cc. 14–15.
sources.publication_status: A-grade — exact contemporary aggregate expenditure figure locked.
sources.bn_title: ১৯১৯ সালের ভারতীয় যুদ্ধব্যয়: ৩১ মার্চ পর্যন্ত £১২৭.৮ মিলিয়ন
sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৯১৯ সালের ১৯ মে ব্রিটিশ সংসদে জানানো হয় যে ৩১ মার্চ ১৯১৯ পর্যন্ত ভারতের সরকারের যুদ্ধব্যয় প্রায় £১২৭.৮ মিলিয়ন, যার মধ্যে ব্রিটিশ সরকারের যুদ্ধব্যয়ের জন্য £১০০ মিলিয়ন অবদান অন্তর্ভুক্ত ছিল।

book_1_integration.part_label: Book 1 — Part II: Expansion of state-backed monetary and financial systems

sources.title: India's Currency and Exchange Crisis After the War, 1919
sources.historical_claim: The 1919 Indian Budget debate recorded that India's currency position had been a major wartime concern, that the post-war rise in silver prices had forced the rupee to 1s. 8d., and that the Government proposed a new Currency Commission to address the resulting currency and exchange problems.
sources.verification_status: Primary contemporary parliamentary record verified through official Historic Hansard.
sources.passage_locator: House of Commons Hansard, 22 May 1919, vol. 116, cc. 621–713; Mr. Montagu's opening statement.
sources.source_identity: House of Commons, East India Revenue Accounts, 22 May 1919, Hansard vol. 116, cc. 621–713.
sources.edition: House of Commons Debates (Hansard), 22 May 1919, vol. 116.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — exact contemporary currency-policy statement.
sources.primary_passage: The currency position in India was a source of great anxiety to the Government throughout the War ... the currency situation is now causing us renewed anxiety owing to the increase in the price of silver which has necessitated a rupee of 1s. 8d. ... I have decided to appoint a new Currency Commission to investigate the situation caused by the rise in the price of silver in a limited world supply.
sources.what_passage_establishes: The statement establishes the Government's contemporary account of wartime currency stress, the post-war silver-price pressure on the rupee, and the decision to create a Currency Commission to investigate the currency and exchange problem.
sources.evidence_limits: This does not by itself establish the later Commission's recommendations, the precise market mechanism producing the rupee rate, or the complete wartime monetary operations that preceded the 1919 policy response.
scholarly_references: House of Commons, East India Revenue Accounts, 22 May 1919, Hansard vol. 116, cc. 621–713.
sources.publication_status: A-grade — exact contemporary currency-policy passage locked.
sources.bn_title: ১৯১৯ সালে ভারতের মুদ্রা ও বিনিময় সংকট: যুদ্ধ-পরবর্তী রুপি ও রৌপ্যের মূল্য
sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৯১৯ সালের ভারতীয় বাজেট আলোচনায় বলা হয় যে যুদ্ধকালে ভারতের মুদ্রাব্যবস্থা নিয়ে সরকারের বড় উদ্বেগ ছিল; যুদ্ধের পর রৌপ্যের মূল্য বৃদ্ধির কারণে রুপির মূল্য ১ শিলিং ৮ পেন্সে ওঠে এবং নতুন কারেন্সি কমিশন গঠনের সিদ্ধান্ত নেওয়া হয়।

sources.title: Gold and Silver (Export, Control, etc.) Bill: Government Control of Bullion Exports and Indian Exchange, 1920
sources.historical_claim: Parliamentary evidence records the post-war continuation of Government power to control gold and silver bullion exports by Order in Council, with contemporaneous evidence linking the control of silver imports to major movements in the Indian rupee exchange.
sources.verification_status: Primary parliamentary debate verified in official Historic Hansard; Government explanation and contemporaneous commercial evidence located in the same debate.
sources.passage_locator: House of Commons Hansard, 10 November 1920, vol. 134, cc. 1320–1326; Government explanation at cc. 1320–1322, 1322–1323; Indian-exchange evidence at c. 1324.
sources.source_identity: Gold and Silver (Export, Control, etc.) Bill, Second Reading, House of Commons, 10 November 1920; Financial Secretary to the Treasury Mr. Baldwin, with subsequent debate including Mr. Samuel Samuel.
sources.edition: House of Commons Debates, 10 November 1920, Series 5, vol. 134, cc. 1320–1326.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — official Hansard text and column locators verified.
sources.primary_passage: The Government will then have power, at any time when the situation makes it necessary, to regulate by Order-in-Council the export of gold and silver bullion. In the same debate, Mr. Samuel stated that wartime restrictions on silver imports had seen the rupee move from 1s. 4d. to 2s. 7d.
sources.what_passage_establishes: The Government's proposed statute would preserve executive authority to regulate gold and silver bullion exports after the wartime Orders in Council expired. The debate also contains a contemporaneous parliamentary statement that wartime restrictions on silver imports were associated with a major rise in the Indian rupee's exchange quotation.
sources.evidence_limits: The Government statement establishes statutory authority and its stated monetary rationale; Mr. Samuel's exchange figures are a parliamentary speaker's contemporaneous account, not an independently tabulated official exchange series. The record does not by itself establish causation between a single restriction and every movement in the rupee, nor does it identify beneficiaries or private bullion-dealer interests.
scholarly_references: House of Commons Debates, 10 November 1920, vol. 134, cc. 1320–1326.
For later Indian currency-policy context, see the Royal Commission on Indian Currency and Finance (1926), while keeping later findings separate from this 1920 primary record.
sources.publication_status: A-grade — direct parliamentary primary evidence; the Government's statutory-control proposition is official, while the exchange-effect portion is explicitly attributed to a contemporary parliamentary speaker.
sources.bn_title: সোনা ও রূপা রপ্তানি নিয়ন্ত্রণ বিল: বুলিয়ন রপ্তানিতে সরকারি নিয়ন্ত্রণ ও ভারতীয় বিনিময় হার, ১৯২০
sources.bn_historical_claim: পার্লামেন্টারি নথিতে যুদ্ধ-পরবর্তী সময়ে অর্ডার-ইন-কাউন্সিলের মাধ্যমে সোনা ও রূপার বুলিয়ন রপ্তানি নিয়ন্ত্রণের সরকারি ক্ষমতা এবং সমসাময়িক আলোচনায় রূপির বিনিময় হারের বড় পরিবর্তনের সম্পর্ক নথিভুক্ত হয়েছে।
sources.bn_historical_claim_note: অনুবাদটি প্রমাণের সীমা বজায় রেখে করা হয়েছে; এটি একক সরকারি নিয়ন্ত্রণকে রূপির সব পরিবর্তনের একমাত্র কারণ হিসেবে দাবি করে না।

book_1_integration.part_label: Book 1 — Part II: Modern monetary and sovereign-finance development

sources.title: East Africa Currency Policy: Indian Rupee, Sterling Link and Imperial Exchange Spillover, 1920
sources.historical_claim: The 1920 Colonial Office debate records the Indian rupee as the statutory monetary unit in East Africa and explains the Government's response to the rupee's wartime appreciation by moving toward a local currency linked to sterling.
sources.verification_status: Primary parliamentary debate verified in official Historic Hansard; ministerial explanation and contemporary parliamentary evidence located.
sources.passage_locator: House of Commons Hansard, 26 April 1920, Colonial Office debate, vol. 128, approximately cc. 901–918; East African currency discussion and ministerial explanation.
sources.source_identity: House of Commons debate on the Colonial Office, 26 April 1920; discussion by Sir F. Banbury and Lieutenant-Colonel Amery, Secretary of State for the Colonies.
sources.edition: House of Commons Debates, 26 April 1920, Series 5, vol. 128.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — official Hansard text and debate locator verified.
sources.primary_passage: The legal unit of value, the statutory unit of account in East Africa has always been the Indian rupee. ... the scheme was prepared at a time when the Indian rupee had risen in exchange value to about 2s. 9d., and it was decided to substitute ... a local currency based on the florin at 2s. sterling.
sources.what_passage_establishes: The debate establishes that the Indian rupee remained East Africa's statutory unit of account and that its appreciation had become a practical imperial monetary-policy problem. The Colonial Secretary explains the proposed transition to a local florin-based currency at a sterling-linked value.
sources.evidence_limits: This is parliamentary evidence about legal status and Government policy, not a complete statistical series. The debate does not by itself establish the full economic incidence of the currency change or prove that Indian policy was the sole cause of East African price and production effects.
scholarly_references: House of Commons Debates, 26 April 1920, Colonial Office, vol. 128.
For later implementation, compare the East Africa and Uganda Order in Council of 26 April 1920 and subsequent 1921 currency debate; keep those later records distinct.
sources.publication_status: A-grade — direct parliamentary primary evidence; the record separates statutory monetary status, Government policy, and attributed parliamentary criticism.
sources.bn_title: পূর্ব আফ্রিকার মুদ্রানীতি: ভারতীয় রুপি, স্টার্লিং-সংযোগ ও সাম্রাজ্যিক বিনিময়-প্রভাব, ১৯২০
sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৯২০ সালের ঔপনিবেশিক দপ্তরের বিতর্কে পূর্ব আফ্রিকার আইনগত হিসাবের একক হিসেবে ভারতীয় রুপির অবস্থান এবং রুপির মূল্যবৃদ্ধির প্রতিক্রিয়ায় স্টার্লিং-সংযুক্ত স্থানীয় মুদ্রার দিকে সরকারের অগ্রসর হওয়া নথিভুক্ত হয়েছে।

book_1_integration.part_label: Book 1 — Part II: Modern monetary and sovereign-finance development

sources.title: Imperial Exchange Policy: End of Wartime Artificial Exchange Support, 1920
sources.historical_claim: The Treasury stated in March 1920 that Britain would not return to wartime artificial support of Empire exchanges where doing so would require new foreign borrowing or new British loans to governments whose exchanges were at a discount to sterling.
sources.verification_status: Primary parliamentary written-answer record verified in official Historic Hansard.
sources.passage_locator: House of Commons Hansard, 4 March 1920, vol. 126, cc. 637–638, Question 75, Exchange (British Empire).
sources.source_identity: Written question and answer in the House of Commons, 4 March 1920; answer by Chancellor of the Exchequer Mr. Chamberlain.
sources.edition: House of Commons Debates, 4 March 1920, Series 5, vol. 126, cc. 637–638.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — exact official Hansard wording and column locator verified.
sources.primary_passage: It is not the policy of His Majesty's Government to return to the method necessarily adopted during the War of giving artificial support to the exchanges, which would involve new borrowings abroad by His Majesty's Government or, conversely, new loans by the British Government to Governments whose exchange is at a discount with sterling.
sources.what_passage_establishes: The Treasury's stated post-war exchange policy was to discontinue wartime artificial exchange support where maintaining it would require additional British foreign borrowing or British lending to governments with depreciated exchanges.
sources.evidence_limits: The answer states Government policy; it does not quantify wartime support operations, identify every affected imperial currency, or establish the later effectiveness of the policy.
scholarly_references: House of Commons Debates, 4 March 1920, vol. 126, cc. 637–638.
For later exchange-stabilisation developments, later records should be kept separate from this March 1920 policy statement.
sources.publication_status: A-grade — direct ministerial statement of post-war exchange policy in Parliament.
sources.bn_title: সাম্রাজ্যিক বিনিময় নীতি: যুদ্ধকালীন কৃত্রিম বিনিময়-সমর্থন বন্ধ, ১৯২০
sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৯২০ সালের মার্চে ট্রেজারি জানায় যে যুদ্ধকালীন কৃত্রিম বিনিময়-সমর্থনে ফিরে যাওয়া হবে না, কারণ এতে নতুন বিদেশি ঋণ বা স্টার্লিংয়ের তুলনায় অবমূল্যায়িত বিনিময়ধারী সরকারগুলোকে নতুন ব্রিটিশ ঋণ দিতে হতো।

book_1_integration.part_label: Book 1 — Part II: Modern monetary and sovereign-finance development

sources.title: Treasury and the Banks: Credit Restraint, Treasury Bills and Money Rates, 1920
sources.historical_claim: In July 1920 the Chancellor of the Exchequer described active consultation with leading bankers and the use of higher money rates, including the Treasury Bill rate, as part of efforts to restrain credit expansion and speculative lending during post-war inflationary pressure.
sources.verification_status: Primary parliamentary debate verified against official Historic Hansard.
sources.passage_locator: House of Commons Hansard, 12 July 1920, vol. 131, cc. 1999–2122; relevant discussion around cc. 2018–2023.
sources.source_identity: Finance Bill Committee debate, House of Commons, 12 July 1920; statement by Chancellor of the Exchequer Mr. Chamberlain concerning credit, money rates and consultation with leading bankers.
sources.edition: House of Commons Debates, 12 July 1920, Series 5, vol. 131, cc. 1999–2122.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — official Hansard text and locator verified.
sources.primary_passage: My responsibility, in so far as I have any responsibility, arises out of an interview which I sought with leading bankers to ascertain whether, in their opinion, they could take such measures as might guard us against the necessity for any further rise in money rates. ... I was confronted with certain circumstances in which ... I was yet being forced into a fresh inflation, not because I was borrowing new money, but because the demands for money were so great that the attraction of Treasury Bills was insufficient as compared with the other opportunities of investment. There was no step that I could take except to raise the rates again. ... I told them that I did not think that they could go on increasing the amount of their overdrafts and loans, or that they ought to allow the overdrafts and loans to be used for speculative purposes.
sources.what_passage_establishes: The Chancellor personally sought consultation with leading bankers; he linked Treasury Bill and money-rate policy to attempts to restrain monetary/credit expansion and warned banks against continued expansion of overdrafts and loans for speculative purposes.
sources.evidence_limits: This is a ministerial parliamentary statement about policy and consultation, not a complete record of private meetings, banking balance sheets, or the independent effectiveness of the measures. It does not establish coordinated control by all banks or a particular banking family's influence.
scholarly_references: House of Commons Debates, 12 July 1920, vol. 131, cc. 1999–2122.
The Cunliffe Committee is mentioned in the debate; later records should separately establish its recommendations and implementation.
sources.publication_status: A-grade — direct ministerial statement in Parliament, with interpretive limits.
sources.bn_title: ট্রেজারি ও ব্যাংকসমূহ: ঋণ-সৃষ্টির নিয়ন্ত্রণ, ট্রেজারি বিল ও অর্থের সুদের হার, ১৯২০
sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৯২০ সালের জুলাইয়ে চ্যান্সেলর অব দ্য এক্সচেকার শীর্ষস্থানীয় ব্যাংকারদের সঙ্গে পরামর্শ এবং ট্রেজারি বিল ও অর্থের সুদের হার ব্যবহারের কথা জানান, যার লক্ষ্য ছিল ঋণ-সৃষ্টির সম্প্রসারণ ও জল্পনামূলক ঋণ নিয়ন্ত্রণ করা।

book_1_integration.part_label: Book 1 — Part II: Modern monetary and sovereign-finance development

sources.title: India's Trade Balance and Private Gold Flows, April 1920
sources.historical_claim: A July 1920 parliamentary answer reported India's April 1920 private-account merchandise trade, remittance demand to London, and net private gold imports into India, providing contemporary evidence of exchange-related monetary flows.
sources.verification_status: Primary written-answer record verified in official Historic Hansard.
sources.passage_locator: House of Commons Hansard, 6 July 1920, vol. 131, cc. 1252–1253W, International Trade (Exchange).
sources.source_identity: Written question and answer, House of Commons, 6 July 1920; answer by Secretary of State for India Mr. Montagu.
sources.edition: House of Commons Debates, 6 July 1920, Series 5, vol. 131, cc. 1252–1253W.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — exact official answer and locator verified.
sources.primary_passage: India's net exports of merchandise on private account amounted in April to 6.87 lakhs. This information was reported by telegram by the Government of India, but as the detailed figures have not yet reached me I am not in a position to state what share in this trade balance relates to trade between India and this country. Exports and imports of commodities form, however, only one element in a country's international account, and during April there was a steady demand for remittance of funds from India to London. In April the net imports of gold into India on private account amounted only to about 14,400 fine ounces, being the equivalent of about 61,200 sovereigns.
sources.what_passage_establishes: The Secretary of State for India reported a private-account merchandise export surplus of 6.87 lakhs in April 1920, steady demand for remittances from India to London, and private net gold imports of about 14,400 fine ounces (about 61,200 sovereigns).
sources.evidence_limits: The answer says detailed trade figures were not yet available, so it does not establish India's complete international balance, the bilateral India-UK share, or the causal relationship among trade, remittances, gold flows and exchange rates.
scholarly_references: House of Commons Debates, 6 July 1920, vol. 131, cc. 1252–1253W.
Contemporary parliamentary evidence on India's post-war currency and exchange position should be read alongside the 1919 currency record and the 1920 East Africa/rupee record.
sources.publication_status: A-grade — direct ministerial written answer containing contemporary quantitative figures.
sources.bn_title: ভারতের বাণিজ্য ভারসাম্য ও বেসরকারি সোনা প্রবাহ, এপ্রিল ১৯২০
sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৯২০ সালের জুলাইয়ের এক সংসদীয় উত্তরে এপ্রিল মাসে ভারতের বেসরকারি পণ্য-বাণিজ্য, লন্ডনে অর্থ প্রেরণের চাহিদা এবং ভারতে বেসরকারি হিসাবে নিট সোনা আমদানির সমসাময়িক পরিসংখ্যান দেওয়া হয়।

book_1_integration.part_label: Book 1 — Part II: Modern monetary and sovereign-finance development

sources.title: Bombay Provincial Development Loan: 6½% Loan, 1920
sources.historical_claim: The Government of Bombay launched a development loan in India in 1920 to inaugurate a five-year programme requiring 30 crores of rupees for industrial housing, reclamation, development and local-body operations; the issue carried 6½% interest, was income-tax free, repayable at par in 1935, and received 9⅓ crores of subscriptions.
sources.verification_status: Primary parliamentary answer verified against the official UK Parliament Hansard record.
sources.passage_locator: House of Commons Hansard, 17 November 1920, vol. 134, c. 1854, 'Provincial Loan, Bombay'.
sources.source_identity: House of Commons oral answer by Secretary of State for India Edwin Montagu concerning the Government of Bombay's recently issued development loan.
sources.edition: House of Commons Debates, 17 November 1920, Series 5, vol. 134, c. 1854.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — exact official answer and locator verified.
sources.primary_passage: The Government of Bombay anticipate that during the next five years they will require 30 crores of rupees to finance industrial housing, reclamation and development, and the operations of Bombay local bodies. With a view to inaugurating this important programme, the Government of Bombay recently issued a development loan in India. The terms of the loan were as follows: Issue price, par; rate of interest, 6½ per cent., free of Income Tax; loan to be repaid at par in 1935. No limit was announced to the amount of subscriptions that the Government would be willing to receive, and when the lists closed at the end of October the gratifying sum of 9⅓ crores had been subscribed.
sources.what_passage_establishes: Bombay had begun raising provincial development finance directly in India through a public loan; the parliamentary answer specifies its 6½% tax-free coupon, par issue and repayment in 1935, while recording 9⅓ crores subscribed against an anticipated five-year requirement of 30 crores.
sources.evidence_limits: The answer does not identify individual subscribers, intermediary banks, underwriting arrangements, secondary-market activity, or the ultimate allocation of proceeds among the listed purposes. It also does not establish that the full 30-crore programme was ultimately financed through this loan.
scholarly_references: House of Commons Debates, 17 November 1920, vol. 134, c. 1854.
The record should be read as evidence of provincial capital-market development in India, not as evidence of a particular private banking group's control.
sources.publication_status: A-grade — direct ministerial statement with precise contemporary loan terms and subscription amount.
sources.bn_title: বোম্বে প্রাদেশিক উন্নয়ন ঋণ: ৬½% ঋণ, ১৯২০
sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৯২০ সালে বোম্বে সরকার শিল্প-আবাসন, ভূমি পুনরুদ্ধার, উন্নয়ন ও স্থানীয় সংস্থার কার্যক্রমের জন্য ভারতে একটি উন্নয়ন ঋণ ইস্যু করে; পাঁচ বছরে ৩০ কোটি রুপি প্রয়োজনের পরিকল্পনার বিপরীতে ঋণের সুদ ছিল ৬½%, আয়করমুক্ত, ১৯৩৫ সালে সমমূল্যে পরিশোধযোগ্য এবং ৯⅓ কোটি রুপির সাবস্ক্রিপশন পাওয়া যায়।

book_1_integration.part_label: Book 1 — Part II: Modern monetary and sovereign-finance development

sources.title: United Kingdom Final Balance Sheet: Dominion, Allied and Indian War Loans, 1920
sources.historical_claim: The 1920 British Budget statement quantified major outstanding government financial assets and liabilities, including loans to Dominions, loans to Allies and relief, and India's remaining liability for the 5% War Loan.
sources.verification_status: Primary parliamentary budget statement verified in official UK Parliament Hansard.
sources.passage_locator: House of Commons Hansard, 19 April 1920, 1920 Budget debate, 'Final Balance Sheet, 1920–21'.
sources.source_identity: 1920 Budget speech by Chancellor of the Exchequer Austen Chamberlain, House of Commons, 19 April 1920.
sources.edition: House of Commons Debates, 19 April 1920, Series 5, 1920 Budget debate.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — official Hansard budget text verified.
sources.primary_passage: At the close of the year we shall have outstanding assets to the following amount: Loans to Dominions, £119,500,000; loans to Allies and for relief, £1,767,000,000; or, taking them as in former years at one-half that figure, £883,500,000; the remaining liability of India for 5 per cent. War Loan, £21,000,000. To these must be added Vote of Credit Assets (£300,000,000), of which a portion may still be required to meet Extraordinary Charges, and Excess Profits Duty payable after the close of the current financial year of £400,000,000, making total assets of £1,724,000,000.
sources.what_passage_establishes: The British Treasury's 1920 budget statement placed loans to Dominions at £119.5 million, loans to Allies and relief at £1.767 billion (with an alternative accounting basis of £883.5 million), India's remaining liability for the 5% War Loan at £21 million, and total stated assets at £1.724 billion after adding other listed items.
sources.evidence_limits: This is a budgetary statement and accounting presentation, not a complete balance sheet under modern accounting standards. It does not establish the identities of lenders or borrowers beyond the categories stated, repayment performance, private ownership, or economic incidence.
scholarly_references: House of Commons Debates, 19 April 1920, 1920 Budget debate, 'Final Balance Sheet, 1920–21'.
Later records should separately establish the evolution and settlement of these wartime intergovernmental loans.
sources.publication_status: A-grade — direct Chancellor's budget statement with contemporary quantitative sovereign-finance figures.
sources.bn_title: যুক্তরাজ্যের চূড়ান্ত হিসাবপত্র: ডোমিনিয়ন, মিত্র ও ভারতীয় যুদ্ধঋণ, ১৯২০
sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৯২০ সালের ব্রিটিশ বাজেট বিবৃতিতে ডোমিনিয়ন, মিত্র ও ত্রাণঋণ এবং ভারতের অবশিষ্ট ৫% যুদ্ধঋণ দায়সহ সরকারের বড় আর্থিক সম্পদ ও দায়ের পরিমাণ দেওয়া হয়।

book_1_integration.part_label: Book 1 — Part II: Modern monetary and sovereign-finance development

sources.title: United Kingdom National Debt Composition at 30 November 1920
sources.historical_claim: A December 1920 parliamentary return quantified the composition of the United Kingdom's approximately £7.736 billion national debt across funded debt, War Loans, Treasury Bills, Ways and Means Advances, National Savings Certificates and other debt.
sources.passage_locator: House of Commons Hansard, 9 December 1920, vol. 135, cc. 2416–2417, National Debt.
sources.source_identity: Official statement laid before the House in answer to Major Nall; Chancellor of the Exchequer's printed statement of approximate debt outstanding on 30 November 1920.
sources.edition: House of Commons Debates, 9 December 1920, Series 5, vol. 135, cc. 2416–2417.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — official statement and figures verified.
sources.primary_passage: The approximate debt outstanding on 30th November, 1920 was as follows: Funded Debt £315,000,000; Terminable Annuities £18,500,000; 3½ per cent. War Loan, 1925/8 £62,700,000; 4½ per cent. War Loan, 1925/45 £12,800,000; 5 per cent. War Loan, 1929/47 £1,949,300,000; 4 per cent. War Loan, 1929/42 £67,200,000; 4 per cent. Funding Loan, 1960/90 £407,000,000; 4 per cent. Victory Bonds £357,700,000; Exchequer Bonds £315,000,000; 4 per cent. and 5 per cent. National War Bonds £1,441,000,000; Treasury Bonds £13,850,000; Treasury Bills £1,111,564,000; Ways and Means Advances £222,614,000; National Savings Certificates £277,900,000; Other Debt £1,163,500,000; £7,735,628,000.
sources.what_passage_establishes: The official statement gives the contemporary scale and composition of Britain's national debt, including £1.9493bn of 5% War Loan, £1.441bn of National War Bonds, £1.111564bn of Treasury Bills and £222.614m of Ways and Means Advances, within a total of £7.735628bn.
sources.evidence_limits: The aggregate statement does not identify ultimate holders, geographic ownership, secondary-market transactions, or the economic incidence of the debt. 'Other Debt' is not broken down in the quoted table.
scholarly_references: House of Commons Debates, 9 December 1920, vol. 135, cc. 2416–2417.
sources.publication_status: A-grade — direct official quantitative debt statement.
sources.bn_title: ৩০ নভেম্বর ১৯২০-এ যুক্তরাজ্যের জাতীয় ঋণের গঠন
sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৯২০ সালের ডিসেম্বরে সংসদে দেওয়া সরকারি বিবৃতিতে যুক্তরাজ্যের প্রায় ৭.৭৩৬ বিলিয়ন পাউন্ড জাতীয় ঋণের বিভিন্ন উপাদান—যুদ্ধঋণ, ট্রেজারি বিল, Ways and Means Advances ও অন্যান্য ঋণ—পরিমাণসহ দেখানো হয়।

book_1_integration.part_label: Book 1 — Part II: Modern monetary and sovereign-finance development

sources.title: British Currency-Note Contraction and Credit Pressure, 1920
sources.historical_claim: The Chancellor reported a £6.5 million reduction in British currency notes between 6 October and 24 November 1920 and attributed importance to money-market pressure against inflated credits and earlier Budget balancing from revenue.
sources.passage_locator: House of Commons Hansard, 2 December 1920, vol. 135, c. 1478W, Currency Notes.
sources.source_identity: Written answer by Chancellor of the Exchequer Austen Chamberlain.
sources.edition: House of Commons Debates, 2 December 1920, Series 5, vol. 135, c. 1478W.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — official written answer verified.
sources.primary_passage: The reduction of currency notes in the period from 6th October to 24th November has been £6,500,000. No special measures have been taken for a deflation of the currency during that period. As to the main causes of the contraction, while I am not prepared to dogmatise, I attach importance to the money market pressure against inflated credits and to the action of the Government early in the year in balancing Budget expenditure from Budget revenue.
sources.what_passage_establishes: The Chancellor reported a £6.5 million contraction in currency notes over the specified period and explicitly associated the contraction with money-market pressure against inflated credit and the Government's budget-balancing policy, while declining to state the causes categorically.
sources.evidence_limits: The answer is a ministerial assessment rather than a full monetary-statistical analysis; it does not establish a single causal mechanism, private-bank behavior in aggregate, or the later persistence of the contraction.
scholarly_references: House of Commons Debates, 2 December 1920, vol. 135, c. 1478W.
sources.publication_status: A-grade — direct quantitative ministerial written answer.
sources.bn_title: ব্রিটিশ কারেন্সি-নোট সংকোচন ও ঋণবাজারের চাপ, ১৯২০
sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৯২০ সালের ৬ অক্টোবর থেকে ২৪ নভেম্বরের মধ্যে ব্রিটিশ কারেন্সি নোট ৬.৫ মিলিয়ন পাউন্ড কমে যায়; চ্যান্সেলর এর সঙ্গে স্ফীত ঋণের বিরুদ্ধে অর্থবাজারের চাপ এবং বাজেট রাজস্ব দিয়ে ব্যয় ভারসাম্য করার নীতির সম্পর্ক উল্লেখ করেন।

book_1_integration.part_label: Book 1 — Part II: Modern monetary and sovereign-finance development

sources.title: India's Sterling Draft Sales and Exchange Support, 1920
sources.historical_claim: The Secretary of State for India reported that the Government of India had sold approximately £50 million of sterling drafts between 1 February and 30 September 1920 in an unsuccessful effort to maintain the rupee exchange at 2s., before discontinuing the sales.
sources.verification_status: Primary parliamentary written-answer record verified in official Hansard.
sources.passage_locator: House of Commons Hansard, 14 December 1920, vol. 135, c. 2128W, Exchange.
sources.source_identity: Written answer by Secretary of State for India Edwin Montagu concerning the Indian Currency Committee recommendations and exchange support.
sources.edition: House of Commons Debates, 14 December 1920, Series 5, vol. 135, c. 2128W.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — exact official answer and locator verified.
sources.primary_passage: In accordance with the recommendations of the report referred to by my hon. and gallant Friend legislation has been passed in India, under which the sovereign has been made a legal tender at the rate of ten rupees. The quotations asked for in the second part of the question are 2s. 1¼d. and 1s. 4¾d. In spite of the sale of sterling drafts, to the extent of approximately £50,000,000 between 1st February and 30th September, it has not been found practicable to maintain exchange at 2s. The sale of these drafts has been discontinued in accordance with the announcement issued on 29th September last, and the existing trade position does not suggest that the Government of India could advantageously resume the sales at the present time.
sources.what_passage_establishes: The Government of India used approximately £50 million in sterling-draft sales between 1 February and 30 September 1920 in an effort to support a 2s. rupee rate; the exchange nevertheless ranged between 2s. 1¼d. and 1s. 4¾d., and the sales were discontinued.
sources.evidence_limits: The answer establishes the scale and dates of draft sales and the Government's stated exchange objective, but not the precise counterparties, reserve source, transaction-by-transaction terms, or ultimate economic effects.
scholarly_references: House of Commons Debates, 14 December 1920, vol. 135, c. 2128W.

This record should be distinguished from the March 1920 general UK policy against artificial exchange support: the December answer concerns the Indian Government's specific sterling-draft operations and their discontinuation.
sources.publication_status: A-grade — direct ministerial quantitative statement of an actual exchange-support operation.
sources.bn_title: ভারতের স্টার্লিং ড্রাফট বিক্রি ও বিনিময় হার-সমর্থন, ১৯২০

sources.title: India Sterling Loan: £7.5 Million for Railway Material, 1921
sources.historical_claim: The Government of India raised a £7.5 million sterling loan in 1921 whose prospectus specified that the entire proceeds would be used to purchase railway material in the United Kingdom; by May about £900,000 had been spent in Britain on railway capital account.
sources.verification_status: Primary parliamentary written-answer record verified against official Historic Hansard.
sources.passage_locator: House of Commons Hansard, 9 June 1921, vol. 142, cc. 2078–2079W, Sterling Loan.
sources.source_identity: Written answer by Secretary of State for India Edwin Montagu concerning the recently issued Indian sterling loan.
sources.edition: House of Commons Debates, 9 June 1921, Series 5, vol. 142, cc. 2078–2079W.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — exact official answer and locator verified.
sources.primary_passage: It was stated on the prospectus issued in connection with the recent Indian sterling loan that the entire proceeds would be utilised for the purchase of railway material in the United Kingdom and no part of the loan proceeds will therefore be expended abroad. About £900,000 was spent in this country in May last on railway capital account.
sources.what_passage_establishes: The 1921 Indian sterling loan was earmarked by its prospectus for railway-material purchases in the United Kingdom, and about £900,000 of the proceeds had been spent in Britain in May on railway capital account.
sources.evidence_limits: The answer does not reproduce the loan's coupon, maturity, issue price, underwriting arrangements, subscriber identities, or the eventual disposition of the remaining proceeds. It establishes stated use and an interim expenditure figure, not the full loan lifecycle.

sources.title: India's Exchange Crisis: Rs.43 Crore Adverse Balance and Limited Government Support, 1921
sources.historical_claim: By the twelve months ending December 1920, India's merchandise-and-treasure balance had turned sharply adverse, while the Secretary of State stated that limited sterling resources and obligations prevented effective Government intervention to support the Indian exchange.
sources.verification_status: Primary parliamentary written-answer record verified against official Historic Hansard.
sources.passage_locator: House of Commons Hansard, 23 February 1921, vol. 138, cc. 956–957W, Exchange.
sources.source_identity: Written answer by Secretary of State for India Edwin Montagu on stabilising the rupee and supporting Indian exchange.
sources.edition: House of Commons Debates, 23 February 1921, Series 5, vol. 138, cc. 956–957W.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — exact official answer and locator verified.
sources.primary_passage: The twelve months ending December last exhibited an adverse balance against India in respect of merchandise and treasure of Rs.43 crores, as compared with the favourable balance of Rs.125 crores in 1919. ... I do not see at present that it is practicable for me, having regard to the extent of my sterling resources and obligations, to intervene with effect in support of the Indian exchange. While I fully appreciate the drawbacks of the present position, the causes are world wide, and beyond the control of individual Governments, and ... there is similar instability in the sterling, franc, and other exchanges.
sources.what_passage_establishes: The official answer records a major reversal in India's merchandise-and-treasure balance between 1919 and the twelve months ending December 1920, and states that the Secretary of State did not consider effective intervention to support Indian exchange practicable given his sterling resources and obligations.
sources.evidence_limits: This is a ministerial statement, not a complete balance-of-payments table. It does not identify the full components of the Rs.43-crore balance, counterparties, private holders, transaction terms, or prove that the cited worldwide causes were the sole or dominant cause of the exchange movement.
scholarly_references: House of Commons Debates, 23 February 1921, vol. 138, cc. 956–957W.
The 1920 exchange-support record separately documents the earlier £50m sterling-draft operation; this record documents the subsequent adverse-balance and support constraint.
sources.publication_status: A-grade — direct ministerial parliamentary statement with quantified balance comparison and explicit resource constraint.

sources.title: Great Depression, 1929–1933
sources.historical_claim: The Great Depression became a global economic and financial crisis, exposing severe weaknesses in banking and monetary systems and prompting major institutional changes.
sources.verification_status: Primary contemporary official record verified — Federal Reserve Board Annual Report 1933
sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৯২৯–১৯৩৩ সালের মহামন্দা বৈশ্বিক অর্থনৈতিক ও আর্থিক সংকটে পরিণত হয় এবং ব্যাংকিং ও মুদ্রাব্যবস্থার গুরুতর দুর্বলতা প্রকাশ করে; এর পর বড় ধরনের প্রাতিষ্ঠানিক পরিবর্তন আসে।
sources.notes: The contemporary 1933 Federal Reserve Board Annual Report directly documents the banking-crisis phase: successive banking difficulties from 1930 through March 1933 and nearly 5,500 bank suspensions between December 1929 and February 1933. The quotation supports the U.S. banking-crisis component of the record; the broader global Depression and subsequent institutional-change claims require separate evidence and are not inferred from this passage alone.

sources.title: Basel Committee established
sources.historical_claim: In December 1974, the G10 central-bank Governors established the Committee on Banking Regulations and Supervisory Practices after major international banking and currency disturbances, creating the institution that became the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision.
sources.bn_title: বাসেল কমিটি প্রতিষ্ঠিত
sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৯৭৪ সালের ডিসেম্বরে আন্তর্জাতিক ব্যাংকিং ও মুদ্রাবাজারের গুরুতর অস্থিরতার পর G10 কেন্দ্রীয় ব্যাংকের গভর্নররা Committee on Banking Regulations and Supervisory Practices প্রতিষ্ঠা করেন, যা পরবর্তীতে Basel Committee on Banking Supervision হয়।
sources.verification_status: Primary-source / contemporary official record verified
sources.notes: The BIS's 12 February 1975 contemporary media release records that the central-bank Governors of the Group of Ten countries and Switzerland had established a standing committee of experts on banking and foreign-exchange regulations and supervisory practices, under George Blunden. The BIS historical record dates the Governors' decision to December 1974, and the 1975 release is a near-contemporary official institutional record of the committee's establishment. This supports Grade A for the establishment claim, while the database should distinguish the December 1974 Governors' decision from the February 1975 public confirmation. The BIS's 12 February 1975 contemporary release directly confirms the committee's establishment; BIS history dates the Governors' decision to the end of 1974.

sources.title: Plaza Accord
sources.historical_claim: The finance ministers and central-bank governors of France, Japan, the United Kingdom, the United States and West Germany agreed at the Plaza Hotel in New York in September 1985 to cooperate in promoting an orderly appreciation of major currencies against the US dollar.
sources.bn_title: প্লাজা অ্যাকর্ড
sources.bn_historical_claim: ফ্রান্স, জাপান, যুক্তরাজ্য, যুক্তরাষ্ট্র ও পশ্চিম জার্মানির অর্থমন্ত্রীরা এবং কেন্দ্রীয় ব্যাংকের গভর্নররা সেপ্টেম্বর ১৯৮৫-তে নিউইয়র্কের প্লাজা হোটেলে প্রধান মুদ্রাগুলোর বিপরীতে মার্কিন ডলারের সুশৃঙ্খল অবমূল্যায়ন/অন্যান্য মুদ্রার মূল্যবৃদ্ধিতে সহযোগিতার জন্য একমত হন।
sources.verification_status: Primary-source statement verified
sources.notes: The 22 September 1985 Announcement of the Finance Ministers and Central Bank Governors of France, Germany, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States is preserved as the contemporary Plaza statement. The text directly records the meeting, the five participating governments, and the agreed policy direction, including that further orderly appreciation of major nondollar currencies against the dollar was desirable and that the participants would cooperate to encourage it. The Federal Reserve's historical archive independently documents the Plaza Agreement and its subsequent foreign-exchange operations.

sources.title: Basel I Capital Accord
sources.historical_claim: In July 1988, the G10 Governors approved the Basel Capital Accord, establishing an internationally coordinated framework for measuring bank capital and setting a target minimum capital ratio of 8% of risk-weighted assets for internationally active banks.

sources.title: Committee on Payment and Settlement Systems established
sources.historical_claim: In 1990, the G10 Governors established the Committee on Payment and Settlement Systems (CPSS) as a permanent central bank committee to monitor and analyse payment and settlement developments, including cross-border and multicurrency arrangements.
sources.bn_title: কমিটি অন পেমেন্ট অ্যান্ড সেটেলমেন্ট সিস্টেমস প্রতিষ্ঠা
sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৯৯০ সালে G10 গভর্নররা Committee on Payment and Settlement Systems (CPSS) প্রতিষ্ঠা করেন, যা আন্তঃদেশীয় ও বহু-মুদ্রাভিত্তিক পেমেন্ট ও সেটেলমেন্ট ব্যবস্থার উন্নয়ন পর্যবেক্ষণ ও বিশ্লেষণের জন্য একটি স্থায়ী কেন্দ্রীয় ব্যাংক কমিটি হিসেবে কাজ করে।
sources.verification_status: Primary institutional record verified
sources.notes: The BIS's official CPSS/CPMI history states that in 1990 the G10 Governors established the Committee on Payment and Settlement Systems as a follow-up to the Committee on Interbank Netting Schemes and the Group of Experts on Payment Systems. The BIS historical timeline places the creation in November 1990 and identifies the committee's remit as policy and oversight issues related to cross-border and multicurrency interbank netting schemes. The 1990 Lamfalussy Report provides contemporary institutional context for the transition from the ad hoc netting committee to the permanent CPSS.

sources.title: BCCI closure and coordinated international supervisory action
sources.historical_claim: On 5 July 1991, banking supervisors in multiple jurisdictions coordinated the closure and provisional liquidation of Bank of Credit and Commerce International (BCCI), following serious findings concerning fraud and falsified financial records.
sources.bn_title: BCCI বন্ধ ও সমন্বিত আন্তর্জাতিক ব্যাংকিং তদারকি পদক্ষেপ
sources.bn_historical_claim: ৫ জুলাই ১৯৯১ সালে গুরুতর জালিয়াতি ও আর্থিক নথি বিকৃতির তথ্যের পর একাধিক দেশের ব্যাংকিং তদারকি কর্তৃপক্ষ সমন্বিতভাবে Bank of Credit and Commerce International (BCCI)-এর কার্যক্রম বন্ধ ও অস্থায়ী অবসায়নের পদক্ষেপ নেয়।
sources.verification_status: Primary-source contemporary official record verified
sources.notes: The Bank of England Banking Act Report 1991-92 identifies the closure of BCCI as the most prominent event of 1991 and records that, following the Bank's receipt of a Price Waterhouse report commissioned under section 41 of the Banking Act, action was taken to protect depositors. It documents the coordinated worldwide operation on 5 July 1991, including provisional liquidation proceedings in the UK and Luxembourg and supervisory action in Grand Cayman and other jurisdictions. The Basel Committee's later report independently documents the same 5 July actions and the cross-border supervisory coordination.
sources.primary_passage: The closure was a co-ordinated worldwide operation by banking supervisors.

sources.what_passage_establishes: The passage directly establishes that BCCI's July 1991 closure was a coordinated worldwide operation by banking supervisors, with the report identifying 5 July as the date of the UK action.
sources.evidence_limits: The record establishes the closure and supervisory coordination. It does not by itself establish the full extent of BCCI's fraud, ultimate liability figures, or all subsequent regulatory reforms; those require separate documentary records.

sources.title: Basel minimum standards for supervision of international banking groups and cross-border establishments
sources.historical_claim: On 28 July 1992, the Basel Committee reformulated certain Concordat principles into minimum standards for the supervision of international banking groups and their cross-border establishments, which G10 supervisory authorities expected each other to observe.

sources.bn_historical_claim: ২৮ জুলাই ১৯৯২ সালে বাসেল কমিটি আন্তর্জাতিক ব্যাংকিং গ্রুপ ও তাদের আন্তঃসীমান্ত প্রতিষ্ঠানের তদারকির জন্য কনকর্ডাটের কিছু নীতিকে ন্যূনতম মানদণ্ডে পুনর্গঠন করে; G10 তদারকি কর্তৃপক্ষগুলো একে অপরের কাছ থেকে এসব মানদণ্ড অনুসরণের প্রত্যাশা করেছিল।

Its introduction states that, following developments in international banking supervision, certain Concordat principles were reformulated as minimum standards that G10 supervisory authorities expected each other to observe. The BCBS history independently dates the reformulation to July 1992 and records that the standards were communicated to other banking supervisory authorities for endorsement.

sources.title: Basel Committee confirms G10 banks meeting minimum capital requirements
sources.historical_claim: In September 1993, the Basel Committee reported that banks in the G10 countries with material international banking business were meeting the minimum capital requirements established by the 1988 Basel Capital Accord.

sources.bn_historical_claim: সেপ্টেম্বর ১৯৯৩ সালে বাসেল কমিটি জানায় যে উল্লেখযোগ্য আন্তর্জাতিক ব্যাংকিং কার্যক্রম থাকা G10 দেশগুলোর ব্যাংকগুলো ১৯৮৮ সালের Basel Capital Accord-এ নির্ধারিত ন্যূনতম মূলধন মান পূরণ করছিল।
sources.verification_status: Primary-source official BIS/BCBS historical record verified
sources.notes: The official BIS Basel Committee history states that the 1988 Capital Accord required a minimum capital-to-risk-weighted-assets ratio of 8% to be implemented by the end of 1992, and that in September 1993 the Committee issued a statement confirming that G10 banks with material international banking business were meeting the Accord's minimum requirements. This provides a clear 1993 institutional checkpoint following the 1992 implementation deadline.

sources.title: Basel Committee risk management guidelines for derivatives
sources.historical_claim: On 28 July 1994, the Basel Committee issued guidance on sound risk management of banks' derivatives activities and distributed it to supervisors worldwide to strengthen prudential supervision of derivatives operations.
sources.bn_title: ডেরিভেটিভস ঝুঁকি ব্যবস্থাপনা বিষয়ে বাসেল কমিটির ১৯৯৪ নির্দেশিকা
sources.bn_historical_claim: ২৮ জুলাই ১৯৯৪ সালে বাসেল কমিটি ব্যাংকের ডেরিভেটিভস কার্যক্রমের ঝুঁকি ব্যবস্থাপনার জন্য সুস্থ ও বিচক্ষণ পদ্ধতির নির্দেশিকা জারি করে এবং ডেরিভেটিভস কার্যক্রমের প্রুডেনশিয়াল তদারকি শক্তিশালী করার লক্ষ্যে তা বিশ্বব্যাপী তদারকি কর্তৃপক্ষগুলোর মধ্যে বিতরণ করে।

The accompanying Basel Committee text states that the paper provides guidance on sound risk management of derivatives activities for supervisory authorities and banking organisations, and that the Committee was distributing it to supervisors worldwide. It also explicitly stresses that capital requirements alone are not sufficient and that sound internal risk management is essential.

sources.title: Basel planned supplement to the Capital Accord for market risk
sources.historical_claim: On 21 April 1995, the Basel Committee issued a revised consultative package to refine the 1988 Capital Accord by incorporating capital requirements for banks' market risks, including a standardised approach and an internal-models approach subject to supervisory approval.

sources.title: Asian financial crisis
sources.historical_claim: The Asian financial crisis began in Thailand in July 1997 after the baht was floated and spread across the region, producing severe financial and economic disruption and requiring international support programs.
sources.bn_title: এশীয় আর্থিক সংকট
sources.bn_historical_claim: ১৯৯৭ সালের জুলাইয়ে থাইল্যান্ডে বাত ভাসমান করার পর এশীয় আর্থিক সংকট শুরু হয় এবং অঞ্চলজুড়ে ছড়িয়ে পড়ে; এতে গুরুতর আর্থিক ও অর্থনৈতিক অস্থিরতা সৃষ্টি হয় এবং আন্তর্জাতিক সহায়তা কর্মসূচির প্রয়োজন হয়।
sources.verification_status: Primary-source contemporary official record verified
sources.notes: The 14 August 1997 Thailand Memorandum on Economic Policies, submitted in connection with the IMF-supported program, records the currency attacks, depletion of Bank of Thailand reserves, suspension of finance companies, and the float of the baht on 2 July 1997. The IMF's contemporaneous 2 July 1997 News Brief independently records Thailand's change to a managed float effective that date. The 20 August 1997 IMF approval release documents the subsequent stand-by arrangement and describes the spread of financial stress. These contemporary official records support the crisis-origin and international-assistance claims; broader claims about the crisis spreading across Asia should be treated as regional consequences rather than inferred solely from the Thai documents.
sources.primary_passage: the combination of a fixed exchange rate, an increasingly open capital account, and high domestic interest rates to combat inflation, attracted short-term capital flows that left the economy vulnerable to sudden shifts in market sentiment and external shocks.

sources.title: Basel Supervisory Guidance on Dealing with Weak Banks
sources.historical_claim: On 11 March 2002, the Basel Committee issued Supervisory Guidance on Dealing with Weak Banks, providing supervisors with practical guidance on identifying weak banks, taking corrective action, resolving problems and managing exit strategies.
sources.bn_title: দুর্বল ব্যাংক মোকাবিলায় বাসেল তদারকি নির্দেশিকা, ২০০২
sources.bn_historical_claim: ১১ মার্চ ২০০২ সালে Basel Committee দুর্বল ব্যাংক মোকাবিলায় Supervisory Guidance প্রকাশ করে। এতে দুর্বল ব্যাংক শনাক্তকরণ, সংশোধনমূলক পদক্ষেপ, সমস্যা সমাধান এবং প্রস্থান কৌশল সম্পর্কে তদারকি কর্তৃপক্ষের জন্য ব্যবহারিক নির্দেশনা দেওয়া হয়।
sources.verification_status: Primary-source official BIS/BCBS publication verified
sources.primary_passage: The objective of this report is to provide guidance to supervisors in dealing with weak banks. It provides a toolkit offering practical guidance in the areas of problem identification, corrective action, resolution techniques and exit strategies.
sources.passage_locator: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, Supervisory Guidance on Dealing with Weak Banks, March 2002, Introduction.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — official BIS-hosted Basel Committee guidance
sources.source_identity: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, Supervisory Guidance on Dealing with Weak Banks, March 2002; official BIS-hosted committee publication.
sources.edition: Supervisory Guidance on Dealing with Weak Banks, March 2002.
sources.publisher: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision / Bank for International Settlements
sources.what_passage_establishes: The passage establishes the issuance and intended supervisory function of the 2002 weak-bank guidance, including its practical toolkit for problem identification, corrective action, resolution and exit.
sources.evidence_limits: The passage establishes guidance, not actual intervention or resolution of any particular bank.
scholarly_references: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, Supervisory Guidance on Dealing with Weak Banks (March 2002).

sources.title: Basel Sound Practices for the Management and Supervision of Operational Risk
sources.historical_claim: On 25 February 2003, the Basel Committee issued Sound Practices for the Management and Supervision of Operational Risk, providing principles for banks and supervisors to manage and evaluate operational risk.
sources.bn_title: অপারেশনাল ঝুঁকি ব্যবস্থাপনা ও তদারকির জন্য বাসেল সাউন্ড প্র্যাকটিসেস, ২০০৩
sources.bn_historical_claim: ২৫ ফেব্রুয়ারি ২০০৩ সালে Basel Committee অপারেশনাল ঝুঁকি ব্যবস্থাপনা ও তদারকির জন্য Sound Practices প্রকাশ করে। এতে ব্যাংক ও তদারকি কর্তৃপক্ষের জন্য অপারেশনাল ঝুঁকি ব্যবস্থাপনা মূল্যায়ন ও পরিচালনার নীতিমালা দেওয়া হয়।
sources.verification_status: Primary-source official BIS/BCBS publication verified
sources.primary_passage: The following paper outlines a set of principles that provide a framework for the effective management and supervision of operational risk, for use by banks and supervisory authorities when evaluating operational risk management policies and practices.
sources.passage_locator: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, Sound Practices for the Management and Supervision of Operational Risk, 25 February 2003, Introduction, paragraph 1.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — official BIS-hosted Basel Committee sound-practices paper
sources.source_identity: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, Sound Practices for the Management and Supervision of Operational Risk, 25 February 2003; official BIS-hosted committee publication.
sources.edition: Sound Practices for the Management and Supervision of Operational Risk, February 2003.
sources.publisher: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision / Bank for International Settlements
sources.what_passage_establishes: The passage establishes the 2003 operational-risk framework and its intended use by banks and supervisory authorities.
sources.evidence_limits: The passage establishes guidance, not actual implementation or operational-risk outcomes at individual banks.
scholarly_references: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, Sound Practices for the Management and Supervision of Operational Risk (February 2003).

sources.title: Basel II: International Convergence of Capital Measurement and Capital Standards — Revised Framework
sources.historical_claim: On 26 June 2004, the G10 central bank Governors and heads of banking supervision endorsed the Basel Committee's revised capital framework, commonly known as Basel II, following the Committee's approval of the text for their review.
sources.bn_title: Basel II: আন্তর্জাতিক মূলধন পরিমাপ ও মূলধন মানের সংশোধিত কাঠামো, ২০০৪
sources.bn_historical_claim: ২৬ জুন ২০০৪ সালে G10 কেন্দ্রীয় ব্যাংকের গভর্নর ও ব্যাংকিং তদারকি কর্তৃপক্ষের প্রধানরা Basel Committee-এর সংশোধিত মূলধন কাঠামো, যা সাধারণভাবে Basel II নামে পরিচিত, অনুমোদন করেন। এর একদিন আগে Basel Committee চূড়ান্ত পাঠটি তাদের পর্যালোচনার জন্য অনুমোদন করেছিল।
sources.verification_status: Primary-source official BIS/BCBS publication and contemporaneous BIS release verified
sources.primary_passage: The present paper is now a statement of the Committee agreed by all its members. It sets out the details of the agreed Framework for measuring capital adequacy and the minimum standard to be achieved which the national supervisory authorities represented on the Committee will propose for adoption in their respective countries. This Framework and the standard it contains have been endorsed by the Central Bank Governors and Heads of Banking Supervision of the Group of Ten countries.
sources.passage_locator: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, International Convergence of Capital Measurement and Capital Standards: A Revised Framework, June 2004, Introduction, paragraph 1.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — official BIS-hosted Basel Committee standard; endorsement corroborated by contemporaneous BIS release dated 26 June 2004
sources.source_identity: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, International Convergence of Capital Measurement and Capital Standards: A Revised Framework, June 2004; official BIS/BIS-hosted publication.
sources.edition: International Convergence of Capital Measurement and Capital Standards: A Revised Framework, June 2004.
sources.publisher: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision / Bank for International Settlements
sources.what_passage_establishes: The passage establishes the agreed 2004 revised capital framework and its endorsement by G10 central bank Governors and Heads of Banking Supervision; the framework contains minimum capital requirements, supervisory review and market discipline.
sources.evidence_limits: The passage establishes agreement and endorsement, not implementation by every national jurisdiction or bank.
scholarly_references: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, International Convergence of Capital Measurement and Capital Standards: A Revised Framework (June 2004).
Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, The Basel Committee's response to the financial crisis and the future of banking regulation (later institutional history).

book_1_integration.part_label: Book 1 — Part IV: Bretton Woods to modern supervisory architecture

sources.title: Basel II application to trading activities and double default effects
sources.historical_claim: On 30 July 2005, the Basel Committee and IOSCO issued final guidance applying Basel II to certain trading-related exposures and double default effects, refining capital treatment for counterparty credit risk and related exposures.
sources.bn_title: Basel II-তে ট্রেডিং কার্যক্রম ও ডাবল ডিফল্ট ইফেক্টের প্রয়োগ, ২০০৫
sources.bn_historical_claim: ৩০ জুলাই ২০০৫ সালে Basel Committee ও IOSCO Basel II-এর অধীনে নির্দিষ্ট ট্রেডিং-সম্পর্কিত এক্সপোজার ও ডাবল ডিফল্ট ইফেক্টের জন্য চূড়ান্ত নির্দেশনা জারি করে; এতে counterparty credit riskসহ সংশ্লিষ্ট এক্সপোজারের মূলধন ব্যবস্থাপনা পরিমার্জন করা হয়।
sources.verification_status: Primary-source official BIS/BCBS publication verified
sources.primary_passage: The proposals in this paper are intended to bring the capital treatment of trading activities and double default effects abreast of the Basel Committee's revised capital framework for banking organisations, also known as Basel II.
sources.passage_locator: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision and IOSCO, The Application of Basel II to Trading Activities and the Treatment of Double Default Effects, 30 July 2005, Introduction.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — official BIS-hosted Basel Committee/IOSCO final paper
sources.source_identity: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision and IOSCO, The Application of Basel II to Trading Activities and the Treatment of Double Default Effects, 30 July 2005; official BIS-hosted publication.
sources.edition: The Application of Basel II to Trading Activities and the Treatment of Double Default Effects, July 2005.
sources.publisher: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision / IOSCO
sources.what_passage_establishes: The passage establishes the final joint BCBS/IOSCO effort to align capital treatment for trading activities and double default effects with Basel II.
sources.evidence_limits: The passage establishes issuance and regulatory treatment, not implementation by individual jurisdictions or banks.
scholarly_references: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision and IOSCO, The Application of Basel II to Trading Activities and the Treatment of Double Default Effects (July 2005).

sources.title: Basel II Comprehensive Framework
sources.historical_claim: In June 2006, the Basel Committee published a comprehensive version of the Basel II Framework, bringing together the June 2004 revised framework, relevant elements of the 1988 Accord, the 1996 market-risk amendment and the July 2005 trading-activities and double-default treatment.
sources.bn_title: Basel II সমন্বিত পূর্ণাঙ্গ কাঠামো, ২০০৬
sources.bn_historical_claim: জুন ২০০৬ সালে Basel Committee Basel II-এর একটি পূর্ণাঙ্গ সংস্করণ প্রকাশ করে। এতে ২০০৪ সালের Basel II Framework, ১৯৮৮ সালের Accord-এর অপরিবর্তিত উপাদান, ১৯৯৬ সালের market-risk amendment এবং ২০০৫ সালের trading activities ও double-default treatment একত্রিত করা হয়।
sources.verification_status: Primary-source official BIS/BCBS publication verified
sources.primary_passage: The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision has today published a comprehensive version of the Basel II Framework. This document brings together the June 2004 Basel II Framework, the elements of the 1988 Accord that were not revised during the Basel II process, the 1996 Amendment to the Capital Accord to incorporate market risks, and the July 2005 paper on The application of Basel II to trading activities and the treatment of double default effects.
sources.passage_locator: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, International Convergence of Capital Measurement and Capital Standards: A Revised Framework — Comprehensive Version, June 2006, opening statement.
sources.passage_status: Passage locked — official BIS-hosted Basel Committee comprehensive framework
sources.source_identity: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, International Convergence of Capital Measurement and Capital Standards: A Revised Framework — Comprehensive Version, June 2006; official BIS-hosted publication.
sources.edition: Basel II Comprehensive Version, June 2006.
sources.publisher: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision / Bank for International Settlements
sources.what_passage_establishes: The passage directly establishes publication of the comprehensive Basel II framework and identifies the prior capital standards and amendments consolidated into it.
sources.evidence_limits: The passage establishes publication and consolidation, not the degree of implementation by individual national authorities or banks.
scholarly_references: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, International Convergence of Capital Measurement and Capital Standards: A Revised Framework — Comprehensive Version (June 2006).
